Philadelphia County by the numbers

Who records deeds in Philadelphia County?

The City's Department of Records acts as the recorder of deeds for Philadelphia County. It sits in City Hall and its main line is (215) 686-2262. The office records deeds, mortgages and other real estate documents for the whole county, and the same borders mean one office serves every neighborhood.

Individuals file either through the mail or at the counter. In-person recording needs an appointment, which you book by email to appointments.records@phila.gov, and recording hours are weekdays, 8 a.m. until 3:30 p.m. Mailed documents go to City Hall, Room 111, 1400 John F. Kennedy Blvd., Philadelphia, PA 19107, with a stamped, self-addressed envelope for the return of the original. Anyone dropping off three or more documents leaves them to be picked up later.

Businesses and title companies usually record electronically through one of three vendors: Simplifile, CSC eRecording or ePN. Those filings are paid by ACH.

What does a Philadelphia deed need before the office will record it?

The office rejects documents that miss its formatting and content rules, so a title company or lawyer normally prepares the deed. The Department itself advises against drafting one on your own and recommends title insurance.

  • White 8.5 by 11 inch paper, typed in 10 point black ink, one side only.
  • A 3 inch top margin on page one with the "Prepared by" and "Return to" details at the left, and 1 inch margins elsewhere.
  • A date, the typed names of every party, and the signatures and notary acknowledgment matching those names.
  • A Philadelphia property with a metes and bounds description and the street address.
  • A signed, certified grantee address on deeds, mortgages and assignments.
  • The full consideration stated, with numbers that match the written amount.
  • The Philadelphia Real Estate Transfer Tax Certificate in duplicate and the Pennsylvania Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value, plus the tax unless the transfer is exempt.

What are the Philadelphia County recording fees?

A standard deed costs $278.75 on the Department's current schedule. The schedule also sets lower fees for a handful of special cases. The table shows the charges homeowners meet most often.

Department of Records recording fees for common documents
DocumentFee
Deed$278.75
Deed, deceased spouse or partner$43.75
Deed, miscellaneous$263.75
Mortgage$248.75
Assignment of mortgage$246.75
Release of mortgage or satisfaction$231.75
Power of attorney$96.50

Source: Philadelphia Department of Records fee schedule.

The office takes cash, money orders, business or certified checks, and Visa, Mastercard, Discover and American Express. Cards carry a 3.5 percent convenience fee, and personal checks are refused. Taxes and fees must be on separate checks: the State tax payable to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, and the City tax and recording fees payable to the City of Philadelphia. A surviving spouse named on the deed can have part of the fee waived, and military discharge papers are recorded and copied free.

What is the Philadelphia realty transfer tax?

The total rate is 4.578 percent of the sale price, which is 3.578 percent for the City plus 1 percent for the Commonwealth. The City share rose from 3.278 percent on July 1, 2025, and the City says the increase pays for affordable housing programs.

The tax is owed once the deed is presented for recording, and the City allows up to 30 days to pay after the property is acquired. On a $250,000 sale the total would be about $11,445, usually split between the two sides at closing. The City can collect the full amount from either party, so buyers insist that it be paid at settlement. Misstating the transaction or never recording it can bring a penalty of up to 50 percent of the tax.

Where no price exists, such as a gift or foreclosure, the tax runs on a computed value: the assessed value times the state's Common Level Ratio, then times the rate. Most transfers among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are exempt, with documents required for each claim.

Do inherited or estate-sold Philadelphia homes pay transfer tax?

It depends on how title moves. A transfer under a will can be exempt, but the tax is due if mortgages, liens or debts on the home remain unpaid at the time of transfer. A home bought from an estate is not exempt. For example, when a will leaves a property to several heirs and one buys out the others, tax is owed on that purchase.

  • Heirs who keep the property usually record a deed from the estate and show the family relationship.
  • Heirs who sell record the deed to the buyer, and the sale carries the full transfer tax.
  • If title is still in a deceased owner's name, ask the title company which estate papers it needs before it will insure the sale.

How do I pay the Philadelphia transfer tax?

Payment can be made three ways, and the title company usually picks the first or second.

  • Online through the Philadelphia Tax Center, by logging in or using the Letter ID printed at the top of the bill.
  • In person, when the deed is filed with the Department of Records.
  • By mail, with two copies of the City certificate, one copy of the state Statement of Value form, and three certified checks: one for the recording fee, one for the City tax and one for the Commonwealth tax.

The tax reaches more than sales. Deeds, leases of 30 years or longer, easements, life estates, entity transfers and transfers of 75 percent or more of a real estate company all trigger it.

What other land records does the Department of Records keep?

The Department keeps the City Archives as well as current land records. Copies of deeds from 1683 to 1955 cost $2 a page, mortgages from 1748 to 1963 are also $2 a page, and a search of deeds, mortgages and other land records runs $20 an hour with a $20 minimum. A plot plan copy is $10. These records help when an old ownership gap needs tracing before a sale, and the Department will certify a copy for $2 per document.

How does recording fit into selling a Philadelphia County house?

Recording comes last in the closing sequence, and the title company usually files it. The seller signs the deed, the buyer or title company assembles the transfer tax certificates, pays the tax and fee, and files the package with the Department of Records.

Before that, the title search checks property tax, water and sewer balances, since each can sit as a lien. A seller with tax or lien problems can still close if the payoff is arranged in advance. A cash buyer working through a title company can handle the transfer tax split and the recording as part of one closing.

More questions about Philadelphia County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Which office files my Philadelphia deed?

At the Department of Records in City Hall, Room 111, either by mail or in person with an appointment. Businesses can also record electronically through a third party vendor.

What fee applies to a standard Philadelphia deed?

The deed fee is $278.75, plus the realty transfer tax, which exempt transfers skip. A deed for a deceased spouse or partner is $43.75. Check the Department's current fee schedule before you send payment.

What is the realty transfer tax rate in Philadelphia?

The rate is 4.578 percent, split into 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the state. It falls due at recording, and the City allows up to 30 days to pay.

Can I record a deed without a lawyer?

The Department says it is possible but advises against preparing a deed yourself. Use a lawyer, title company or other professional, and consider title insurance.

Does the Department of Records take personal checks?

No. It accepts cash, money orders, business or certified checks, and cards with a 3.5 percent fee. Taxes and fees go on separate checks.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Standard recording fee for deeds and for mortgages is $200.00 (extra $10 per parcel over 30; $5 per name over 30).
  • E-recording available via CSC, eRecording Partners Network, ERX/Xerox, Simplifile; some deed types (sheriff deeds, corrective deeds, trust transfers, deeds taxable in multiple jurisdictions) must be paper.
  • Realty transfer tax collected at recording, paid by separate check; total 2% to 5% with 1% to State; Statement of Value REV-183 needed when consideration not on deed or for certain exemptions.
  • Deeds must specify local transfer tax disbursement by percentage and dollar amounts and include parcel Block and Lot numbers.

Allegheny County by the numbers

Where are deeds recorded in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania?

Deeds go to the Division of Real Estate, which sits in Room 101 of the County Office Building at 542 Forbes Avenue in Pittsburgh. The division does the recorder's work in this county, and it also collects the state and local transfer taxes.

The counter keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For questions, call 412-350-4636 and choose Option 2. The recording page says most documents can be eRecorded online, so a title company in another city can submit a deed without anyone walking into Room 101.

A homeowner who sells in Allegheny County will usually never visit the counter. The title agent prepares the deed, records it, and sends the tax and fee payments that the division requires.

What does the Allegheny County Division of Real Estate charge to record a deed?

The standard recording fee for a deed is $200.00, and a mortgage costs the same, under the schedule effective January 1, 2026. Large documents add charges only when they pass 30 parcels or 30 indexed names.

Allegheny County recording fees effective January 1, 2026
Document typeStandard fee
Deed and deed related documents$200.00
Mortgage and mortgage related documents$200.00
Power of attorney$50.00
Notary public bond and commission$80.00
Financial statement$175.00
Military service dischargeNo fee

Source: the Division of Real Estate recording fee sheet. Each parcel past 30 on a deed adds $10.00, and each indexed name past 30 adds $5.00. Deed related documents include leases, rights of way, declarations of trust, oil and gas documents and sewage permits, all at the same $200.00.

How much is the transfer tax on a sale in Allegheny County?

It runs from 2% to 5% of the price depending on where the house is, and 1% of that goes to the state. The remainder goes to the municipality and the school district that cover the property.

The division collects every layer of the tax at recording, with one check for transfer tax and a second check for the recording fee. The county's own worked examples show the spread on a $40,000 sale:

  • A house in Shaler Township pays 1% to the state, 0.5% to the township and 0.5% to Shaler Area School District, for $800.00 in total.
  • A house in the City of Pittsburgh pays 1% to the state, 3% to the city and 1% to Pittsburgh School District, for $2,000.00 in total.

Scale those percentages to a real price and the difference is large. On a $200,000 sale, 2% is $4,000 and 5% is $10,000. Ask the closing agent for the exact municipal and school rates before the settlement statement is final.

When no price appears on the deed, or when an exemption applies, a Statement of Value on Pennsylvania form REV-183 is required. Certain family transfers can skip the form if the deed carries a sentence explaining the relationship. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, at 717-783-8104, handles exemption questions.

What formatting rules apply to an Allegheny County deed?

A deed must be typed in black ink on white or manila sheets, 8 1/2 by 11 inches or 8 1/2 by 14 inches, in a font of at least 10 points. Continuous paper is rejected.

  • Leave a one inch margin at the top of the first page for the certification stamp.
  • Print a name and a full address with zip code in the Record and Mail to area, outside that top margin.
  • Handwriting is limited to signatures, acknowledgments and a few listed exceptions.
  • Keep out tape, glue, staples, correction fluid and highlighting.
  • Double-sided pages are fine, though each side that carries text counts as a separate page for the fee.

The same page sets a formatting rule for the Certificate of Residence, and the county publishes content requirements for each document type separately.

How can I pay recording fees in Allegheny County?

Paying in person takes cash, a business check, a money order or a cashier's check. Personal checks, debit cards and credit cards are refused.

Firms that record often can open a draw down account in the office during business hours, which saves the trip to the counter with a check each time. The recording page lists online payment as an option, and the county posts a separate sheet for copies and their associated fees.

Anyone who sees an unfamiliar deed or mortgage filed against their property can use the county's web form to report suspected deed or mortgage fraud.

Where does the common level ratio come into a deed?

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue issues a new Common Level Ratio factor for each county every year, effective July 1, and the Division of Real Estate links to it from its transfer tax page. The factor sits in the same list of helpful items as the Statement of Value, so a filer working on a gift or low-price deed will see both together.

The county's appeal board, meanwhile, lists 49.3% as the common level ratio for the 2027 tax year, applied to current market value in assessment appeals that began in September 2026. A ratio near 49% signals that county assessments, frozen to a 2012 base year, run well below current market prices. Ask the closing agent which figure belongs on the Statement of Value before the deed is signed.

What is Allegheny County like for someone selling a house?

Allegheny County covers 745 square miles, and the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet at Downtown Pittsburgh to form the Ohio. The Youghiogheny River joins the Monongahela at McKeesport, about ten miles to the southeast. With 130 municipalities, the county has more local governments than any other in Pennsylvania, and neighboring municipalities can carry different transfer tax rates.

The Census Bureau counted 1,225,035 residents in its July 2025 estimate, second in the state behind Philadelphia, and it lists 614,484 housing units.

Allegheny County housing figures from Census QuickFacts
MeasureAllegheny County
Owner-occupied rate, 2020-202465.2%
Median owner-occupied value, 2020-2024$227,600
Median gross rent, 2020-2024$1,153
Median household income, 2020-2024$78,548
Building permits, 20253,191

About 35% of housing units are renter occupied, which matters when a seller owns a duplex or a house with tenants in place.

What should an Allegheny County seller check before the deed is recorded?

  1. Confirm the municipality and school district, since those two set most of the transfer tax.
  2. Review the deed against the formatting rules above so the division does not reject it.
  3. Decide who pays transfer tax; the Department of Revenue says both grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for the tax, so settle the split in writing.
  4. Choose eRecording or hand delivery, and for hand delivery plan on a business check, cashier's check, money order or cash.

Buyers of rental houses have a second step. Effective September 18, 2026, Act 29 of 2026 requires a new owner of non-owner-occupied real estate to send contact details to the county's chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a knowingly false filing can bring a fine of up to $500. A seller who is handing a tenant-occupied house to an investor can mention that duty to the buyer.

More questions about Allegheny County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the standard recording fee for a deed in Allegheny County?

It is $200.00 for a deed and for a mortgage under the fee sheet effective January 1, 2026. Parcels beyond 30 add $10.00 each and indexed names beyond 30 add $5.00 each.

Does Allegheny County take personal checks or cards at the recording counter?

No. The Division of Real Estate does not accept personal checks, debit cards or credit cards. It takes cash, business checks, money orders, cashier's checks and draw down accounts, and online payment exists for eRecorded filings.

Why is the transfer tax so different between Pittsburgh and the suburbs?

The 1% state share is constant, while the municipal and school district shares change by location. On the county's $40,000 example, Shaler Township totals 2% and the City of Pittsburgh totals 5%.

Can a deed be recorded without visiting Room 101?

Yes, the county says most documents can be eRecorded online. For hand delivery, the address is 542 Forbes Avenue, Room 101, and the counter keeps weekday hours.

Does a military discharge cost anything to record in Allegheny County?

No. Military service discharge papers, street or alley vacations and ordinances are listed with no recording fee.

Selling in Montgomery County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Montgomery County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Fee schedule effective Nov 24, 2025: base deed fee $87.75 (up to 4 names, 4 pages, 1 parcel); over 4 names $1 each, over 4 pages $4 each, extra parcel $15.50; two separate checks (recording fee and transfer tax).
  • E-recording available but deeds with trusts cannot be e-recorded; all documents must be registered by the Board of Assessments before recording.

Fees

Selling in Montgomery County?

What we could not confirm

  • No 2027 sale dates published

Montgomery County by the numbers

Where does Montgomery County, Pennsylvania record a deed?

Deeds for Montgomery County go to the Recorder of Deeds on the third floor of One Montgomery Plaza, 425 Swede Street in Norristown, in Suite 303. Posted hours run weekdays from half past eight until four o'clock, and quick questions can be texted to 267-355-3404.

The county created the office in 1784, the same year it was carved out of Philadelphia County. Its job covers deeds, mortgages, powers of attorney, notary commissions, subdivision and highway plans, and military discharge papers.

For a seller the visit happens last. Papers get signed at the closing table, they travel to Norristown, and the recording date marks the moment the buyer shows up as owner in the public record. That sequence explains why a closing agent keeps asking you for a parcel number.

What does the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds charge?

Montgomery County starts a deed at $87.75, per the schedule dated November 24, 2025. The price assumes no more than four names, four pages and a single parcel, and every extra is billed on top.

Montgomery County recording charges, schedule effective November 24, 2025
ItemCharge
Deed or mortgage, starting price$87.75
Additional page past the fourth$4.00
Additional name past the fourth$1.00
Additional parcel$15.50
Relocation deed$175.50
Satisfaction of a mortgage$81.75
Document rejection$10.00
Returned check$30.00

Source: the county's Recording Fee Schedule page. A few smaller charges apply too, listed below.

  • Statement of Value forms cost $1.50 for the pair of originals the office wants. A relocation deed needs four originals, at $3.00.
  • Mail a lone document with no return envelope and it costs $2; a bundle costs $10.
  • Cards add a 2.65% convenience charge.
  • Where land sits in two or more taxing authorities, the first unique parcel ID in each one carries a $5.50 fee.

How does Montgomery County collect transfer tax at recording?

The recorder collects it during recording, at a combined 2 percent. One point goes to the state, and under the state's rule the seller and the buyer answer for it jointly.

Montgomery County asks for two separate checks when a deed is recorded: one for the recording fee and one for the realty transfer tax. Payee names the county will honor include "Montco Recorder of Deeds" and "Montgomery County ROD," and each check should print the account holder's address.

Form REV-183, the Statement of Value, rides along whenever the tax is not simply paid on a stated price. Land spread over two or more municipalities calls for a split of value in the deed, so each local tax collector gets the right piece. The fee page also posts a Common Level Ratio Factor, 3.25 as of July 1, 2025 and 3.36 as of July 1, 2026. Ask the office how it applies to a deed that carries no sale price.

Some transfers owe nothing, such as particular gifts inside a family or inherited property. Whether a given family deed qualifies is a question for the closing attorney or the recorder's staff.

Why does a Montgomery County deed stop at the Board of Assessments first?

Montgomery County requires every document, on paper or electronic, to be registered by the Board of Assessments first. The board sits directly across the hall from the recorder on the third floor of One Montgomery Plaza.

Every document also needs a Parcel Identification Number, which is a 12-digit number in this county. If a parcel number appears anywhere on a document, it has to be registered unless the document says in so many words that the number is for reference only. Questions about parcel mapping belong with the Board of Assessments, not the recorder.

Older advice about registering a deed with the township before recording no longer holds. The county rescinded pre-registration on December 9, 2008. Some municipalities still want the deed registered after it is recorded, and the municipality may charge for that. The submitter handles it.

Can a deed be filed online in Montgomery County?

Yes, within limits. The county has taken electronic recordings since fall 2006 and works with Simplifile, the eRecording Partners Network and CSC. Documents usually come back the same day or the next.

The county lists what cannot go through that channel, so a seller's closing agent knows to bring paper.

  • Deeds that contain a trust must be mailed or delivered, because an electronically recorded document becomes public automatically.
  • Mortgages in default, plans and post-construction stormwater documents cannot be submitted electronically.
  • Documents with more than 10 parcels, packages of more than 10 documents and packages above 100 pages are turned away.
  • Scans must be at least 300 DPI, black and white, as TIFF images.

If an electronic filing is rejected and you think the rejection was wrong, the county asks you to call 610-278-3289 the same day so staff can decide whether the rejection fee comes back.

Which errors make Montgomery County return a deed?

Most returns come from small mismatches. The county repeats the Pennsylvania recorders' association standards on its requirements page, and it adds its own.

  • The document must be an original, not a copy.
  • The acknowledgment date cannot be earlier than the document date, and it needs county, state, names, titles, the notary's signature, seal and commission expiration.
  • The number written out must match the numeral on a deed or mortgage.
  • Deeds, mortgages and assignments need a certified grantee or mortgagee address, signed.
  • Blanket documents are refused.
  • Paper submissions need a stamped, self-addressed envelope big enough for the documents.

Each rejection costs $10, so a package that fails twice costs more than one that is checked before it leaves the closing office.

Who is selling in Montgomery County, and where?

Only Philadelphia and Allegheny counties have more people than this suburb of Philadelphia, where Norristown is the seat and Lower Merion Township is the biggest municipality. The 2025 federal estimate is 877,643 residents, and roughly 71 percent of homes are lived in by their owners.

Prices run high: the typical owned home is valued at $436,700 and the typical household earns $113,915, based on the latest five-year survey. Employers cluster around Blue Bell, Lansdale, Fort Washington, Horsham and King of Prussia.

The county is made up of dozens of townships, boroughs and home rule municipalities, and the local share of transfer tax follows whichever one the house sits in. School district names such as Lower Merion, North Penn, Abington and Norristown Area matter when you compare tax bills.

What should be in the closing folder for a Montgomery County sale?

Bring the paperwork that the recorder will otherwise bounce. A few items cause most of the delay.

  • The 12-digit parcel number, checked against the Board of Assessments.
  • Two original Statement of Value forms, fully filled in.
  • Two checks, one for the recording fee and one for transfer tax, each with the account holder's address.
  • A prepaid return envelope if the deed comes back by mail.
  • A plan for any trust deed, since those cannot be filed electronically.

Your title company normally handles all of this. It still helps to ask who is paying the recording fee and the buyer's half of the tax, because the sales contract can shift those costs from the default.

More questions about Montgomery County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the price of recording a Montgomery County deed?

The base fee is $87.75 for up to four names, four pages and one parcel, plus $1 per extra name, $4 per extra page and $15.50 per extra parcel. Transfer tax and a $1.50 Statement of Value fee are separate.

Does Montgomery County take one check or two for a deed?

Two. The county wants one check for the recording fee and a second for the realty transfer tax, both payable to the Recorder of Deeds, each showing the account holder's address.

Who owes the transfer tax on a Montgomery County sale?

State law makes them jointly responsible. The sales contract normally sets who really pays, and the combined rate collected at the Norristown counter is 2 percent.

Why can't a trust deed go through e-recording in Montgomery County?

No. Deeds with a trust must be recorded by mail or in person, because electronic recordings are public at once. Mortgages in default and plans are also excluded.

What if my deed has no parcel number yet?

Contact the Montgomery County Board of Assessments, which is across the hall from the recorder in Norristown. Every document must carry a registered 12-digit parcel number before it can be recorded.

Bucks County by the numbers

Where is the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds?

The office is at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, in Doylestown, and the phone is 215-348-6209. It is open weekdays from 7:45 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., but every document to be recorded has to be submitted by 4 p.m. Papers that reach the counter after noon can slip to the following workday.

The Recorder keeps real estate records back to 1684, the era of the county's founding under William Penn. Besides deeds and mortgages, the office handles as many as 25 other kinds of documents, including subdivision plans, UCC filings, mausoleum and sewer permits, and notary commissions. Official records survive on microfiche, microfilm and PDF/A, and the office has stopped preparing bound books.

The county's assessment board works in step with the Recorder. Its deed registry staff check every document and attach tax parcel labels before recording, so a deed with a wrong parcel number or an old owner name can stall at that desk.

What will Bucks County charge to file a deed?

The county's schedule is built on one parcel, four names and four pages. Each page beyond four adds $4, each name beyond four adds $1, and each parcel beyond one adds $10. For the base amount on a deed or mortgage, use the recording fee calculator the county links, which was built by the state's recorders association. The Statement of Value form is not counted as a fee page.

Each parcel after the first$10
Official search per name or item for a court order$5
Special handling per document$25
Rejected document returned$10
Paper copy of a receipt$0.50
Credit card service fee3.0%

Checks and money orders are made out to the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. The calculators do not include certified copies, and staff verify final amounts when the document is recorded. Call 215-348-6209 to confirm a number before you send anything.

How much transfer tax do Bucks County sellers face?

The rate is 2%, split evenly between the state and the local taxing bodies, and the Recorder takes payment at the time of filing. The tax applies to the value of the interest conveyed, which is not always the sales price. Neither the state nor local governments say who pays, so most purchase agreements split it between buyer and seller. The new owner is on the hook if the amount paid turns out to be short.

Since January 2026 the office has refused personal checks for transfer tax. Accepted methods are cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card. Title agents usually handle this at settlement, so confirm which method your closer will use.

  • Some transfers are exempt, such as conveyances between spouses, from parents to children, across three generations, and among siblings.
  • A one-time transfer between former spouses is allowed.
  • If an investigator finds a higher value, the state can bill extra tax and interest and mails the determination to you directly.
  • State revenue officials describe their share as 1% of the value, collected with any local tax by the county recorder.

When do you need a Statement of Value in Bucks County?

A Statement of Value, the state's REV-183 form, is needed whenever transfer tax is not paid or the true value is missing from the deed, as with a $1 consideration. It sets the value or gives the reason for an exemption. The county accepts only the June 2019 version of the form, and a paper copy must come in duplicate.

The form uses the Common Level Ratio Factor, which the county posts for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. State investigators later check whether the stated value or exemption holds up. If it does not, the state issues the determination and the extra tax and interest go to the state, with a receipt sent to the Recorder for recording.

For a deed recorded electronically, attachments such as a trust agreement, mortgage or assignment add a $1 per page copy fee. The office prints them for the Department of Revenue and then deletes them from the public record. Mailing those pages in on paper avoids the charge.

How can you submit a deed for recording in Bucks County?

You can e-record through Simplifile, CSC or ePN, bring the paper deed to the counter, or mail it. A mailed package needs the correct checks payable to the Recorder and a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself. Deeds, mortgages, general powers of attorney, satisfactions and copy requests should come straight to the Recorder's office.

The office stopped issuing book and page numbers on July 1, 2012, so every recorded document carries only an instrument number. Paper receipts ended in 2012 as well. Receipts now go by email, which requires the Submitter Information Form on file with the office.

  • Free services include the Fraud Alert System, which tells an owner if something is recorded against the property.
  • You can request a free email copy of your own deed.
  • Military discharge papers (DD-214) are recorded free.
  • In-office notary service is available.

What else should Bucks County sellers check before filing?

Bucks County is the northern edge of the Philadelphia area, covering 622 square miles between the Delaware River and Montgomery County, with Doylestown as its seat and Bensalem the largest township. Census Bureau estimates for 2020 to 2024 give $445,700 as the middle home value among owners, and 77.8% of households own. The county's 2020 population was 646,538.

On a house of that price, 2% transfer tax is a real line item, so settle early who bears it. Check that the municipality named on the deed matches the tax bill, since the local half of the tax depends on it. The assessment board says there is a gap between recording and updates on its public site, and it can be reached at 215-348-6219 for ownership questions.

Sellers who want a quick close can work with a cash buyer who handles the paperwork. Give the closing agent the parcel number, every owner name and the school district well before the settlement date. Bucks County has 54 townships and boroughs, so a short list of those three details can save a rejected filing and the $10 return charge.

More questions about Bucks County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What are the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds office hours?

Counter service runs weekdays, 7:45 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. Documents to be recorded have to be submitted by 4 p.m. A package received after noon may wait for the following workday.

Can I pay Bucks County transfer tax with a personal check?

No. Since January 2026 the Recorder of Deeds does not take personal checks for realty transfer tax. Accepted methods are cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card, and cards carry a 3.0% service fee.

What is the fee for each extra page on a Bucks County deed?

Each page after the fourth costs $4. Names after the fourth cost $1 each and parcels after the first cost $10 each. The REV-183 Statement of Value does not count as a fee page.

Does Bucks County require a Statement of Value?

Yes, when transfer tax is not paid or the deed does not show the true value, for example a $1 consideration. Use the June 2019 version of REV-183, in duplicate if submitted on paper. The state may later send a determination if the stated value looks low.

How far back do Bucks County deed records go?

The Recorder of Deeds holds records from 1684 to the present. They are kept on microfiche, microfilm and PDF/A, and the office does not prepare bound books anymore. Documents recorded since July 1, 2012 carry an instrument number only.

  • E-recording accepted since late 2020 via Simplifile, CSC, EPN, Indecomm; vendor pricing from vendors.

What we could not confirm

Delaware County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Delaware County?

Deeds for Delaware County property are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds in the Government Center, Room 108, 201 W. Front Street, Media, PA 19063. The office keeps real property records back to 1789, the year the county was created from part of Chester County, and the phone number is 610-891-4152.

The counter is open 8:30am to 4:30pm, but documents are accepted for recording only from 8:30am to 3:30pm. A seller whose closing runs late in the day should ask the title company how it will get the deed in before the cutoff, because e-recording and hand delivery both follow the same recording window.

One office handles every deed, but each deed also touches a municipality. The recorder collects the local share of transfer tax for the township, borough or city where the house sits, so the municipality named on the deed shapes the final bill. Media sits near the middle of the county, which makes the Government Center a short drive from most parcels.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Delaware County?

A four-page Delaware County deed costs $117.25 to record under the fee schedule dated December 1, 2025. The $38.00 base fee covers up to four pages, four names and ten folio numbers, and the rest of the total is made up of county and state add-on charges.

Delaware County Recorder of Deeds fees, schedule dated December 1, 2025
Document (4 pages)Total fee
Deed$117.25
Mortgage$115.25
Satisfaction, release or assignment$84.25
Agreement, power of attorney or general miscellaneous$43.00
Certification (4 pages)$7.00

Breaking the deed total down shows where the money goes:

  • Base fee: $38.00
  • County Affordable Housing charge: $18.00
  • Judicial computer, access to justice and criminal justice add-on: $41.25, which rose by $1.00 on December 1, 2025
  • County Improvement Fund: $5.00
  • Demolition of Blighted Properties charge: $15.00

Extra pages on a deed are $4.00 each, and every name after the fourth or folio after the tenth adds $1.00. Veterans discharge papers are recorded free.

How much transfer tax does a Delaware County seller pay?

Most Delaware County sales carry 2% in realty transfer tax: 1% to the state and 1% to the local taxing bodies. A few places charge more, so the municipality printed on your deed decides the rate.

  • Radnor Township: local 1.5%
  • Upper Darby Township: local 1.5%
  • Chester City: local 1.5%
  • Upper Providence Township: local 2%
  • Everywhere else in the county: local 1%

On a $300,000 sale, the standard split is $3,000 to the state and $3,000 locally. The same sale in Upper Darby would be $3,000 state plus $4,500 local, and in Upper Providence $3,000 plus $6,000. Contracts often split the tax between buyer and seller, so read the agreement of sale before assuming who writes the check.

Chester City dropped its separate property registration form and $10 fee for sales after September 1, 2023. All Chester City properties now fall under the single 1.5% local rate.

When a deed covers land in more than one municipality, it has to say what share of the value belongs to each taxing body, using the Pennsylvania Statement of Value.

What paperwork and payments does the recorder require?

The office asks for three separate checks when a deed is recorded in person. Each has a different payee, so mixing them into one check will get the package returned.

  • One check for the recording fee, made out to Recorder of Deeds
  • One check for state transfer tax, made out to Recorder of Deeds, Agent
  • One check for local transfer tax, also made out to Recorder of Deeds, Agent

Every document needs a 1-inch top margin on each page, a rule announced on November 17, 2025, so the office can stamp recording data electronically without covering text. All documents are also subject to Solicitor approval before recording, which is worth building into the closing timeline.

E-recording submitters have a correction window. Fees have to be right, and the office told submitters on September 1, 2024 that they have until 11:30am the next business day after a month ends to flag incorrect fees. The county does not run title searches, so title work stays with the title company or an attorney.

What is the Common Level Ratio for Delaware County?

The recorder's 2026-27 Common Level Ratio factor is 1.83, announced on June 22, 2026. It applies to any document dated July 1, 2026 or later.

The ratio changes every fiscal year, so a deed dated before July 1, 2026 uses the earlier factor. If your document needs the factor at all, ask the office which one applies to the date on your deed.

How do you search Delaware County records and get copies?

Records from 1799 to the present can be viewed online through the county's public access site, and copies cost less there than in the office. Online copies are $0.50 per page, and copies bought at the counter are $1.00 per page. Electronic certified copies are $12.50 through the same public access site, while paper certifications are $7.00 for four pages plus $1.00 for each added page.

  • Property Alert: a free service that emails you when a document is recorded against your Property ID number
  • Return envelope: add $1.00 to a mailed request if you do not enclose one
  • Microfiche copies: $1.00 per page

Homeowners who worry about deed fraud can sign up for Property Alert before listing. It costs nothing and shows quickly if someone records a document against the parcel.

What should a Delaware County home seller know?

Delaware County covers 191 square miles and sits southwest of Philadelphia, where it is the only Pennsylvania county bordering both Delaware and New Jersey. Media is the county seat, Upper Darby is the largest township, and Chester is the main city on the Delaware River.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table lists 580,937 residents for July 2025 and 230,160 housing units. Median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $332,200, owner-occupancy is 69.6%, and median gross rent is $1,372. Median household income is $89,546. These figures run well above Elk County, where the median home value is $133,600.

The county had 216,946 households in 2020 to 2024, at 2.56 people per household, and the Census Bureau counted 217 building permits for 2025. About 41.9% of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree, and the mean commute is 28.1 minutes. Industry clusters along the river: the Trainer refinery and the Port of Chester sit on the Delaware shoreline, and the lowest point in Pennsylvania is at Marcus Hook, where the river leaves the state.

That price level makes transfer tax a real number in a Delco sale. A seller in a 1.5% township pays noticeably more than a seller across the line in a 1% township, so check the municipality before pricing an offer.

More questions about Delaware County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the cost to record a deed in Delaware County?

A four-page deed costs $117.25 under the December 1, 2025 schedule. Extra pages are $4.00 each, and names after four or folio numbers after ten add $1.00 each.

What are the transfer tax rates in Delaware County?

The standard rate is 1% state plus 1% local. Radnor, Upper Darby and Chester City charge 1.5% locally, and Upper Providence charges 2% locally.

What hours does the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds accept recordings?

Recording hours are 8:30am to 3:30pm, although the office stays open to 4:30pm. The office is in Room 108 of the Government Center in Media.

Do I need separate checks to record a deed in Delaware County?

Yes. The office asks for one check for the recording fee, one for state transfer tax and one for local transfer tax. Tax checks go to Recorder of Deeds, Agent.

Can I look up Delaware County deeds online?

Yes. Records from 1799 to the present are available online, with copies at $0.50 per page. Copies bought in the office are $1.00 per page.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Base deed recording fee $94.75 (1 UPI, 4 pages, 4 names); $20 UPI fee per UPI number.
  • Realty transfer tax 1% (state) with local exceptions Malvern and Tredyffrin 1.5%, Coatesville 2.5%; separate checks for municipal and state; no cash or credit card.

Chester County by the numbers

What does the Chester County Recorder of Deeds do when a house sells?

The office in West Chester files the deed that moves a Chester County house from seller to buyer, collects the realty transfer tax due on that deed, and keeps the permanent land record. Until a deed is recorded here, the public record still shows the old owner, which can stall a buyer's loan or a later resale.

The county describes the office as the custodian of all land records and indexes for transfers, going back to 1688. It also records mortgages, satisfactions, powers of attorney, subdivision plans and notary commissions. The tax money it collects is passed on to the Commonwealth, the county's 73 municipalities and its 14 school districts. Staff cannot draft a deed, search for liens or give legal advice, so the drafting usually falls to a title company or attorney.

Where is the Recorder of Deeds office and when can I file?

The office is at 313 W. Market Street, Suite 3302, West Chester, and the phone number listed on the county page is 610-344-6330. It is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., but documents for recording must be handed in by 4 p.m.

  • Same-day recording runs 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Same-day recording of large exhibits such as maps and subdivision plans stops at 3:00 p.m.
  • The search library is open until 4:15 p.m.
  • Fees must be paid at the moment of recording, and the office will not record an unofficial copy of a document that is already on record.

Bring a self-addressed stamped envelope with any paper filing. The county adds postage and a $2.00 fee when one is missing.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Chester County?

A standard deed costs $94.75 to record under the schedule effective December 1, 2025. That base covers one UPI, up to four pages, one notation fee and four names. The same base applies to a mortgage and to a deed of correction.

Chester County recording fees, schedule effective December 1, 2025 (source: Chester County Recorder of Deeds)
DocumentBase fee
Deed$94.75
Re-recorded deed or mortgage$96.75
Deed in blank or relocation deed$183.50
Satisfaction, assignment, release, easement$81.75
Power of attorney$20.50
Miscellaneous document$40.50

Extras stack on top. A UPI costs $20.00 per number, a document that misses the PRIA formatting standards carries a $25.00 non-compliance fee, and each exhibit adds $5.00. The base fee already contains a $41.25 judicial administration charge set by the Department of Revenue.

What is the transfer tax on a Chester County sale and who pays it?

The county fee page puts the rate at 1% of the consideration or computed value, whichever is higher, with higher rates in three places: Malvern and Tredyffrin at 1.5%, and Coatesville at 2.5%. Ask the recorder for the combined state and local figure that applies to your deed.

State law makes both the grantor and the grantee jointly liable for the tax, and the Department of Revenue notes that certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy are exempt. Who covers the bill in a sale is a matter for the sales agreement.

  • Transfer tax is paid by separate checks, one for the municipality and one for the state, made out to the Chester County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Only business checks, cashier's checks and money orders are taken for tax. Cash and credit cards are refused for tax.
  • Recording fees go on a third check or other accepted payment.

What payment and paperwork rules cause rejected deeds?

Most rejections come from payment mistakes and missing page-one details. The recorder takes cash in person for recording fees only, and personal, estate and trustee checks are refused at all times. Checks older than 180 days are not accepted, no more than ten documents may share one check, and a returned check triggers a $25 bank fee on top of the $10.00 rejection fee for returned documents.

  • Type a valid UPI on the first page. A computer-printed label on page one is acceptable.
  • State the grantee's exact mailing address and certify it with a signature, as 16 P.S. Section 9781 requires.
  • Attach a Statement of Value when the deed does not state the full value, unless a family exemption applies. The Common Level Ratio factor, updated each July 1, belongs on that form.
  • For land in more than one municipality, show the local tax split in dollars on the deed.
  • Match every name across the caption, signature and notary acknowledgment, including Sr., Jr. and III.

What should a Chester County seller check before the deed goes in?

Start with the title trail. A prior mortgage that was paid off should show a recorded satisfaction, and the satisfaction, assignment and release category carries its own $81.75 base fee if one is missing. If the house came through an estate, the Statement of Value and the family-transfer rules matter more than they do on an ordinary sale, so the title company should review them early.

Also confirm the grantee's mailing address with the buyer. Tax bills are sent to the address on the deed, and the county asks that it be exact, current, legible and scannable. A deed sent in with a tax check from a personal or estate account will be turned away, so closing funds for transfer tax should be arranged as a cashier's check or money order ahead of time.

  • Order a copy of the vesting deed from the recording office if the seller's own copy is lost. Certified copies run $0.50 per page plus $5.00 for certification when made by staff.
  • Ask the title company whether the property sits in Malvern, Tredyffrin or Coatesville, where the higher tax rates apply.
  • Confirm the deed shows the correct UPI and not the tax parcel number, since the two are formatted differently.

Can a Chester County deed be e-recorded?

Yes. Chester County takes electronic filings through Simplifile and CSC eRecording, which is how most title companies deliver a closing package. For a deed that owes tax, the consideration and the state and municipal tax amounts must appear on the first page.

Each package is limited to ten documents, and a single document cannot list more than ten UPI numbers. E-recording is not available for deeds of correction, re-recorded deeds or Statements of Value with exhibits attached. Those go in on paper. Resubmitting a document costs a $10 return fee each time, and a document recorded in error is not refunded.

What does the Chester County housing market look like for sellers?

Chester County sits in the Philadelphia metropolitan area, with West Chester as the seat and Coatesville as its only city. The Census Bureau estimated 557,116 residents in July 2025 across about 751 square miles of Piedmont hills and valleys, with 217,440 housing units.

For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied home value of $485,600, a median household income of $127,208 and median gross rent of $1,763. Owners occupy 75.1% of homes. Houses in the south of the county, in the Brandywine and Octoraro watersheds, sell alongside suburban homes near the Main Line, so transfer tax can differ sharply from one township to the next.

More questions about Chester County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How long does it take to record a deed in Chester County?

Same-day recording is offered until 4:00 p.m. on business days, and e-recorded packages through Simplifile or CSC are the usual route for closings. Large plans must arrive by 3:00 p.m. for same-day handling.

Can I pay the Chester County transfer tax by credit card?

No. Transfer tax must be paid by business check, cashier's check or money order made out to the Chester County Recorder of Deeds. Credit cards may be used only for recording fees and copy requests, with a 3.5% in-person fee.

Do I need a Statement of Value to record a deed in Chester County?

Yes, when the deed does not state the full and complete value of the property, unless a family exemption applies. It is a Department of Revenue form and is recorded with the deed, so its pages count toward the recording fee.

Can the Recorder of Deeds correct a mistake in a recorded deed?

Not by editing it. A deed of correction costs $94.75 and needs a written explanation on page one, the book and page of the deed being fixed, a new acknowledgment and a Statement of Value. Deeds of correction cannot be e-recorded.

Is the transfer tax the same everywhere in Chester County?

No. The listed rate is 1% of consideration or computed value, but Malvern and Tredyffrin charge 1.5% and Coatesville charges 2.5%. Check the municipality where the house sits before you price a sale.

Lancaster County by the numbers

Where does a Lancaster County deed get recorded, and until what hour?

Deeds go to the Recorder of Deeds at 150 North Queen Street, Suite 315, Lancaster, PA 17603. The office is open from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, and recording itself concludes at 4:30 p.m.

The county's recorder website notes that payments are not taken over the phone. It also says that since October 1, 2025 staff no longer print trusts or other supporting papers as a courtesy, so a submitter who wants to skip a 25 cent per page printing charge must send those pages already printed, or attach them to an electronic filing.

For a seller, this office comes at the very end. The deed is signed and acknowledged at closing, then recorded here, and the county's public search shows the new owner afterward.

What does it cost to record a deed in Lancaster County?

The posted base fee for a deed or mortgage of up to four pages is $71.25. Every page after the fourth adds $2.00, and the office says it does not issue refunds.

Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds base fees, up to four pages, from the office's fee schedule
Document typeBase fee
Deed or mortgage$71.25
Assignment, release, satisfaction, installment sale agreement, easement$59.75
Agreement, termination, modification, subordination$58.75
Power of attorney or deputation (miscellaneous)$18.50

The recorder's bulletin board adds that the JCP fee rose from $40.25 to $41.25 under Act 45 of 2025. Because that line sits on the home page and the fee page lists a round base figure, call the office for the exact total on your package.

A veteran's discharge, the DD-214, is recorded free.

How should I pay at the Lancaster County recorder's counter?

Cash, certified checks, corporate checks, money orders and credit cards are accepted to record documents. Personal checks are refused for amounts over $75 and are never taken for transfer tax. Blank checks are not accepted either.

  • Card payments carry a 2.5% charge on transactions over $50, and $1 on smaller ones.
  • A returned check costs $25.00.
  • There are no refunds, so the amount has to be right the first time.
  • Mailed or couriered packages need a self-addressed stamped envelope of the right size and with enough postage.

The county says that when a document type has no listed fee, the Recorder sets one. If your deed has attachments or several parcels, ask before sending money.

What rules does Lancaster County apply to the deed itself?

Cover pages are no longer required, and staples are banned. Documents go on white 8.5 by 11 paper in type no smaller than 10 point.

  • The notary acknowledgment date cannot come before the date on the document, and the acknowledgment needs the state, county, date, the person appearing, the notary's signature and the notary's expiration date. The seal itself is optional for Pennsylvania notaries.
  • The tax parcel ID, with its district code, must appear on every deed.
  • Deeds, mortgages and assignments need a signed, certified address with a zip code for the buyer or lender. On a deed a P.O. box is not allowed as that address, though the deed may say tax bills should go to a box.
  • Land in more than one municipality must state the percentage split of local transfer tax, in whole numbers.
  • Written amounts must match numbers, and no Social Security or bank account numbers should appear.
  • A transaction is limited to 10 documents, and blanket assignments or releases are rejected.

Corrective or confirmatory deeds need a Statement of Value, an explanation and a full copy of the deed being fixed.

How does Pennsylvania realty transfer tax work in Lancaster County?

The Recorder collects it at the same moment the deed is recorded. The Commonwealth's rate is 1 percent of the transferred value, and the Department of Revenue holds both buyer and seller liable. Local taxes are collected alongside it and shared by municipalities and school districts.

Exemptions exist for certain family transfers, transfers to governments, and property passing by will or intestate succession. Whenever tax is not paid in full, a fully completed Statement of Value must accompany the deed, and the county counts that form as a page toward the four-page base. Easements need one too.

The office also warns that a deed with the wrong property location is the submitter's responsibility. The correct tax must go to the right municipality, school district and state, and the submitter has to claim any refund from the places paid by mistake.

What is Lancaster County like for a home seller?

Lancaster County spans 984 square miles, of which 944 are land, and it was carved out of Chester County on May 10, 1729. The 2020 census counted 552,984 residents, the sixth-highest total among Pennsylvania counties. Lancaster city is the seat; Ephrata, Elizabethtown, Columbia, Lititz and Millersville are among the larger boroughs. Farmland, the Amish community and tourism shape much of the county.

Lancaster County housing and income figures, Census Bureau QuickFacts

Rain falls on about 124 days a year, around 44 inches in all, with roughly 21 inches of snow, according to NOAA normals reported for Lancaster. Basements and roofs take the weather, and buyers will look at both.

What else does the Lancaster County recorder file besides deeds?

The office handles mortgages, satisfactions, assignments, powers of attorney, leases, Uniform Commercial Code filings, notary commissions and veterans' discharges. Several of these touch a house sale, so know the charges ahead of time.

  • A notary commission and bond costs $32.00, and registering the notary's signature adds $4.75.
  • Subdivision, stormwater and state highway plans start at $15.00 for the first page and add $2.00 per page; condominium plans start at $30.00.
  • Plans must be at least 18 by 24 inches and no larger than 24 by 36, and both Mylar and paper are accepted.
  • A UCC-1 or UCC-3 filing costs $100.00 each.
  • Notaries can register their signature at the Recorder's office, which saves a trip to the Prothonotary's office in a separate building.

A seller paying off a mortgage should ask the lender when the satisfaction piece will be filed. At the posted $59.75 base, it is a separate recording with its own book and page reference back to the original mortgage.

What should I check before the deed leaves for the courthouse?

Run through these items with the title agent.

  • Parcel ID and district code on the deed, matching the county record.
  • A certified buyer address that is not a P.O. box.
  • Dollar figures that agree in words and numbers.
  • A completed Statement of Value if the transfer is taxed in part or exempt.
  • Payment in an accepted form: no personal check over $75 and none at all for transfer tax.
  • No staples and no cover sheet.

If the deed is going by mail, put the package together a few days early and enclose the return envelope. The office's public records search lets you confirm afterward that the deed appears under the buyer's name.

More questions about Lancaster County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the base fee for a deed at the Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds?

The posted base fee is $71.25 for a deed or mortgage of up to four pages, plus $2.00 for each added page. The recorder's bulletin says the JCP fee rose to $41.25 under Act 45 of 2025, so confirm the total with the office.

Can I pay Lancaster County transfer tax with a personal check?

No. Personal checks are not accepted for the payment of transfer tax, and they are refused for any amount over $75. Use cash, a certified or corporate check, a money order or a credit card, with the card fee added.

Does a Lancaster County deed need a cover page?

No. Cover pages are no longer required, and staples must not be used. Use white 8.5 by 11 paper and type of at least 10 point.

Can I use a P.O. box as the buyer's address on a Lancaster County deed?

No. The certified grantee address on a deed cannot be a P.O. box. You may state on the deed that tax bills should be mailed to a P.O. box, but the certified address must be a street address with a zip code.

What time does the Lancaster County recorder stop recording?

Recording concludes at 4:30 p.m., though the office remains open until 5:00 p.m. on weekdays. Documents that come in after 4:30 p.m. wait for the next business day.

Berks County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Berks County?

Deeds for Berks County property are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds on the third floor of the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, Reading, PA 19601. Counter hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, and the phone is 610-478-3380. Documents can also arrive by e-recording, by mail or over the counter.

The office does more than file deeds. It also collects state and local real estate transfer taxes, affordable housing fees, judicial fees and redeterminations, records subdivision and land development plans, highway maps and real estate UCC liens, and swears in notaries. Every document recorded since the county was founded in 1752 is available as an image and index on its online search site, with original handwritten and typed books kept for 1752 to 1953.

Property owners can use the Property Alert tool, which the county offers as fraud protection for people who want to know when something is recorded against their address.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Berks County?

A deed, agreement, easement, lease or order of court carries a base fee of $88.00 for up to four pages, and every added page is $4.00. The county's fee schedule took effect on November 14, 2025, and a Statement of Value counts as an extra page when fees are figured. The base fee includes one tax parcel, and each additional parcel is $15.00.

Berks County recording fees, from the Recorder's fee schedule effective November 14, 2025
ItemFee
Deeds, easements, leases, mortgages and related releases or satisfactions (4 pages)$88.00
Powers of attorney, modifications, terminations and similar instruments (4 pages)$87.00
Each additional page$4.00
Each additional tax parcel$15.00
UCC financing statement$115.00
Clean and Green agreement$41.00
Subdivision or land development plan set$100.00
Certification$2.00
Copy, 8.5 by 11$0.50 per page

There is an extra charge to index more than 15 names on one document. Statements of Value that arrive through e-recording are charged a $0.50 per page copy fee for printing and mailing to the Department of Revenue.

What is the transfer tax rate in Berks County?

It depends on where the house sits. The Recorder's fee schedule lists a transfer tax rate of 5% in the City of Reading and 2% in all other Berks municipalities. On a $240,000 sale outside Reading that would be $4,800, and inside Reading it would be $12,000, before any recording fee.

How the payment is made matters here. The office no longer accepts cash or personal checks for transfer tax, an announcement dated December 6, 2022, and the fee schedule repeats that personal checks are not accepted. Overpayments of $10 or less are forfeited, and checks 180 days old or older are refused. Checks are made payable to Berks County Recorder of Deeds.

  • Ask your closing agent whether the title company will pay by company check or wire.
  • Confirm which municipality and school district appear on the deed, especially for Wyomissing Borough, where deeds must name Wyomissing or Wilson School District.
  • Read the purchase agreement to see who pays the tax, since the split is a negotiated term.

What does the Statement of Value need in Berks County?

A Statement of Value is required on every deed that does not state the full and complete value of the property, unless a family exemption applies, in which case the exemption has to be stated in the deed. It must also accompany easements and rights of way. The form is completed in duplicate under Department of Revenue rules, and it is the Pennsylvania REV-183.

The form uses the Common Level Ratio, which changes each July 1. For documents accepted from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 the Berks County factor is 3.12. Since the office treats the form as an additional page, include it when you estimate fees so the check comes out exact.

What documents does the Berks County Recorder reject?

Berks County is specific about format. Documents should be on white 8.5 by 11 inch paper at 20 pound weight, in a font no smaller than 10 point, with a one inch margin at the top and one inch margins on the sides and bottom. Legal size paper is no longer accepted, and light copies will not be scanned legibly, so use dark print and black ink.

  • A Property Identification Number (UPI) is required on every document that references real estate, and the grantee's mailing address must be exact, current and legible.
  • The written amount on a deed must match the numerical amount.
  • The acknowledgment needs the state and county, date, signers, notary signature and a clear stamp with an expiration date.
  • Do not include Social Security numbers or bank or loan numbers, since the Recorder may redact or reject the document.
  • The submitter's name and company must be typed in the Return To area, with a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

Documents received by 3:30 p.m. are generally recorded that same day and held until the next day before being returned.

What is Berks County like for a home seller?

Berks County sits in south central Pennsylvania, about 50 miles northwest of Philadelphia, and it covers 866 square miles with the Schuylkill River running through it. Reading is the county seat and the fourth most populous city in the state. The county was formed on March 11, 1752 from parts of Chester, Lancaster and Philadelphia counties and takes its name from Berkshire in England.

It is the largest of these four counties by far. Census QuickFacts estimates 440,072 residents in 2025, up 2.6% from the 2020 base, with 172,559 housing units and 163,236 households. The owner-occupied rate is 71.3%, and the median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 was $257,300, with median gross rent at $1,181. The county issued 582 building permits in 2025, which is more than the other three counties combined in this group.

QuickFacts shows 9.7% of residents as foreign-born and 21.3% speaking a language other than English at home. A document written in a foreign language has to be recorded with an English translation sworn or affirmed by the translator.

How do you get a recorded document back or obtain a copy?

The submitter decides where the recorded document goes, because the office requires a postage-paid, addressed envelope with each one. Title companies and attorneys often address it to themselves and forward it, and others address it to the new owner. If a copy never shows, check with the closing agent first, then request a copy from the Recorder.

Certified copies ordered online are $10.00 per document, regular copies from the website are 50 cents a page, and copies made in the office, other than your own home's deed, are also 50 cents a page. Credit card payments add a processor fee that is not a county charge. After a mortgage payoff, the lender has 60 days to file the satisfaction, and Pennsylvania lenders do not hold deeds, so no new deed will arrive.

More questions about Berks County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the base fee to record a deed in Berks County?

The base fee is $88.00 for up to four pages and one tax parcel. Every extra page is $4.00 and each extra parcel is $15.00, under the schedule effective November 14, 2025.

What is the Berks County transfer tax on a home sale?

It is 5% in the City of Reading and 2% in every other Berks municipality, according to the Recorder's fee schedule. The office no longer takes cash or personal checks for it.

How do I add or remove a name on my Berks County deed?

A new deed has to be prepared and recorded. The office suggests an attorney, who can often file it too, and the office phone is 610-478-3380.

What is the Berks County Common Level Ratio for 2026 to 2027?

The factor is 3.12 for documents accepted from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. It changes every July 1 and goes on the Statement of Value.

Does the Berks County Recorder record military discharge papers?

Yes, recording a DD-214 and the Veterans ID card are free. You need to bring in the original discharge papers if you have not recorded them before.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Deed recording fee $81.25; extra page $2.00, extra name $0.50, extra PIN $10.00, electronic notation $2.00.

What we could not confirm

  • Upset/judicial sale timeline not on county site (lehighcountytaxclaim.com not used)

Lehigh County by the numbers

Where is a Lehigh County, PA deed filed?

Deeds for Lehigh County property are recorded by the Recorder of Deeds Division, in Room 122 of the Lehigh County Courthouse at 455 W. Hamilton Street, Allentown, PA 18101. The phone number is 610-782-3162, with counter service Monday to Friday between 8:00 and 4:30. Parcel identification, called GIS PIN certification, ends earlier, at 3:45 in the afternoon, so bring a deed that needs a new PIN in the morning or early afternoon.

The office closes on major holidays and on any day the President Judge of the Court of Common Pleas directs. Whoever runs your closing normally files the deed and the payoff papers on your behalf. The fees below still matter to you, since they appear as lines on the settlement statement.

What are the Lehigh County deed recording fees?

A deed of any type costs $81.25 to record under the fee schedule effective January 1, 2026. The fee covers up to four pages, four names and one PIN certification. Anything beyond those limits is billed separately.

Lehigh County recording fees, effective January 1, 2026 (source: Lehigh County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule)
DocumentFee
Deed, all types$81.25
Mortgage$81.25
Satisfaction piece$71.75
Release of mortgage$71.75
Assignment of mortgage$71.75
Deed of dedication$69.75
Easement or right-of-way$69.75
Quiet title action$28.50
Power of attorney$18.50

Extras are small but add up on a complicated parcel:

  • Each page over four costs $2.00, and each name over four costs $0.50.
  • Each additional PIN costs $10.00, so a deed that covers several parcels costs more.
  • Each electronic notation costs $2.00.
  • A rejected document costs $10.00 each time, and a returned check costs $20.00.
  • Mailing documents back costs $3.00 each unless you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

An overpayment of $10.00 or less is forfeited, and the office does not refund fees for a document sent twice by mistake. Double-check the amount before you send it.

Can I record a Lehigh County deed electronically?

Yes. The office accepts electronic filings through Simplifile, CSC and ePN. Because those platforms calculate fees and taxes as you submit, fewer documents are rejected, and the county says documents are usually recorded the same day. A rejected filing can be corrected and sent back right away.

Maps and plans, including subdivision plats, can be electronically recorded through the same three vendors. The division does not keep a paper copy of a map that was recorded electronically.

Certified copies cannot be bought online. They are made at the recorder's counter for $1.50 per document on top of the copy charge. Plain copies are $0.50 per page in person and $1.00 per page by mail.

How are old Lehigh County deeds searched?

The division holds records back to 1812, the year Lehigh County was formed from part of Northampton County. All of it is public except military discharge papers (DD-214), which the office records for free and keeps private. Staff are not authorized to do your search or research for you, so you search yourself.

  • LANDEX Webstore: free searching, with a fee to view or print a document, aimed at occasional users.
  • LANDEX Remote: a pay-as-you-go service at $0.15 a minute and $0.10 for each page loaded, built for heavy users, with an Index Book tab covering 1812 to 1983.
  • Lehigh County Online Records Access: requires an account and a yearly fee arranged through the county Fiscal Office.
  • In person: the public review area downstairs in the courthouse, open Monday to Friday between 8:00 and 4:00

Heirs with a thin paper trail can use the index books to look for an old deed or an unreleased mortgage ahead of any buyer's title search.

What transfer tax is due when a Lehigh County house sells?

The commonwealth taxes a transfer at 1 percent of what the real estate is worth, and the recorder takes it at filing along with the recording fee. The revenue department's page makes grantor and grantee jointly responsible. A local share for the school district and municipality can be added, and it varies from one place to another. Cities can differ from townships, so get the combined figure for your parcel from the recorder before you set a price.

Certain family transfers, transfers under a will or by intestacy, and transfers to government bodies are exempt. A claimed exemption is explained on the state's REV-183 Statement of Value.

What else can end up on the Lehigh County record for a house?

A sale is not the only event that touches a parcel. Farmland owners record Act 319 preferential assessment filings at $33.00 with no extra charge for added pages or names, and covenant filings under Act 515 carry the same $33.00. An Agricultural Security Area ordinance costs $28.50. Easements and rights-of-way cost $69.75. A lease over 30 years costs $59.75. Financing statements under the Uniform Commercial Code cost $110.00 flat.

Release paperwork matters for sellers more than most. When a loan is paid off at closing, the lender files a satisfaction piece ($71.75) or release of mortgage ($71.75), and the mortgage stays on the record until that happens. For an inherited house, check the record for old mortgages that were paid off long ago but never released. A notary commission and bond cost $33.50 in the same office.

Plans and maps follow a different scale. A subdivision, survey or stormwater plan costs $35.00 for page one and $25.00 for every page after it, and a condominium plan costs $40.00 and $25.00. Highway, mining and railroad maps cost $15.00 and $3.00. These matter if you are splitting a lot before you sell.

What is the Lehigh County market area like?

Lehigh County covers 348 square miles in the Lehigh Valley, about 64 miles northwest of Philadelphia and 93 miles west of New York City. The county dates to March 6, 1812, with Allentown as its seat. The 2020 count was 374,557 people, of whom 125,845 lived in Allentown, and the 2025 estimate is 384,383.

Blue Mountain forms the northern edge of the county and South Mountain the southern edge, with the Lehigh River draining most of the land between them. Winters are cold and summers are hot and humid; Allentown averages about 32 inches of snow in a year.

  • Cities and boroughs: Allentown, Bethlehem (mostly in Northampton County), Emmaus, Catasauqua, Fountain Hill, Slatington, Coplay, Macungie, Coopersburg and Alburtis.
  • Colleges: Cedar Crest, Muhlenberg, DeSales University, Penn State Lehigh Valley and Lehigh Carbon Community College.
  • Travel: Lehigh Valley International Airport sits in Hanover Township, LANta runs the local buses, and I-78 and PA 309 meet in the county.

The oldest continuously occupied building in the county is Shelter House in Emmaus, built in 1734, and the county contains housing from every era since. Older homes can bring title questions, such as old easements or a lien that was never released, which the recording office's records can help answer.

More questions about Lehigh County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the Lehigh County recording fee for a deed?

A deed costs $81.25 under the schedule effective January 1, 2026. That covers four pages, four names and one PIN certification, with extra pages at $2.00 and extra names at $0.50.

Where is the Lehigh County Recorder of Deeds?

The office is in Room 122 of the courthouse at 455 W. Hamilton Street in Allentown. It is open weekdays from 8:00 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon, and the number is 610-782-3162.

Can I get a certified copy of a Lehigh County deed online?

No. Certified copies are not available online and must be made at the office, at $1.50 more per document than a regular copy. Regular copies cost $0.50 per page in person.

How far back do Lehigh County records go?

The records start in 1812, when the county was formed. LANDEX covers index, deed, mortgage, map and miscellaneous records from 1812 to the present.

Are Lehigh County deeds recorded the same day?

Electronic filings through Simplifile, CSC or ePN are usually recorded the same day. Paper filings depend on the queue, and a rejected paper filing costs $10.00.

Northampton County by the numbers

Where do Northampton County deeds get recorded?

The Recorder of Deeds works from Room L116 of the county government center at 669 Washington Street in Easton. Phone 610-829-6210. Staff are at the counter until half past four, but a recording that needs a parcel certification must be in by 4:00 p.m.

The division records, images and stores deeds, mortgages and other real estate papers filed in the county. Each document gets a volume and page reference, then it is imaged and made available for viewing and copying. It also collects the fees and taxes on property transfers and passes them along.

Sellers reach this office at the end of the transaction. The title company gets the deed signed, carries it to Easton, and the recording puts the buyer's name on the public record. Most deeds need a parcel certification, so a courier who shows up at 4:15 may be told to come back tomorrow.

What are the Northampton County recording fees?

Filing a deed runs $76.25 on the schedule that began December 1, 2025. The price assumes four pages and four names at most, with parcel certification added on top.
