Notations beyond the first cost $2 each on mortgage documents. A land contract or article of agreement must carry a Certificate of Residence. Notary commissions and bonds cost $33.50 and are taken in cash, money order or a business check only.

What does Butler County charge to copy records?

Mail requests for record books or instrument numbers cost $1 per page, while a certificate and seal of office is $1.50. A service fee of $2 applies per document when you supply the book and page, and $4 per document when you do not. Plan book copies by mail run $2 per page, and an Act 287 search costs $2 per township.

  • Maps and plans: $45 covers page one, then $40 for each page after.
  • Highway plans: $15 covers page one, then $3 for every page after.
  • GRID setup: $7 per name.

These charges matter to sellers who need a copy of an old easement or plat for a title company. Order by instrument number when you can, since the lower service fee applies when the book and page are known.

What transfer tax applies when a Butler County house sells?

Pennsylvania imposes a 1% state realty transfer tax on the value of real estate transferred by deed, and the county recorder collects any local tax with it. State revenue officials hold the grantor and grantee jointly liable for the tax. Ask the Butler County Recorder of Deeds for the total rate that applies to your municipality and school district before you price the sale.

Some transfers escape the tax, such as certain family conveyances, transfers to government units, and property passed by will or intestacy. A deed that reflects one of those exemptions needs the state's Statement of Value to explain it. The county also posts a Common Level Ratio Factor for each July 1 to June 30 period. Its page lists the earlier factor of 16.67 for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026.

How do Butler County tax sales touch a seller?

The Tax Claim Bureau runs an Upset Sale on the second Monday of September for properties two years behind on taxes. A buyer at that sale takes on past due taxes, liens and mortgages. Properties that fail to sell move to a Judicial Sale, where bidding starts at costs plus deed recording and transfer fees and the property is sold free and clear if all parties were properly notified.

Anything still unsold goes to the Repository List. A bidder there fills out a bid form, and the Bureau presents the highest bid to the three taxing districts for approval.

The Bureau is at 124 West Diamond Street, with a mailing address at P.O. Box 1208, and its phone is 724-284-5326. It is open Monday through Friday, opening at half past eight and closing at 4 p.m. An owner behind on taxes should call there before the September sale.

Which place name goes on a Butler County deed?

Use the legal municipality, which is often a township, and not the mailing-address village. Butler is the only city in the county. Communities such as Renfrew, Lyndora, Herman, Sarver, Cabot, Boyers and Forestville have their own post offices and zip codes but lie entirely inside townships, so a deed that names the village instead of the township can point the recorder, the assessor and the school district at the wrong place.

  • Take the municipality and school district from the latest tax bill, not from a listing.
  • Match every owner name to the prior deed, since names over four add $1 each.
  • Count pages before you sign, because each page past four adds $2.

Eight counties touch Butler County, among them Allegheny, Armstrong, Lawrence and Venango. A parcel near a boundary belongs to one county only, so confirm the county of record before you send a package.

What should Butler County homeowners know about the area?

Butler County covers 795 square miles north of Pittsburgh, was created from Allegheny County on March 12, 1800, and is named for Revolutionary War General Richard Butler. The city of Butler is the seat, and Cranberry Township is the largest township. The 2020 census counted 193,763 residents, and an estimate for 2025 stands at 200,169.

History here includes John Roebling's wire rope works at Saxonburg and the Jeep, which American Bantam developed in the county in 1941. Moraine State Park, with its 3,000-acre Lake Arthur, draws weekend traffic. The Allegheny River touches the northeast and southeast corners, and the county's climate is humid continental, with July averages near 72 degrees in the borough of Butler.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a median value of $294,200 for owner-occupied homes, median household income of $89,843 and a 76.9% owner rate. The county issued 1,246 building permits in 2025. Public school districts include Butler Area, Seneca Valley, Mars Area, Knoch, Moniteau and Slippery Rock Area, among others. Main roads are I-79, I-76, I-80, US 19 and US 422.

More questions about Butler County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the base fee to record a deed in Butler County?

The base fee is $87.75 for a deed, mortgage or re-recorded deed that has four names, four pages and one parcel. Names over four cost $1 each, pages over four cost $2 each and extra parcels cost $0.50 each. The fee started on November 19, 2025.

Where is the Butler County Recorder of Deeds?

The office is in the Government Center, Floor L, at 124 West Diamond Street in Butler. Phone 724-284-5340. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1208, Butler, PA 16003.

Do I need a Certificate of Residence in Butler County?

Yes for an article of agreement or an installment land contract, which the county says must carry one. The base fee for either document is $59.75 for four pages. Pages over four are $2 each and names over four are $1 each.

Who collects transfer tax on a Butler County sale?

The county Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording. The state rate is 1% of the value, and local taxes can add to that. Ask the office for the rate for your municipality and school district.

When is the Butler County upset tax sale?

The Upset Sale is held on the second Monday of each September. It covers properties that are two years delinquent. Unsold properties move to a Judicial Sale and then to the Repository List.

Centre County by the numbers

What does the Centre County Recorder of Deeds handle?

The Bellefonte office records the deeds, mortgages and related papers for every parcel in Centre County, and it acts as the county's agent for realty transfer tax. Its stated mission is to record, protect, preserve and reproduce the legal documents that relate to real estate here.

Official county land records begin in 1800, the year Centre County was formed. The office also records notary commissions, oaths and veterans' discharge papers, and it collects fees for the Affordable Housing Fund and the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts. Each year it sends transfer tax checks averaging more than $5.6 million to 37 political subdivisions and six school districts. More than 10,000 people visit in person each year.

Where is the office and what are its hours?

The Recorder of Deeds is in the Willowbank Office Building, 414 Holmes Street, Suite 1, Bellefonte, PA 16823. The phone number on the county page is 814-355-6801, and the office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

  • Documents are accepted as close to 5 p.m. as practical, and there are no Saturday or evening hours.
  • Papers can be mailed in, provided every recording requirement is met and the correct fee is enclosed.
  • A deed that still needs its UPI can be sent straight to the Assessment Office, which stamps it and forwards it to the recorder.
  • E-recording runs through Simplifile and CSC.

Return time is usually one to two days, though holidays, volume and staffing can stretch it. The county advises contacting whoever recorded the paper if nothing has arrived after three weeks.

How much does recording cost in Centre County?

A deed or mortgage costs $71.25 for four pages and four names, per the county fee bill, with $2 for each added page and $0.50 for each added name. Fees are set by the Commonwealth through the General Assembly and can change.

Centre County recorder fee bill (source: Centre County Recorder of Deeds)

Photocopy, per page$0.50

Cash, check or card is accepted for recording fees. Card payments add $3.99 or 2.95% of the transaction, whichever is higher.

What is the transfer tax in Centre County, and does State College pay more?

Yes. The county's tax page sets 1% for the state and 1% local on the consideration or value, except in State College Borough at 3%, Ferguson Township at 2.75% and Taylor Township at 1.5%. The state share goes to the Department of Revenue, and the local share splits between the municipality and the school district.

The office will not accept a deed without the tax due. In most sales agreements the buyer and seller divide the tax equally, yet the new owner answers for any shortfall if the amount paid is questioned. Unlike some counties, Centre County does not require separate checks for the state and local shares, and all checks are payable to the Centre County Recorder of Deeds.

For a house near Penn State's University Park campus, the municipality can move the tax bill by thousands of dollars on the same price, so confirm the borough or township before you set a net figure.

Which transfers are exempt, and when is a Statement of Value required?

The county names conveyances between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and brothers and sisters as exempt, and a transfer between ex-spouses is exempt too. Most nonprofit corporations are not. For anything unusual the office suggests asking an attorney.

A Statement of Value is a state form that sets the value of a property or explains why tax is not owed. The office forwards each one to the Department of Revenue for review. It is required whenever the true value is not shown on the deed, such as a $1 consideration, or when tax is not paid at recording. The county's own checklist adds that an exemption claim not based on family relationship must state its reason, and a deed on land in more than one municipality must show the local tax split in dollars.

How do I get a copy of a Centre County deed or check who owns a parcel?

Every paper recorded in the office is public except military discharges, so anyone can look at a deed or mortgage. A copy sent by request costs $0.50 per page, plus $1.50 if you want it certified, and the request should include a self-addressed stamped envelope. Give the full owner name, the property location and an approximate purchase date. A certified copy of a deed stands in for a lost original.

The county also runs an online subscription portal, WEBIA, that covers the recorder, register of wills, tax claim and maps. Records recorded before 1989 sit in separate Deed, Mortgage and Miscellaneous books, and everything since 1989 is in Record Books, which matters when a title searcher asks for a book and page.

Staff will not run a search for you or prepare a deed. If a surviving spouse owned the home as tenants by the entireties, nothing usually needs to be recorded at death, because the survivor explains the death in the next deed or mortgage. Other ownership forms can need different handling, so check with an attorney.

What mistakes get a Centre County document rejected?

The county lists ten instructions for filers, and most failures trace back to names, notary blocks or the UPI.

  • Names in the caption, signature block and acknowledgment must match exactly. Variants like John J. Doe and J Joseph Doe cause rejections.
  • The acknowledgment must show county, state, date, the person or officer appearing, and the notary's signature, seal and expiration date. It should not predate the document date.
  • The written amount must match the numeric amount on deeds and mortgages.
  • Every deed needs a pre-authorized UPI from the Centre County Assessment Office before it is recorded. Call 814-355-6721 with questions.
  • List the property's municipality, and every one if there are several.
  • Leave a one-inch by three-inch space for the recorder's stamp at the top of page one.
  • Include a self-addressed, postage-paid envelope big enough for the return.

What should Centre County sellers know about the local market?

Centre County is home to the State College metropolitan area, with Bellefonte as the seat and State College as the largest borough. Census Bureau figures put the 2025 population at 157,393 across about 1,109 square miles, with a 2020 density of 142.7 people per square mile. The 2020 to 2024 median value of owner-occupied homes is $323,500, and only 61.8% of homes are owner-occupied.

Median household income runs $74,291 and median gross rent is $1,207. Public school districts include State College Area, Bellefonte Area, Bald Eagle Area, Penns Valley Area, Philipsburg-Osceola Area, Keystone Central and Tyrone Area, so a seller in one township may be dealing with a different school district tax than a neighbor a few miles away. The county's Common Level Ratio was listed at 6.10 as of July 1, 2026.

More questions about Centre County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Do Centre County buyers and sellers need separate transfer tax checks?

No. The county's FAQ says it is not necessary to present separate checks for state and local transfer tax. All checks are payable to the Centre County Recorder of Deeds, and the office accepts cash or check for fees.

How much is the transfer tax in State College?

State College Borough is listed at 3% of the consideration or value, compared with 1% state plus 1% local in most of the county. Ferguson Township is 2.75% and Taylor Township is 1.5%.

Can I record a deed without a UPI in Centre County?

No. Every deed needs a UPI issued by the Centre County Assessment Office, sold as a $10.00 stamp, before it can be recorded. A separate check payable to the County of Centre covers it.

Can the Recorder of Deeds change a deed that is already recorded?

No. Once recorded, a document cannot be altered. A new deed showing the change has to be recorded, and a wrong name or description is usually fixed with a deed of correction prepared by an attorney.

Do I have to record a deed at all in Centre County?

A signed and delivered deed is valid, but recording protects the buyer. If it is left off the record, the former owner could still borrow against the property, and tax bills may keep going to the old owner.

Monroe County by the numbers

How do you contact the Monroe County recording office?

Look for Room 106 of the Administration Building at One Quaker Plaza in Stroudsburg. The main number is 570-517-3969. Doors open at 8:30 in the morning and close at 4:30 in the afternoon on weekdays, with major holidays off.

Walk-in recording and title searches are available, though the county says appointments are strongly encouraged because space is limited. Packages can also arrive by post, or electronically through Simplifile, CSC and EPN. Its record books begin in 1836, the year Monroe County was formed from parts of Northampton and Pike counties, and filings made since August 1995 sit on the Landex system.

Beyond the recording fee itself, the office collects realty transfer tax for the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue and for every municipality and school district in the county. It also collects for the Monroe County Affordable Housing Agency, the Commonwealth Court Computer Automation fund, the Equal Access to Justice program and an archive fund for historical preservation of the land records.

A fax line is also listed, 570-517-3873. The Recorder also runs a free Record Alert System, which sends a notice whenever a document is filed under the subscriber's name. An owner who wants to know about any filing against a property can sign up for it.

What does the Monroe County fee bill charge to file a deed?

A deed or mortgage costs $87.75 under the fee bill that took effect November 17, 2025 and was revised the next day with no fee increase. The bill adds $2.00 for each page over four, $0.50 for each name over four, and $10.00 for each tax code number on a document.

Source: Monroe County Recorder of Deeds fee bill. Realty transfer tax is listed as 1 percent state and 1 percent local.

The bill also sets payment rules. It turns away personal checks, demands the exact amount because the office makes no change and gives no refunds, and adds a $2.00 charge to any document that is rejected. Include a postage-paid return envelope so originals can come back.

What must a Monroe County deed contain before the Recorder will accept it?

The county wants an original that is signed, dated and acknowledged in front of a notary, showing the notary's seal, signature and expiration date. Fees and transfer taxes are all due the moment the deed is presented.

  • A tax code number for the parcel.
  • A property description that names the municipality.
  • Payment of the transfer tax. If the tax is unpaid or the deed does not show true value, as with a $1.00 deed, a Statement of Value goes in as two copies and the county forwards it to the state.
  • A return envelope with postage already on it.

Staff will not draft a deed for anyone. Once recorded, a deed stays as written, so adding a spouse or fixing an error means recording a new deed or a deed of correction. Originals go back to the buyer, and mortgages go to the lender. On the lender side, Act 197 lets a satisfaction piece be recorded without the original mortgage or a certified copy of it.

Who pays transfer tax on a Monroe County sale?

The state share and the municipal share are 1 percent apiece, applied to the property's value, which the county warns can differ from the sale price. Contracts often split the bill between the two sides. Even so, a deed is turned away unless the tax is paid when it is presented, and the new owner carries the risk if the amount is questioned later.

The county FAQ lists the family exemptions as a husband and wife, from parent to child, from grandparent to grandchild, and among brothers and sisters, and it adds deeds between former spouses. Non-profit corporations get no break. State revenue guidance also exempts deeds handed to government units and property that passes by inheritance.

A state investigator can decide that a property was worth more than the value stated, or that a claimed exemption fails. The Department then mails the owner a determination. Extra tax and interest are paid to the state, a matching municipal sum is paid at the recorder's office, and the deed is recorded again for regular fees.

What happens to unpaid Monroe County property tax?

Delinquent real estate taxes go to the Monroe County Tax Claim Bureau, which handles 20 municipalities and four school districts and receives about 9,000 delinquent returns a year. It was created when Act 542 of 1947, the Pennsylvania Real Estate Tax Sale Law, took effect, with the aim of putting tax-delinquent properties back on the productive rolls.

The bureau is down the hall in Room 104 of the same building, at 570-517-3172, and works weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30. Its page offers a lien certificate, which a seller with overdue taxes should request so the closing agent can see what must come out of the proceeds. Counter payments can be made with a money order, a cashier's check or a card, and repository sales run through Bid4Assets.

Anyone behind on taxes should call the bureau before listing, because the balance has to be settled as part of any sale.

What does the Pocono setting mean for a Monroe County seller?

Stroudsburg is the county seat of this Pocono county in northeast Pennsylvania, which the 2020 census put at 168,327 people. It borders Northampton County and the Lehigh Valley to the south, the Delaware River and New Jersey to the east, and Pike, Wayne, Carbon and Luzerne counties on its other sides. About 608 square miles are land.

The county grew fast in the late twentieth century as New York commuters and Pocono tourism arrived, and the 2020 census listed 79,114 housing units, 21.3 percent of them vacant. About three in four occupied homes (76.6 percent) had an owner living in them.

Public schools run through four districts: East Stroudsburg Area, Pleasant Valley, Pocono Mountain and Stroudsburg Area. Interstates 80 and 380 are the main highways, and East Stroudsburg University anchors the town of the same name. Part of the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area, a park of nearly 70,000 acres, lies inside the county, and the Appalachian Trail runs along its southern edge. The Monroe County Transit Authority, known locally as the Pocono Pony, runs fixed bus routes.

More questions about Monroe County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the Monroe County deed recording fee?

A deed or mortgage starts at $87.75. The bill adds $2.00 for every page past four, $0.50 for every name past four, and $10.00 for each tax code number on the document.

Can I pay a Monroe County recording fee with a personal check?

No. The fee bill rules out personal checks and requires the exact amount, with no change or refunds. Ask the office which payment forms it takes before sending a package.

Does Monroe County take e-recording?

Yes. Simplifile, CSC and EPN are the three e-recording routes the county lists, and paper still works by post or at the Stroudsburg counter.

Which Monroe County deeds are exempt from transfer tax?

Family deeds between spouses, down the line from parent or grandparent, or among brothers and sisters are exempt, and so are deeds between ex-spouses. Non-profit corporations are not exempt. For any other case the county advises talking to an attorney.

Who collects overdue Monroe County property tax?

The Tax Claim Bureau, Room 104 at One Quaker Plaza in Stroudsburg. Its counter takes money orders, cashier's checks and cards, and the bureau can issue a lien certificate for a sale.

Schuylkill County by the numbers

What is the first thing Schuylkill County needs before it records a deed?

A tax parcel certification stamp from the Tax Assessment Office. The county requires that stamp on deeds, mortgages, easements, rights of way, land leases and several other instruments, and it has to be completed before the Recorder of Deeds will accept the paper.

The Tax Assessment Office charges its own fee for the stamp, $20 per instrument according to the county Recorder of Deeds page. Questions about the certification go to the assessment office at 570-628-1025. This step is separate from the recording fee and from realty transfer tax, so a seller or closing agent should expect three different amounts on a Schuylkill County deed.

The county also recommends e-recording, which folds the recorder and assessment steps into one submission. That saves postage and avoids the rejection charge described below.

How can I pay the Schuylkill County recorder?

Not with a personal check. Since 2016 the office has refused personal and personal business checks. The list of what it does accept is short.

  • A check from a law firm
  • A certified bank check
  • A money order
  • Cash

Payment goes to "Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds." If a document is rejected for any reason and was sent by mail, UPS or FedEx, the office charges a $3 rejection and return fee, and the sender must include a self-addressed stamped envelope of adequate size for the return. E-recording avoids that charge entirely.

The office also states plainly what it will not do. It does not supply forms, help prepare legal documents, notarize anything, run real estate searches, certify that a property is free and clear or give legal advice. If you need a title search, that comes from a title company or attorney.

How do I get a copy of a Schuylkill County deed?

Mail or courier a written request that gives the exact book and page number and the year of the document. The office does not search for documents and does not do genealogy research, so a request without those details cannot be filled.

For each document under 40 pages the county charges $8.50 for an uncertified copy and $10.00 for a certified copy. Enclose a self-addressed envelope of adequate size with prepaid postage. The online land records database at uslandrecords.com is the better route when you only know the owner's name, but it needs a computer, internet access and a credit card to pay for printed pages.

What transfer tax applies when a Schuylkill County house sells?

The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value of the property, and Pennsylvania's Department of Revenue makes the grantor and grantee jointly liable. County recorders collect it, often alongside a local transfer tax shared between the municipality and the school district.

The local portion depends on where the house sits in the county, from Pottsville to the smaller boroughs and townships. Ask the recorder or your closing agent for the combined percentage on your deed before closing day, so the settlement sheet matches what the office will collect.

The Department of Revenue also exempts a list of transfers, including certain transfers between family members, transfers to government units and property passing by will or intestate succession. A house inherited in Schuylkill County therefore moves to the heirs without that tax, but a sale by the heirs afterward is a new transfer.

Why does the Schuylkill County reassessment matter to a seller?

Schuylkill County's last countywide reassessment before this one dated to 1996. Property owners sued in 2018, arguing that assessments no longer met the uniformity requirement in the state constitution, and the county signed a consent decree on May 16, 2022 that committed it to a new countywide assessment.

The county's reassessment page describes a vendor, Vision Government Services, collecting property data in the field and appraising every parcel with computer-assisted mass appraisal. Its stated schedule had notices mailed on or before July 1, 2025, a formal appeal route to the Schuylkill County Board of Assessment Appeals, and new assessed values taking effect January 1, 2026.

For someone selling, the practical point is that the tax bill a buyer will pay can differ from the bill you paid in earlier years. If your assessment changed, read the notice, and ask the Tax Assessment Office how the new value applies to your parcel before you promise a buyer a tax figure.

What kind of county is Schuylkill, and who lives in it?

Schuylkill County was created on March 1, 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton counties and takes its name from the Schuylkill River, which starts here. Pottsville is the county seat and only city. Anthracite coal was found near Pottsville in 1790, and the county sits in northeastern Pennsylvania's Coal Region. Population peaked at 235,505 in 1930 and has drifted down since, with 143,049 counted in 2020.

The county covers 783 square miles and borders eight other counties. Blue Mountain and the Appalachian Trail lie to the south, Broad Mountain crosses the middle, and the eastern edge around Tamaqua reaches the Poconos. Interstate 81, US 209 and PA 61 are among the main routes, and the county sits about 97 miles northwest of Philadelphia.

  • Population estimate, July 1, 2025: 145,085, up 1.4 percent from the 2020 base
  • Housing units, July 1, 2025: 67,679
  • Owner-occupied rate, 2020 to 2024: 76.1 percent
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $153,000
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $876
  • Median household income, 2020 to 2024: $68,313
  • Mean travel time to work: 27.3 minutes

These figures come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for Schuylkill County. Median home value of $153,000 sits well below the Pike County figure of $272,600, which is the clearest sign of how different the two northeastern counties are for sellers.

What should a Schuylkill County seller check before the deed is signed?

Begin with the parcel stamp, because a deed without it cannot be recorded. Then confirm the payment method: if the closing agent hands you a personal check for the recording office, expect it to be refused.

Look at the paperwork next. A seller with a vacant or inherited house may be facing repairs, back taxes and an unclear title at the same time. Gather the prior deed, any mortgage satisfaction and the latest tax notices. If heirs share ownership, every owner of record has to sign.

Finally, ask the title company who will submit the deed. Electronic submission through the county's recommended route is quicker, and the recorder confirms the recording by book and page, which you should keep with your closing papers.

More questions about Schuylkill County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Does Schuylkill County accept personal checks for recording?

No. The recorder has refused personal and personal business checks since 2016. It accepts law firm checks, certified bank checks, money orders and cash, made payable to Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds.

What is the parcel certification stamp?

It is a tax parcel ID certification the Tax Assessment Office applies before a deed or mortgage can be recorded. The assessment office charges $20 per instrument. Call 570-628-1025 with questions.

What happens if my document is rejected?

A mailed or courier submission that is rejected for any reason incurs a $3 rejection and return fee. You must also supply a self-addressed stamped envelope. E-recording avoids the fee.

How much does a copy of a recorded deed cost?

$8.50 for an uncertified copy and $10.00 for a certified copy, for documents under 40 pages. Send a written request with the book and page number, the year and a prepaid return envelope.

Is there transfer tax on an inherited house in Schuylkill County?

Title passing by will or intestate succession is exempt from Pennsylvania realty transfer tax. If the heirs then sell, that sale deed is taxed at the state rate of 1 percent plus any local tax, unless another exemption applies.

What fees come with filing a Lebanon County deed?

A standard deed or mortgage costs $91.75 to record under the fee schedule that took effect November 12, 2025. That base price covers up to four pages and four names, and it already contains the affordable housing fee, the records improvement fee, the parcel identifier fee and the court and access-to-justice surcharges, so those do not show up as separate line items.

A few smaller charges can matter on a sale:

  • A Statement of Value that has attachments adds $2.00 for each attachment page. The duplicate copy for the state carries no charge.
  • Sending a document by email to the office costs $5.00 plus $0.50 for each page.
  • A returned check costs $30.00.
  • Copies run $0.50 per page on sheets up to tabloid size, and oversized pages add $5.00.

The office takes cash or checks only. Write the check to the Recorder of Deeds for the exact amount, because fees and transfer taxes must be paid when the document is presented.

What does a Lebanon County deed need before the office will record it?

The deed must show a Uniform Parcel Identifier, called a UPI, on page one, and that number must be certified by the county Assessment Office. The certification happens electronically inside the courthouse. If you do not have the number, call Assessment at 717-228-4425 or use the county property viewer to look the parcel up by address.

The county's recording instructions add several other requirements:

  • A signed certificate of residence for the grantee on every deed, and for the mortgagee on every mortgage or assignment.
  • Type no smaller than 10 point, and a legal acknowledgment before a notary.
  • A typed English translation attached to any document written in another language.
  • Page numbers or numbering that shows the filing order when several documents belong to one transaction.
  • Where a parcel straddles two or more municipalities or school districts, the percentage lying in each, so the local levy can be split.
  • A return envelope, addressed and stamped, big enough to carry the originals home.

A Statement of Value, the state's REV-183 form, is filed in duplicate with its attachments. It is required when the deed does not state the full price, when the transfer is a gift or has no consideration, when an exemption is claimed, and when the property was sold at a tax claim or sheriff sale. The county notes that a statement is not needed when full consideration is paid, when the transfer is between close family members, or when the grant is an easement to a public utility. Fill in every block, sign it, and date it with the settlement or acceptance date.

How much realty transfer tax is due on a Lebanon County sale?

The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of a property's value, paid at the counter with the filing fee. Per the state revenue department, grantor and grantee answer for it jointly. A local levy rides on top, divided between the school district and municipality that cover the house. Call the office or your settlement agent to learn the combined percentage for your street address.

Exemptions cover some family transfers, inheritance by will or intestacy, and government transfers. Anyone claiming one is pointed to the state rules, and the REV-183 must lay out the basis. The county FAQ also gives Lebanon County's assessed ratio, known as the common level ratio, as 1.39 percent that also appears on the Statement of Value.

In a typical sale the settlement agent works out the tax and delivers a check. The purchase agreement says which side absorbs the cost.

How long does recording take, and can I record electronically?

According to the county, most filings are back with their owners the next business day, by pickup, mail or electronic return. Each document is received, reviewed and keyed in, sent to Assessment to certify the UPI, returned for recording, and then proofread. Documents are recorded in the order they arrive, so a heavy day can lengthen the wait.

Electronic recording is accepted through Simplifile, CSC and ePN, three vendors the office lists by name, and confirmation can come back in minutes. A mailed filing needs a check for the exact amount plus the return envelope.

Landex, the county's records vendor, also runs record alerts tied to a parcel number. Owners of a rental house or of a home left empty after an inheritance may want to ask the Recorder of Deeds how to sign up.

How do I look up deeds and mortgages recorded in Lebanon County?

Lebanon County was established in 1813, and its recorded documents from 1925 to the present can be searched online through Landex. Anything older has to be viewed at the office in Room 107. Anyone may view the records, with one exception: military discharge papers (DD214 forms) are kept private. Veterans can record a DD214 for free and may get a Veterans ID Card.

Phone help is limited, because the office is not insured for title searching. Plan to do your own search online, or hire a title company if the chain of ownership is complicated. A deed describes the land and not the buildings on it, so adding a house to a lot does not produce a new deed.

Notary commissions are handled in the same office. The notary fee is $42.00, which includes the Prothonotary fee, paid by one check payable to the Recorder of Deeds.

What is the Lebanon County setting like for a home sale?

Lebanon County covers 362 square miles in south central Pennsylvania, about 72 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It was cut from Dauphin and Lancaster counties in 1813, and the city of Lebanon serves as seat and biggest town. Census figures show 143,257 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 146,380 for 2025.

Swatara Creek drains most of the valley toward the Susquehanna, while Tulpehocken Creek near Myerstown runs east toward the Schuylkill. Interstates 78 and 81, the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76), and US 22, 322 and 422 all pass through. Dauphin, Lancaster, Berks and Schuylkill counties border it.

  • Larger communities by 2010 count: Lebanon, Palmyra, Cornwall, Myerstown and Cleona.
  • Colleges: Lebanon Valley College, Evangelical Seminary and the Lebanon campus of Harrisburg Area Community College.
  • Climate: a humid continental pattern, with Lebanon city averages near 29 degrees in January and 74 in July.

Whether a house sits in Lebanon city, a borough such as Palmyra, or a township changes which municipality and school district receive the local transfer tax, so confirm your municipality before you estimate closing costs.

More questions about Lebanon County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the base deed fee in Lebanon County?

Under the schedule effective November 12, 2025, the base fee is $91.75 and includes up to four names over four pages. Each extra page costs $4.00 and each extra name $1.00. The county accepts cash or check only.

Does Lebanon County require a parcel number on a deed?

Yes. The Uniform Parcel Identifier belongs on the first page and must be certified by the Assessment Office. Call 717-228-4425 to get the number for your property.

Can I record a Lebanon County deed by email or mail?

Mail works with an exact-amount check and a stamped envelope for the return. Email submission is accepted for $5.00 plus $0.50 per page, and electronic recording through Simplifile, CSC or ePN is also available.

How soon will my recorded deed come back?

Most documents are returned the next business day. The wait depends on how many documents were filed ahead of yours, since the office records in order of arrival.

Who owes transfer tax on a Lebanon County sale?

Seller and buyer both answer to the state for it, and the tax is payable at the counter at filing. Who bears the cost in practice is set by the sales contract, so check it with your closing agent.

Franklin County by the numbers

Who records deeds in Franklin County, Pennsylvania?

The Franklin County Register & Recorder records them, from the Administration Building at 272 North Second Street in Chambersburg, PA 17201. The phone is 717-261-3872 and the fax is 717-709-7211.

One office wears several hats. Besides land records, deeds and mortgages, it handles probate for executors and administrators, records military discharges, and acts as the collection agent for the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue on state realty transfer tax and inheritance tax.

Franklin County was carved out of Cumberland County in 1784 and named for Benjamin Franklin. A deed signed at a Franklin County closing finishes its trip here, where it becomes part of the land record searched by every later buyer, lender and title agent.

How can a deed be submitted in Franklin County?

The county accepts deeds by e-recording through Simplifile, CSC or EPN, by mail, or in person at the Chambersburg office. Department hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, and the office is closed on weekends and county-observed holidays.

Searching is done remotely through Landex, and questions about that system go to 717-274-5890. Probate filings are by appointment only, which does not apply to recording.

  • E-recording: Simplifile, CSC or EPN, with electronic rejection notices that explain the reason.
  • Mail or overnight delivery: rejected documents come back unrecorded with a written explanation.
  • In person: the clerk reviews the document at the counter before it is accepted.

In each case the county scans the document and sends it to the Tax Assessment Office for UPI certification, then it comes back to the recorder for recording. The UPI stamp prints on the ending page. A document with a missing or wrong parcel number is returned with a note on what to fix.

What does it cost to record a deed in Franklin County?

A deed or a mortgage is $92.75 on the schedule posted for July 2026, and every document is priced at four pages and four names. The listed fees already include one UPI certification, and each extra certification adds $20.00.

Franklin County Recorder of Deeds fees for common home-sale documents
DocumentFee
Deed$92.75
Deed of distribution (Statement of Value required)$92.75
Mortgage$92.75
Satisfaction of mortgage$81.75
Assignment$81.75
Easement (Statement of Value required)$79.75
Power of attorney to sell real estate$38.50
Statement of Value$1.00

Source: Franklin County Register & Recorder fee schedule on franklincountypa.gov.

Beyond those, each page past four costs $2.00 and each name past four costs $0.50. Copies are $0.25 per page, copies of subdivisions $0.50, and certification of a document $1.50. The posted schedule is also marked with a common level ratio of 13.89 for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.

How does realty transfer tax work on a Franklin County deed?

The county schedule states that a state tax of 1% and a local tax of the same amount are due at recording. Together that is 2% of the price, or of the assessed value where no price applies.

Every deed must either state the true consideration or carry a Statement of Value. If a full or partial exemption is claimed, the Statement of Value is mandatory unless the deed itself notes the exemption, and it must be fully completed. Corrective deeds and any deed recorded more than 30 days after signing also require one.

  • A deed of distribution from an estate requires a Statement of Value.
  • A property in two or more taxing districts must show the value in each district on the deed so the local share lands in the right place.
  • Pennsylvania lists family transfers, transfers by will or intestacy, and transfers to government units among the exempt categories.

The state's Department of Revenue says both grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable, so an unpaid tax can reach either side of a Franklin County sale.

What if the Franklin County house came through an estate?

The same office that records the deed also opens the estate, so an heir can handle both in Chambersburg. Probating requires an appointment, and the deed that moves title out of the estate is recorded as a deed of distribution with a Statement of Value attached.

The Register of Wills side of the posted schedule steps up with the size of the estate. Letters and probate run $30.00 for an estate up to $1,000 and $80.00 for one between $75,001 and $100,000, then $35.00 for each additional $100,000 or fraction. Surcharges apply at probate: a $5.00 automation fee and a $41.25 JCP fee.

  • Short certificates are $5.00 each, and a lender or bank often asks for one.
  • An inheritance tax return or supplemental return is $20.00.
  • Certification of inheritance tax paid is $5.00.
  • An inventory and appraisement is $10.00.

Because the county collects Pennsylvania inheritance tax through this office, an heir who intends to sell the inherited house can finish the estate paperwork and the recording at the same counter.

Which other recordings can matter when a Franklin County house sells?

A deed is the main document, but the schedule shows several others that turn up around a sale. Releasing a loan is recorded as a satisfaction or release of mortgage at $81.75, and a partial release costs the same.

Leases are $38.50 unless they run 30 years, which needs a Statement of Value and costs $79.75. A right of way is $78.75, an installment sales agreement $79.75, and a memorandum $38.50. Farm owners may also record an Ag Security Map at $35.00, and plans on 8.5 by 14 paper are $35.00.

A seller who had a prior mortgage should confirm that its satisfaction was recorded before closing, since a lien that was paid off but never released can still appear in a title search of the Franklin County land record.

Can a Franklin County owner get alerts when a document is recorded against a parcel?

Yes. The Recorder of Deeds offers a free Landex Record Alert that notifies an owner when a document carrying their parcel number is recorded or corrected. Sign-up is by email address or mobile number.

The service keys on the parcel number, which is 20 characters including dots and dashes and appears on a tax bill. The county describes the alert as a courtesy tool and adds that it does not replace an owner's own diligence, paid monitoring or a lawyer. Anyone who suspects fraud is told to contact local law enforcement quickly.

For a seller, the alert is a useful check before listing. An owner who signs up can see any mortgage, easement or release that gets recorded against the parcel while a sale is pending.

What do the Census numbers say about selling a house in Franklin County?

Franklin County is the fastest-growing of the four counties compared by Census QuickFacts, with an estimated 160,652 residents in July 2025, up 3.0% from the April 2020 base. The median owner-occupied home is worth $249,800 for 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 73.5% of housing.

Median household income is $77,003, poverty is 9.3%, and the county issued 1,033 building permits in 2025. Fayette County issued 196 that year, Huntingdon 64 and Indiana 40, so Franklin County leads the group in new building by a wide margin.

The county covers 772 square miles of land in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, mostly drained by the Potomac, with Chambersburg at its center. About 55.5% of residents lived in urban areas in 2020. Whoever sells a Franklin County house finishes at the Chambersburg office, so the deed paperwork above is the last item to confirm with the closing agent.

More questions about Franklin County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How much is the UPI certification in Franklin County?

The first certification is built into the listed recording fee, and each additional UPI certification is $20.00. A deed covering two parcels therefore adds $20.00 to the posted price.

Can I e-record a deed in Franklin County?

Yes. The Register & Recorder accepts e-recording through Simplifile, CSC or EPN, as well as mail and in-person submissions at the Chambersburg office.

What is the Statement of Value fee in Franklin County?

The Statement of Value is $1.00. It is required when a deed claims an exemption from transfer tax, when a deed is corrective or recorded after 30 days, and for deeds of distribution.

When is the Franklin County recorder open?

Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The office is closed on weekends and county-observed holidays. Probate filings need an appointment.

Who do I call about the Landex search system in Franklin County?

Call 717-274-5890 for Landex questions. The Register & Recorder's main line at 717-261-3872 handles recording, fees and probate appointments.

Fayette County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Fayette County, Pennsylvania?

Deeds for Fayette County property are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds office in the courthouse at 61 E Main Street in Uniontown, PA 15401. The office phone is 724-430-1238 and the fax is 724-430-1458.

Fayette County records go back to 1784, and the county's own FAQ explains that the area belonged to Westmoreland County before that. The same office also records mortgages, releases, satisfaction pieces, plans, powers of attorney, leases, notary bonds and military discharges (DD-214 forms are the one record that is not public).

For a seller, the recorder is the last stop. The deed signed at the closing table becomes the public record of the new owner only once this office stamps it, assigns an instrument number and a volume and page, and prints the recording time on every page.

What hours does the Fayette County Recorder of Deeds keep?

Weekday service runs 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., with the front counter shut from 12 to 1 daily. Recording itself runs 8 a.m. to noon and 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., so a deed that arrives during the lunch closure waits for the afternoon session.

  • Office hours: 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed 12 to 1.
  • Recording hours: 8 a.m. to noon and 1 p.m. to 4 p.m.
  • Veteran ID program: 10 a.m. to noon and 1 p.m. to 3 p.m.

Anyone sending a Fayette County closing package should plan to arrive well before 4 p.m. and to hold a payment ready, since the county states that all recording fees and transfer taxes are payable at the time of recording.

What must a deed show before the Fayette County recorder accepts it?

A deed needs a typed parcel number, a proper notary acknowledgment and correct tax paperwork, or it is sent back unrecorded. Fayette County's recording requirements page lists the rules, and most rejections come from small gaps in them.

  • A PIN (the tax assessment parcel number) must be typed on the first page, and the Tax Assessment Office issues a UPI number for it before the document is recorded.
  • The acknowledgment must name the county, state and date, the person or corporate officer appearing, and carry the notary's signature and commission expiration date. The acknowledgment date cannot come before the date of the document. An embossed seal is now optional.
  • The deed must name the municipality, county and state where the land sits.
  • The written dollar amount must match the numerals on every deed and mortgage.
  • Grantee, mortgagee and assignee need a mailing address with ZIP code.
  • Any document that points back to an earlier mortgage must cite its book and page numbers, not a document number alone.
  • A re-recorded document has to explain why it is being recorded again.

Typing or writing on a notary stamp is a violation of the Pennsylvania notary law according to the county, so a stamp that is smudged or altered is a common reason for a bounce. Every document also needs a printed name so it can be returned to the right attorney or title company, along with a self-addressed stamped envelope unless the office holds it for pickup.

What will the recorder charge for a Fayette County deed?

The total depends on the base fee for the document type plus add-ons, and the office will quote the current deed figure by phone at 724-430-1238. The fee schedule on the county website, last dated June 28, 2023, lists the add-ons that apply to a typical home sale.

Fayette County Recorder of Deeds add-on fees

Source: Fayette County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule PDF and recorder FAQ on fayettecountypa.org.

A parcel-by-parcel UPI charge matters on rural sales. A farm assembled from three tax parcels needs three PIN numbers certified, so the UPI line alone reaches $60 before the base fee.

How is realty transfer tax paid on a Fayette County sale?

The county's recording requirements say recording fees and realty transfer tax can go in one check made out to Fayette County Recorder of Deeds. The fee schedule describes the transfer tax as 1% state plus 1% local.

The deed has to state the price paid, or it must carry a Statement of Value that explains why no tax is due. An original goes into the document as a page and a duplicate goes to the state. Questions about the tax can be emailed to the Department of Revenue realty transfer tax division at ra-bitrealtytransfertax@pa.gov.

When a property lies in more than one local taxing district, the deed must show whole-number percentages for the division of the local share. The state's own page confirms that buyer and seller are both liable and that the recorder passes the 1% to the Department of Revenue.

How do you search Fayette County land records?

Index searches for most documents from 1950 to the present are free through the US Land Records site, while images are pay-per-access. Documents recorded before January 1, 2001 are also kept in books in the office, and public search stations in the Uniontown courthouse show the rest.

The recorder indexes by name, with the legal description and municipality, and not by street address. For an address or parcel lookup, the county sends people to the Tax Assessment property search or the Mapping Room, reachable at 724-430-1350, extension 229.

  • Archive Viewer indexes cover deeds and mortgages from 1950 to 1974, plans from 1791 to 1988 and agreements from 1854 to 1949.
  • Liens and judgments are not filed here. The Prothonotary on the first floor of the courthouse handles them at 724-430-1272.
  • Subdivision plans are recorded in this office, while zoning questions go to Planning, Zoning and Community Development on the fourth floor at 724-430-1210.

What do the numbers say about selling a house in Fayette County?

Fayette County has 790.76 square miles of land and an estimated 123,021 residents in 2025, down 4.5% from the April 2020 base, according to Census QuickFacts. Owners occupy 72.4% of homes, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $143,200.

Median household income is $58,236 and 14.7% of residents live in poverty. Only 196 building permits were issued in 2025, so little new construction competes with resale houses. The county was part of Westmoreland until 1783 and grew on coal, coke and steel, and the Census also shows a median gross rent of $793 for owners weighing a rental instead of a sale.

Uniontown, where the courthouse stands, anchors the county, and the National Road, the Monongahela and Youghiogheny valleys and the Connellsville Amtrak stop shape where homes cluster. A seller who wants a quick closing in Fayette County mainly needs a clean deed, a certified parcel number and a buyer whose title agent knows the Uniontown office schedule.

More questions about Fayette County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How much is the UPI fee in Fayette County?

The posted schedule shows $20.00 for each PIN number certified. A deed that covers two tax parcels therefore adds $40.00 to the recording bill.

Can I record a deed in Fayette County without a parcel number?

No. The county requires a PIN typed on the first page, and the Tax Assessment Office issues the UPI number before recording. A deed without it comes back unrecorded.

Can one check cover the recording fee and transfer tax in Fayette County?

Yes. The county's recording requirements allow fees and realty transfer tax in a single check payable to Fayette County Recorder of Deeds, as long as the amount is exact.

Does the Fayette County recorder search for liens?

No. The recorder does not file liens or judgments. Those go through the Prothonotary's office in the courthouse at 724-430-1272, while the recorder shows mortgages and whether they were satisfied.

Where do I get a copy of my recorded deed in Fayette County?

Visit the Uniontown office, where copies are $0.50 per page, or find the document through the US Land Records index. A certified copy costs $0.50 per page plus $3.00 for the certification.

Cambria County by the numbers

Where is the Cambria County Recorder of Deeds?

The office is on the first floor of the Cambria County Courthouse, 200 South Center Street, Ebensburg, PA 15931, and the phone is (814) 472-1473. Staff are in from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays, though recording stops at 3:30 p.m. sharp. The office also answers information requests by phone.

Records date to 1804. Documents from 1986 to the present are searchable online through the county's Tyler portal, the index for 1924 to 1985 is on a separate historical site, and anything older than 1924 is available only in the office. There is no subscription fee to view, and print or download costs $0.50 per page.

After recording, the office scans each document and hands it straight back. It accepts cash or checks payable to Recorder of Deeds, and staff will quote recording fees or copy prices if you call ahead. Military discharge papers are recorded and copied for veterans free of charge.

What does it cost to record a deed in Cambria County?

The county's current fee schedule is dated December 1, 2025 and is posted as a PDF on the recorder's page. The office quotes exact totals by phone, so call before you mail a package. Two surcharges are spelled out on the office's notices and apply to nearly every sale document.

Cambria County Recorder of Deeds charges named on the office's notices
ItemAmount or rule
Act 152 of 2016 fee on all deeds and mortgages$15.00, charged since March 1, 2017
Added charge since December 1, 2025$1.00 on deeds, mortgages, easements, satisfactions, assignments, leases, orders and similar documents

Why does a Cambria County deed need UPI approval?

Since August 1, 2016, the county's Assessment Office has to approve a Uniform Parcel Identifier certification before many documents can be recorded. The list covers deeds, decrees of distribution, awards of real estate, mortgages, rights of way, easements, leases, condemnations, declarations of taking, consents, assignments of leases and rents, sewage and water permits, highway occupancy permits, statements of adverse possession and boundary line agreements. The Recorder will not accept those papers without the approval.

The Assessment Office is at 200 South Center Street and its phone is (814) 472-1451. A UPI staff member sits in the Recorder's office, and approval is unavailable from 1:00 to 2:00 p.m. each day. The office urges closers to email documents ahead of time for pre-approval, using the UPI address on its page.

  • Send the deed to UPI review before the closing date, not on the day.
  • Keep the parcel description identical to the prior deed.
  • Avoid a closing slot that depends on approval between 1:00 and 2:00 p.m.

How do you e-record or pay transfer tax in Cambria County?

The office takes e-recording for certain document types through Simplifile, Indecomm Global Services, CSC Global and ePN. The recorder's page lists a phone number for each vendor. Paper originals can still be brought to the counter.

The Recorder also collects Pennsylvania realty transfer tax and distributes it. The state levies 1% of the value of the real estate, and local governments may add their own share, so ask the office for the combined rate that fits your municipality and school district. Some transfers are exempt, including certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy.

Both buyer and seller can be held liable for the tax, according to the state's Department of Revenue. Settle in the purchase agreement who pays it, and confirm that your closing agent has the funds in an accepted form.

What happens to Cambria County tax-delinquent houses?

The county Tax Claim office collects delinquent school, municipal and county real estate taxes and runs the tax sales. Its phone is (814) 472-1445, and it sits at 200 South Center Street. The Judicial Tax Sale for 2026 was scheduled for Monday, October 12, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. in Courtroom 1, with bidder registration ending October 2.

Since April 1, 2025, a $250.00 fee has been added to the costs of every property sold at an upset, judicial, private or repository sale, under Cambria County Ordinance 5 of 2024. Private sales are capped at 50 properties, and each bidder may list up to four per sale. For the 2025 tax year and later, delinquent school taxes in Cambria Township, Ebensburg Borough and Jackson Township, the Central Cambria School District, are collected by Portnoff Law Associates, at (866) 211-9466.

A seller who owes back taxes should get a certification from the Tax Claim office, and the office takes certification orders online. Ask the Tax Claim office what is owed for each tax year before you set a closing date.

Who handles assessments and homestead filings in Cambria County?

The Cambria County Assessment Office, in the courthouse at 200 South Center Street, keeps property records and values real estate for taxation. It does not set millage or collect taxes. The county is a fourth-class county under the General County Assessment Law, and the phone is (814) 472-1451 with hours of 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.

The same office runs the Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion program under Acts 50 and 1 and the Clean and Green preferential assessment program under Act 319. It posts an appeal form, appeal board rules, millage rates and a homestead application for 2026, along with the schedules for the 2026 appeal hearings. Sellers who plan to appeal before listing should read the board rules first.

  • Assessment Office: values property and takes appeals.
  • Tax Claim office: collects delinquent taxes and holds tax sales.
  • Recorder of Deeds: records the deed and collects transfer tax.

What is Cambria County like for a home seller?

Cambria County is an older industrial county in the Appalachian Regional Commission area, and its home prices run far below the state's suburban counties. It covers 694 square miles, was created in 1804 and organized in 1807, and takes its name from the Latin word for Wales. Ebensburg is the seat, and Johnstown, the home of the old Cambria Iron Company, is the largest city.

Population peaked at 213,459 in 1940 and was 133,472 in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 128,968. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 data show a median home value of $121,000, median household income of $58,418, median gross rent of $739 and an owner rate of 76.4%. Residents 65 and older make up 26.2% of the population, and 14.5% live in poverty.

Main roads are US 22, US 219 and US 422, plus PA 36, PA 56 and PA 53. Prince Gallitzin State Park and the trailhead of Laurel Ridge State Park are in the county. Winters are cold, with average January temperatures near 28 degrees in Johnstown and 24 in Ebensburg.

More questions about Cambria County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What time does the Cambria County Recorder of Deeds stop recording?

Recording stops at 3:30 p.m. on weekdays, even though the office stays open until 4:00 p.m. The office opens at 9:00 a.m. Monday through Friday. Plan the deed to arrive well before the cutoff.

Does Cambria County charge an extra fee on deeds?

Yes. A $15.00 fee applies to all deeds and mortgages under Act 152 of 2016, in place since March 1, 2017. Since December 1, 2025 an added $1.00 applies to deeds, mortgages, easements and many other documents.

Where can I search Cambria County deeds online?

Records from 1986 to now are on the county's Tyler web portal, linked from the recorder's page. The 1924 to 1985 index is on SearchIQS. Records before 1924 are available only in the office, and printing costs $0.50 per page.

Does a deed in Cambria County need approval before recording?

Yes. Since August 1, 2016 the Assessment Office has to approve the UPI for deeds, mortgages, easements, leases and similar documents. Approval is not offered from 1:00 to 2:00 p.m., so send the document in advance.

What extra fee does Cambria County add to tax sale costs?

A $250.00 fee is added to the costs of every property sold at an upset, judicial, private or repository sale since April 1, 2025. The charge comes from Cambria County Ordinance 5 of 2024. Call the Tax Claim office at (814) 472-1445 for details.

Blair County by the numbers

Where is the Blair County Recorder of Deeds?

The Register of Wills and Recorder of Deeds share one office in the Blair County Courthouse, 423 Allegheny Street, Suite 145, Hollidaysburg, PA 16648. The phone is (814) 693-3095. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., except legal holidays, and it stays open over lunch.

Blair County was formed in 1846 from parts of Huntingdon and Bedford counties, so its recorded land records begin that year. Everything recorded is a public record that anyone can view during business hours, with one exception: military discharge records are impounded. Remote access to records runs through Landex, and the office also lists a free Record Alert service that texts or emails you when a document is recorded under up to five names you register.

What does it cost to record a deed in Blair County?

A deed is $87.75 and so is a mortgage, under the Recorder's posted fee schedule. That price covers up to four names and four pages, and each extra name is $0.50 and each extra page is $2.00. Checks are made payable to Blair County Recorder of Deeds, and the FAQ page states in capital letters that the office does not accept credit cards.

Blair County recording fees, from the Recorder of Deeds fee schedule
DocumentFee
Deed$87.75
Mortgage$87.75
Release of mortgage$61.75
Satisfaction piece$64.75
Assignment of mortgage$61.75
Easement or right of way$59.75
Subordination of mortgage$20.50
Power of attorney$18.50
Copy made in the office$0.25 per page
Copy mailed or emailed$1.00 per page
Certification$2.00

Recording a veteran's discharge, and certified copies of it, carry no charge. The schedule says that if a fee is not listed, the Recorder of Deeds sets it.

What paperwork does Blair County require with a deed?

Three rules appear on the fee schedule and trip up many filings. Deeds claiming an exemption from realty transfer tax must carry two statements of value. All deeds, mortgages and assignments must have a signed certificate of residence giving the precise address of the grantee, mortgagee or assignee. And the office does not accept blanket assignments, releases or satisfactions.

  • Every document needs a self-addressed, stamped envelope in the correct size for its return.
  • Documents should name the correct municipality and say whether it is a city, township or borough.
  • Some instruments, such as awards of real estate and decrees of distribution, must be filed with a statement of value.
  • Leases of 30 years or more are $59.75 and need a statement of value, while shorter leases are $18.50.

Ask the Recorder at (814) 693-3095, or your closing agent, what transfer tax rate applies to your municipality and school district before you set a net figure.

What time should a deed arrive at the Blair County courthouse?

Plan to submit by 3:15 p.m. The office states that recordings and filings submitted after 3:15 p.m. are not guaranteed to be processed the same day. The FAQ page describes the recording and filing desk as closing at 3:45 p.m., so the earlier time is the safer one for a closing that needs a same-day record.

Electronic filing avoids the trip. The office accepts e-recording through Simplifile, CSC at eRecording.com and ePN, and the county's own wording is to save time, postage and checks. Mail and counter drop-off also work, as long as the return envelope is included.

The office keeps a posted holiday calendar. The 2026 calendar lists closures on Veterans' Day, Thanksgiving, the day after Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, so a closing near those dates has to be filed around them.

What is Blair County like for a home seller?

Blair County covers 527 square miles in the Altoona metropolitan area, and Altoona is the largest city while Hollidaysburg is the county seat. The county also contains boroughs such as Bellwood, Duncansville, Roaring Spring, Martinsburg and Williamsburg, and Canoe Creek State Park lies in Frankstown Township. I-99, US 220, US 22 and a set of state routes carry traffic through, and its neighbors are Centre, Huntingdon, Bedford, Cambria and Clearfield counties.

Census QuickFacts estimates 119,541 residents in 2025, down 2.7% from the 2020 base. There are 56,086 housing units and 50,558 households, and 72.4% of homes are owner-occupied. The median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 was $161,100, the lowest of the four counties covered here, and median gross rent was $885. Only 86 building permits were issued in 2025. About 24.5% of residents are 65 or older.

Wikipedia classes the climate as warm-summer humid continental. Altoona's record high is 103 degrees, and winters are cold enough that a buyer inspecting an older house will want to see the roof and heating system.

Which other documents does the Blair County office record?

The fee schedule runs well past deeds and mortgages. Agreements, affidavits, bills of sale, powers of attorney, ordinances, waivers and sewage permits are $18.50 each. Articles of agreement, installment sales agreements, declarations of taking and notices of condemnation are $59.75, and an order of court is $20.50.

  • Subdivision plans: $30.00 for the first page and $10.00 for each additional page.
  • Surveys and plans: $10.00 for the first page and $5.00 for each additional page.
  • Highway plans: $18.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each additional page.
  • UCC financing statements: $100.00.
  • Notary public bond, oath and commission: $38.50.

A satisfaction by order of court is $64.75, matching the cost of an ordinary satisfaction piece. If you hold a paid-off mortgage that was never released, the satisfaction is the filing that clears it from the index before a sale.

What office rules should a seller know about in Blair County?

Photography and any image capturing equipment are strictly prohibited inside the office, so bring paper notes rather than a phone camera when you look up a record. The office also gives only general information by phone and will not search records or give legal advice for you. A title examiner or attorney handles anything more detailed.

Plan the visit around the time cutoffs and the document rules above. Bring a check, since no credit cards are taken, and the self-addressed stamped envelope for any mailed or dropped-off filing. Deeds claiming a tax exemption need two statements of value, so a family transfer takes more preparation than an arm's length sale does.

How do you get a copy of a Blair County deed?

Records are on line through Landex, or you can come to the office during business hours and a staff member will help find the reference and photocopy it. Counter copies are 25 cents a page. A request by mail, email or fax needs the full name, the property location and the year of purchase, costs $1.00 per page, and needs a stamped, self-addressed envelope. Certifying a copy costs $2.00 more.

A certified copy can replace a lost or destroyed deed. A recorded document cannot be changed afterwards. To add, delete or change a name, a new deed has to be recorded, and employees may not prepare deeds, so an attorney drafts it. If a spouse dies and the house was held as tenants by the entireties, the name usually does not need to be removed until the property is sold or mortgaged, and the next deed will state the date of death.

More questions about Blair County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How much is a deed recording fee in Blair County?

It is $87.75 for a deed with up to four names and four pages. Each extra name costs $0.50 and each extra page costs $2.00.

Does the Blair County Recorder of Deeds take credit cards?

No. The FAQ page states that credit cards are not accepted, and checks are made payable to Blair County Recorder of Deeds.

Can a Blair County deed be recorded electronically?

Yes. The office accepts e-recording through Simplifile, CSC at eRecording.com and ePN.

What certificate of residence does a Blair County deed need?

Every deed, mortgage and assignment needs a signed certificate of residence with the precise address of the grantee, mortgagee or assignee.

How do I find the earliest Blair County records?

Records start in 1846, when the county was formed from Huntingdon and Bedford counties. Search them online through Landex or visit the office in Hollidaysburg.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Lycoming County, PA Recorder of Deeds sale
  • Turn the Lycoming County, PA Recorder of Deeds offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Lycoming County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Deed fee $79.75 (4 names, 4 pages, 1 UPI); additional UPI $10.00; copies $0.50.
  • UPI required before recording, $10 per UPI at recording.
  • Exempt transfers need REV-183 Statement of Value (family transfers stated in document); SOV also for nominal consideration.

What we could not confirm

  • Millage seen only in search snippet
  • E-recording availability not found on official pages
