Lycoming County by the numbers

Where does a Lycoming County deed get recorded?

Deeds for property anywhere in Lycoming County are recorded by the Register and Recorder in Williamsport, the county seat. The office keeps land records going back to 1795, the year the county was carved out of Northumberland County on April 13, and the county's website says all deeds from 1795 to the present can be viewed online through the searchiqs.com/palyc portal.

A deed is the last paper in a sale. The buyer's title company or attorney usually carries the signed deed to the recorder after closing, and the recording date is when the public record shows the new owner. The county's own instructions are blunt about corrections: a name cannot be added, removed or changed on an existing deed, so a new deed has to be drafted and recorded, and the office points owners to a real estate attorney or title company for that, and the county site links a find-a-lawyer page.

Lycoming is the largest Pennsylvania county by land area, about 1,229 square miles, and it touches nine other counties. That size matters for sellers because a house in Jersey Shore, Montoursville or Hughesville is recorded at the same Williamsport counter as one on a city street.

What does the Uniform Parcel Identifier step involve in Lycoming County?

Every instrument that affects real estate needs a Uniform Parcel Identifier, called a UPI, before the Recorder will accept it. The county requires this for deeds, easements, rights of way, mortgages, mortgage assignments, releases, satisfactions and leases, and a 2017 ordinance amendment extended the rule to every instrument involving a specific interest in real estate.

The UPI is assigned or verified by the Land Records Office in the Department of Planning and Community Development, on the third floor of the Third Street Plaza at 33 West Third Street in Williamsport. The county price is $10.00 per UPI, collected when the document is recorded, and a single-UPI document has that charge folded into the base recording fee.

  • Bring or mail the original document to Land Records, or email a draft to upi@lyco.org or fax it to 570-320-2135 for review ahead of closing.
  • The county says turnaround is roughly 5 to 10 minutes at the counter and no more than one business day.
  • Staff stamp the UPI in the upper left corner of the first page so the Recorder can collect the right fees.
  • One document can list several lots and still need just one UPI.
  • Land Records answers questions at 570-320-2130 and keeps weekday hours from 8:30 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon

A seller who is splitting off part of a parcel should expect the new piece to be labeled as part of the original UPI, which is one more reason to start the paperwork before the closing date.

Which charges stack up on a Lycoming County deed filing?

Pricing for the deed itself comes off a fee sheet that the Register and Recorder publishes and updates. Get the latest sheet before closing day so the check matches.

What can be stated from county pages is the shape of the charges. The recording fee covers a set number of pages and names, the UPI charge is $10.00 for each parcel identifier, and realty transfer tax is paid on top. The table below lays out the pieces that apply to a typical sale.

Charges that attach to a Lycoming County deed recording
ItemWho sets itAmount or rule
Base recording feeLycoming County Register and RecorderPer the current fee sheet
UPI certificationLycoming County Land Records$10.00 per UPI
Commonwealth realty transfer taxPennsylvania Department of Revenue1 percent of value
Local transfer taxMunicipality and school districtShared by the district and municipality, rate varies
Name or ownership changeRecorderRequires a new recorded deed

Source: Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds and UPI pages, and the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue.

How is realty transfer tax handled when a Lycoming County house sells?

The commonwealth levies 1 percent of the property's value, and under state law the grantor and the grantee each answer for it. The Williamsport office gathers it alongside the local share and passes the state portion up to Harrisburg.

The county's recorder page lists the school districts used for transfer tax purposes, which is the quickest way to see how local tax is split. The eleven names are:

  • Canton, East Lycoming and Jersey Shore
  • Loyalsock, Montgomery and Montoursville
  • Muncy, South Williamsport and Williamsport
  • Southern Tioga and Wellsboro, which reach into neighboring Tioga County

A few transfers escape the tax, among them some gifts inside a family, deeds to public bodies and estates passing at death. If a seller thinks one of those fits, the closing agent needs to hear it early because the deed must carry supporting language.

How do appeals and the 2027 value question work for Lycoming County owners?

Owners who believe the assessment is too high can file a yearly appeal from July 1 to September 1, which applies to the following tax year, or file within 40 days after a change of value notice arrives. A separate form is needed for each parcel, and the filing fee is $15.00 for residential property and $50.00 for everything else, including commercial, industrial and Clean and Green.

The appeal has to argue market value. The county states that tax bills and the owner's ability to pay cannot be appealed, and that the law presumes the assessment is correct until the owner shows otherwise. The board will not split a property into land and buildings, so the appeal covers total value.

  • Useful evidence: a certified appraisal from the last three years, sales of similar homes within the past three years, photos of a run-down interior and, for rural lots, perc test results.
  • An annual appeal never changes the current year, so taxes are still paid on time.
  • On a change-of-value appeal, the county suggests paying with a letter saying the tax is paid in protest.
  • A ruling that still looks wrong can go to the Court of Common Pleas, and the clock for that is 30 days.

Sellers can ask the Assessment Office which value will drive the next tax bill, since that is the number a buyer inherits.

What is Lycoming County like for someone about to list a house?

Lycoming County sits in north central Pennsylvania on the West Branch Susquehanna River, about 130 miles northwest of Philadelphia and 165 miles east-northeast of Pittsburgh. Residents numbered 114,188 in the 2020 census, and owners lived in 67.2 percent of occupied homes. Williamsport, the seat and only city, had 29,381 residents in 2010, and the next largest places are South Williamsport, Montoursville, Jersey Shore and Muncy.

The river and its tributaries, including Lycoming, Loyalsock and Muncy creeks, drain the whole county into the Chesapeake Bay watershed, so a house near any of them is worth describing accurately to buyers. Winters run cold, with downtown Williamsport averaging 26.5 degrees in January against 72.4 in July, and heating systems and roofs get a real test every year.

Roads help a sale. Interstates 99 and 180 and US 15 and 220 serve the valley, and Williamsport Regional Airport offers commercial flights to Washington, D.C.

More questions about Lycoming County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Does the Lycoming County recorder fix a misspelled name on an old deed?

Not on the old deed itself. A recorded deed stays as written, and the county says a new deed must be prepared and recorded to add, remove or change a name. A title company or real estate attorney can draft it.

How much is the UPI charge in Lycoming County?

It is $10.00 for each UPI, paid when the document is recorded. A document with one UPI has that charge included in its base fee, and extra UPIs on the same document cost more.

Can I check Lycoming County deeds from home?

Yes. The county says deeds from 1795 to the present can be viewed online at searchiqs.com/palyc, and the same records can be searched at the recorder's office in Williamsport during business hours.

What deadline applies to a Lycoming County assessment appeal?

Yearly appeals go in between July 1 and September 1 and apply to the next tax year. After a change of value notice, the window is 40 days counted from the notice date.

Who covers the realty transfer tax on a Lycoming County sale?

The grantor and grantee each answer for the 1 percent state tax, with local tax added on top. The sales contract normally sets how the two split it, and the recorder collects it at filing.

Northumberland County by the numbers

Where does Northumberland County record deeds?

Deeds are recorded by the Register and Recorder at 201 Market Street, first floor, in Sunbury. The phone is 570-988-4143. On Mondays the office is open from 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., and Tuesday through Friday it runs 9:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. It closes every day from noon to 1:00 p.m.

One office holds two jobs. It records land documents, and it also serves as register of wills for estates and issues marriage licenses. Heirs who sell an inherited house therefore use both functions: first to open the estate, later to record the deed out of it.

Probate visits require an appointment, booked at 570-988-4985. The lunch closure matters for recording: a package that arrives at 12:15 p.m. waits until 1:00.

What are the recording charges at the Sunbury office?

Filing a deed costs $86.25 on the December 1, 2025 schedule, whether it is taxable, nontaxable or a quit claim. The price assumes four pages, four names and a single tract.

Northumberland County Recorder of Deeds charges since December 1, 2025
DocumentCharge
Deed of any kind$86.25
Mortgage$86.25
Satisfaction piece$64.75
Lease of 30 years or more$71.25
Right of way agreement$59.75
Affidavit affecting real estate$18.50
Statement of Value$2.00

Source: the county's Recorder of Deeds fee schedule. Extras are small. Each page after the fourth adds $2.00, and each added name or added tract adds fifty cents (no tract charge on a mortgage). A marginal notation is $2.00.

A wrong fee gets the document rejected, and a payment that is too high counts as wrong. Add it up before writing the check.

How does transfer tax get paid on a Northumberland County sale?

A taxable deed owes the state's 1 percent, a local 1 percent and the recording fee. Northumberland tells filers that separate checks are not required, so a single check can cover all three amounts.

Under the state's rules the grantor and grantee share liability for the state portion. The state also exempts some deeds, such as particular family transfers, deeds to a government body and inherited property.

An exempt deed still travels with a Statement of Value, priced at $2.00 here, and the title agent or attorney should state the reason for the exemption on the form.

What paperwork rules apply in the Northumberland County recorder's office?

The county's requirements page is brief, so each item on it matters.

  • The document submitted must be an original.
  • If the recorded deed must come back by mail, enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself.
  • No blanket assignments or satisfaction pieces.
  • The exact recording fee is required or the document is refused.

Electronic filing covers deeds, mortgages, assignments, satisfactions, mortgage releases, UCC filings and powers of attorney. The county sends filers to two vendors, CSC E-Recording Solutions and Simplifile, to sign up.

How does the register of wills affect selling an inherited house in Northumberland County?

An heir cannot sign a deed until someone has authority to act for the estate. In this county that authority comes from letters issued by the Register and Recorder, and the fee rises with the size of the estate.

  • Letters in an estate under $1,000 cost $142.75.
  • An estate between $50,001 and $100,000 costs $267.75.
  • Each additional $100,000, or fraction of it, adds $100.00.
  • Letters used for litigation only cost $102.75.

Those prices come from the December 2025 schedule and include the filing of the inventory and the inheritance tax return. The same office charges $50.00 for a certified copy of an instrument and $10.00 for a short certificate, which a title company may ask for. Call the office before the visit, since probate meetings run by appointment.

Heirs sometimes need smaller filings too. A disclaimer costs $15.00, a renunciation is $10.00 per name, a receipt and release in the register of wills is $10.00 per name, and a creditor's claim is $75.00. Whoever is handling the estate should add these to the budget before the house is listed.

What is the Northumberland County housing picture for sellers?

Created in 1772, this fifth class county lies along the Susquehanna River in central Pennsylvania. Sunbury is both the seat and the biggest city, Shamokin is the other city, and the county spans 478 square miles, 19 of them water.

Anthracite mines and factories carried the economy until the 1950s, when the mines began to close. Leading employers listed for 2023 include Weis Markets, Knoebels Amusement Resort, the state government and Geisinger Health System. The 2025 population estimate is 89,920, which is 1.9 percent below the 2020 base.

Housing costs are low. The latest five-year survey shows a $162,400 median home value, $60,583 in median household income and 75.5 percent owner occupancy, against a $436,700 median home value in Montgomery County.

Which places in Northumberland County do sellers come from?

Every town in the county files with the Sunbury office. Sunbury had 9,905 people in the 2010 census and Shamokin had 7,374, and Milton ranked third. The rest is a patchwork of boroughs, townships and small villages strung along the Susquehanna River and its West Branch, with mountains to the north and south and rolling hills in between.

The climate is humid continental. Sunbury averages about 27 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 73 in July, and Mount Carmel runs a couple of degrees cooler, which is worth remembering when you schedule showings and inspections in winter.

Recording fees do not shrink with the price. An $86.25 deed fee is the same on a $90,000 house as on a $900,000 one, so on a low-priced sale it takes a bigger bite and belongs in the closing estimate as its own line.

How is an old mortgage cleared when a Northumberland County house sells?

The lender files a satisfaction piece or a release of mortgage with the recorder, and each costs $64.75 to record under the current schedule. A partial release costs the same. An assignment of a mortgage from one lender to another is $61.75.

The county refuses blanket satisfaction pieces, so each one has to name the specific mortgage it clears. A paid-off mortgage that still shows in the public record is something to ask the title company to hunt down. Ask the lender how long it takes to file, so the record is clear for the buyer.

How should I prepare for closing on a Northumberland County house?

Work through this list before the deed leaves the title office.

  • Work out the exact fee from the schedule, including extra pages and names.
  • Bring a stamped, self-addressed return envelope.
  • Check the hours, including the noon closing.
  • Decide ahead whether the closing agent will file electronically through CSC or Simplifile.
  • For an inherited home, schedule the probate appointment well before the closing.

More questions about Northumberland County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What will a deed cost to file in Sunbury?

$86.25, under the schedule that started December 1, 2025, for a deed of four pages, four names and one tract. Each extra page adds $2 and each extra name adds 50 cents.

Do I write one check or several for a taxable deed in Northumberland County?

No. Northumberland says separate checks are not required on taxable deeds, so one check may cover the state tax, the local tax and the recording fee.

Can a deed be recorded electronically in Northumberland County?

Yes. CSC E-Recording Solutions and Simplifile handle electronic deeds, mortgages, assignments, satisfactions, releases, UCC filings and powers of attorney for the county.

When can I visit the Sunbury recorder?

Mondays it runs until 4:45 p.m. and Tuesday through Friday until 4:15 p.m., always opening at 9:00 a.m. A lunch closure from noon to 1:00 p.m. applies every day.

What happens if I send the wrong fee to the Northumberland County recorder?

It comes back unrecorded, and that includes a payment that is too high. Calculate the fee from the current schedule before mailing.

Adams County by the numbers

Who records deeds in Adams County, Pennsylvania?

The Adams County Recorder of Deeds records them, from an office in the Adams County Courthouse at 117 Baltimore Street, Room 102, in Gettysburg. Staff answer at 717-337-9826 on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., and the office shuts for every holiday on the county calendar.

Recordings stop at 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the doors close, so a closing package that arrives at 4:20 waits for the next business day. The same office acts as the Department of Revenue's agent for realty transfer tax and hands the money on to the state, the municipality and the school district.

Anyone selling a house in Adams County meets this office at the very end of the sale: the deed is signed at closing, then recorded here, and the recording date is when the new owner shows up in the public record.

What does the Adams County recorder charge to record a deed?

A deed or a mortgage costs $71.25 to record under the fee bill that took effect December 1, 2025. That covers the first four pages and the first four names, and a few add-ons apply after that.

Adams County Recorder of Deeds fees, schedule effective December 1, 2025

Source: the county's Recording Fee Bill. The schedule says that if a document type carries no listed fee, the Recorder of Deeds sets one, and it adds that all fees are payable at the time of recording.

Payment for the recording fee can be cash, check, or a debit or credit card, though a vendor fee is added to card payments. The office cannot make change on a check, so an overpayment of $10 or less is kept as an overpayment and shows that way on the receipt. Anything above $10 means a new check.

How is realty transfer tax paid when a house sells in Adams County?

Check only, with no cash taken, at the moment the deed is recorded. The county's fee bill describes a 1% state tax plus a local tax of the same amount, and it calls for three separate checks: one to the state, one to the township or borough, and one for the recording fee.

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue explains that buyer and seller are both liable for the tax. Its page also lists transfers that escape the tax, such as certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy.

  • A Statement of Value is required whenever the tax is not paid in full, including when a family exemption is claimed.
  • When land lies in two or more municipalities, the deed has to state how the value splits so the local share goes to the right place.
  • The county's fee bill lists grandparent to grandchild and sibling transfers among the exemptions it recognizes.
  • A Certificate of Residence has to be completed and signed on every deed and mortgage before the office will record it.

The Statement of Value is a Revenue form with no recording charge at this office, and the county directs people with questions on it to the Department of Revenue.

What paperwork rules does the Adams County office enforce?

Documents must relate to real estate, carry original signatures, and be properly notarized. The date on the document cannot come after the date of the notary acknowledgment.

Adams County stands apart from many Pennsylvania counties on a few points. It does not use the Uniform Parcel Identifier system, so no UPI fee is collected and no parcel number or street address is required on a document being recorded. It also sets no margin rules, and it takes both letter and legal size paper.

  • Include a self-addressed stamped envelope; finished documents are mailed back about two weeks after the recording date.
  • Assignments of mortgage must cite the book and page of the original mortgage.
  • Subdivision plans must be 18 by 24 inches, signed by the township or borough and the county planning commission, and recorded within 90 days of approval.
  • Remote online notarization is accepted only during a declared emergency.

How can I get a document to the Adams County recorder?

There are three routes: an in-person visit, the secure drop box outside the courthouse entrance, or mail by USPS, FedEx or UPS. Appointments are preferred but not required, and they can be made by phone or by email to registerrecorder@adamscountypa.gov.

The courthouse lobby has public terminals for searching records, and a copier that runs on a button picked up from the Register and Recorder or the Prothonotary. There is no terminal inside the recording office itself, and photographing screens, books or microfilm is prohibited.

The office also runs a free fraud alert service called PropertyCheck, which emails or texts an owner whenever a document is recorded against their property. A seller who plans to hold other property in the county may find that useful.

Ask the recorder whether a title company can send a closing package electronically, because the office pages open to the public describe paper, drop box and mail only.

What does Adams County look like for a seller?

Adams County covers about 522 square miles in south central Pennsylvania, and Gettysburg sits at the center of it, ringed on three sides by the national military park. Thirteen historic roads meet at or near the borough, and most of the farmland outside it has kept its nineteenth century layout.

The Census Bureau estimated 107,594 residents in July 2025, up 3.6% from the 2020 base, while Allegheny and Armstrong counties both lost residents over the same stretch.

Adams County housing and income snapshot, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureAdams County
Housing units, July 202544,750
Owner-occupied rate, 2020-202478.9%
Median owner-occupied home value, 2020-2024$268,500
Median household income, 2020-2024$84,092
Building permits, 2025476

With a median home value of $268,500 and nearly four in five households owning, most sales here are owner to owner. The county also lists a Tax Services office among its recording resources, which a new owner can contact after the deed is on record.

What should I have ready before closing in Adams County?

A short checklist keeps a deed from bouncing at the counter.

  • The signed, notarized deed with the notary's venue, expiration date and a legible stamp.
  • Three checks drawn on the correct accounts: state tax, local tax and recording fee, with the amounts matching the deed's stated consideration.
  • A completed Certificate of Residence and, if any tax is excused, a filled-in Statement of Value.
  • A stamped return envelope addressed to the new owner or the title agent.
  • Arrival before the 4:00 p.m. cutoff on a weekday that is not a county holiday.

Whoever delivers the deed to the courthouse, the same steps apply, so agree before closing on who will carry the package in and who gets the recorded original back.

More questions about Adams County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the base recording fee for a deed in Adams County?

The base fee is $71.25 for a deed or mortgage under the schedule effective December 1, 2025, plus $4.00 for each page after the fourth and $1.00 for each name after the fourth. Transfer tax is paid separately, by check.

When does Adams County stop accepting documents each day?

The cutoff is 4:00 p.m. on business days, even though the office stays open until 4:30 p.m. For a special circumstance the office asks you to call or email before you come.

Is cash accepted for transfer tax at the Adams County courthouse?

No. Realty transfer tax must be paid by check, and the office asks for separate checks for the state tax, the local tax and the recording fee. Recording fees themselves can be paid in cash or by card with a vendor fee.

Must a deed carry a parcel number to be recorded here?

No. The county does not use the UPI system, and a parcel identification number or property address is not required on documents submitted for recording. A Certificate of Residence is required, though.

Where should a signed deed be delivered or mailed?

Send it to the Recorder of Deeds at the Adams County Courthouse, 117 Baltimore Street, Room 102, Gettysburg, PA 17325, or use the drop box at the entrance. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope; return mail takes about two weeks.

Carbon County by the numbers

What does the Carbon County Recorder of Deeds do?

The Recorder of Deeds is an elected county office that preserves the land records for Carbon County, from deeds and mortgages to easements and rights of way. When a house sells in Jim Thorpe, Lehighton, Palmerton or any other Carbon County town, the deed has to be recorded here before the public record reflects the new owner.

Each document goes through three steps: indexing the information into the public retrieval system, scanning, and verifying the index entries. The county stores one copy on its public system, Landex, and two archive copies on secure servers at separate locations. The office is also the collection agent for realty transfer tax and the court-related fees that go to the state, plus the Affordable Housing Program fee that supports income-based housing in the county.

How much does the Carbon County recorder charge?

A deed or mortgage costs $102.75 under the fee sheet effective November 17, 2025. That covers four pages, four names and one parcel number.

Carbon County recording fees effective November 17, 2025 (source: Carbon County Recorder of Deeds)
DocumentFee

Agreement of sale$74.75

Longer documents pay more. Deeds and mortgages cost $4.00 for each page past four, other documents cost $2.00 per page past four, every name beyond four adds $0.50, and each extra parcel number adds $15.00. Pay the exact amount by cash, personal check, business check or money order. A wrong amount is returned with a $5.00 rejection fee, though an overpayment of $10.00 or less is kept by the county.

What is the realty transfer tax in Carbon County?

The county page states that the office collects 2% of the total consideration or the fair market value, and that money is split among the state, local school districts and municipalities. A Pennsylvania Statement of Value, form REV-183, is required whenever you are not paying tax on full market value.

  • All trusts require a Statement of Value.
  • Easements need one unless the grantee is a public utility.
  • A transfer out of an estate needs one unless full tax is being paid.
  • The form goes in duplicate and its pages do not count toward the page total.
  • A family transfer, such as a parent to children, must be typed on the deed if no tax is being paid.

Use the Common Level Ratio factor for the year your document is dated. For factors older than five years, call the office at 570-325-2651.

Where do I file and what is the deadline each day?

Carbon County takes recordings by mail, in person and through e-recording partners CSC and Simplifile. The office phone number on the county page is 570-325-2651. The county sets the cut-off for recording at 3:30 p.m., so a closing that wraps up late in the day may not record until the next business day.

Documents must pertain to real estate, be in English or carry a translation, and bear original, properly notarized signatures. Mailed filings need a self-addressed stamped envelope, and an office mailbox holder is asked to collect recorded papers at least weekly. Remote online notarization is accepted when the certificate says the notarial act involved the use of communication technology.

Why can a Carbon County deed be rejected?

The county's recording requirements run to 21 items, and the same few errors come up repeatedly.

  • The document date must be the same as or earlier than the acknowledgment date.
  • Grantor names, signatures and acknowledgments must match exactly, and the names should match the prior deed's grantee.
  • Reference documents must show the book and page of the earlier recorded paper.
  • The municipality, whether a township or borough, should be stated above the legal description. For land in several localities, show the percentage split for local transfer tax through the Statement of Value.
  • Deeds, mortgages, easements, releases and assignments need a signed mailing address certification, because that address tells the Assessment Office where to send property tax bills.
  • Notary blocks need the right venue, a legible stamp and a current commission expiration date.

How can I look up or monitor Carbon County records online?

The county publishes its records through Landex. Landex Webstore gives the public remote access to documents from 1988 to the present, and a separate Landex Remote service serves title searchers. Anyone can also sign up for a Landex Record Alert using a name or a tax parcel number, which sends a notice when a new document is recorded against that name or parcel.

An alert is a cheap way for a seller to confirm that a satisfaction of mortgage has been recorded after payoff, or for an heir to watch for filings against an inherited house. The recorder's staff can also help trace a property back through earlier owners and purchase prices, and can help replace a document that was lost.

  • A re-recorded document needs a new acknowledgment and new signatures.
  • Several documents filed together should be labeled, such as POA, deed and mortgage, so they record in the right order.
  • Sales agreements must list the full address of both buyer and seller.

Why do releases and satisfactions matter when selling?

A seller with a mortgage needs the lender's satisfaction recorded so the title is clear for the next owner. The county explains the difference. A satisfaction is used when the whole loan is paid off, and the lender signs a satisfaction of mortgage that is recorded to clear the title. A release, also called a partial release, is used when part of the property or one name is taken off the mortgage and the loan stays active on the rest.

Satisfactions and releases can reference only one mortgage each, and blanket documents are not accepted. Another rule affects trust transfers. Since October 1, 2024, the office no longer accepts e-recorded deeds into a trust, so those deeds must be brought in or mailed. For tax parcel numbers on agreements, easements, leases and rights of way, the county advises calling its GIS department at 570-325-8519 first.

What is the Carbon County market like for sellers?

Carbon County was divided from Northampton County in 1843 and takes its name from coal. Jim Thorpe, founded in 1818 as Mauch Chunk, is the seat, and Palmerton is the largest borough. The Lehigh River cuts a gorge through the county, Blue Mountain forms its southern edge, and I-80 and the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-476) cross it.

Census Bureau figures show 65,868 residents in 2025 on about 381 square miles and 34,816 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 the median home value was $211,400, owner-occupancy was 76.4%, median gross rent was $994 and median household income was $67,554. Mean travel time to work was 32.5 minutes. About 24.3% of residents are 65 or older.

More questions about Carbon County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What time does the Carbon County Recorder of Deeds stop recording?

The cut-off for recording is 3:30 p.m. Documents arriving after that time wait for the next business day, so plan closings with that in mind.

How much is the realty transfer tax in Carbon County?

The office collects 2% of the total consideration or the fair market value of the property. That money is distributed to the state, the local school district and the municipality.

Can a deed into a trust be e-recorded in Carbon County?

No. Since October 1, 2024, the office accepts deeds into a trust only in person or by mail. Other documents can still be e-recorded through CSC or Simplifile.

Do I need a UPI to record a Carbon County deed?

Yes. All real estate documents need a Uniform Parcel Identifier before recording. Call the Assessment Office at 570-325-5254 to get one, and add $15.00 for each parcel beyond the first.

What happens if I pay the wrong recording fee in Carbon County?

The document is returned and a $5.00 rejection fee is charged per document. The one exception is an overpayment of $10.00 or less, which the county keeps.

Pike County by the numbers

What does the Pike County Recorder of Deeds do?

The office records and indexes real estate documents for Pike County, such as deeds, mortgages and mortgage satisfactions. It also acts as a collection agent for the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, which is why realty transfer tax is paid at the same counter as the recording fee.

The county's Recorder of Deeds page lists the office at 506 Broad Street in Milford, staffed on weekdays from 8:30 am until 4:30 pm, with a phone line at 570-296-3508. Checks go to "Pike County Recorder of Deeds." A returned document carries a $10 return fee.

Recording comes last in a sale and decides whether the buyer's name shows up in the public index. A deed that sits in a drawer, or one that is rejected, leaves the seller on record as the owner. That matters for property tax bills, liability and any lien searches that follow.

How do I record a deed in Pike County?

You can deliver the deed to the Milford office or send it through an electronic recording vendor. The county names two vendors on its recorder page, and both handle title companies and law offices every day.

  • Simplifile, phone 800-460-5657
  • CSC, phone 866-652-0111
  • Walk it in or mail it to 506 Broad Street, Milford, PA 18337, with a check for the fee and, if the deed carries transfer tax, a payment for that

The county's published fee schedule changes from time to time, so ask the office for the current deed fee before you write a check. A check in the wrong amount is one of the reasons a package comes back.

When a title company or attorney closes your sale, they normally prepare the deed, calculate the tax and file it. Ask them for the recording confirmation or the book and page reference after closing, and keep it with your sale papers.

Why do Pike County deeds get returned?

The recorder publishes a short checklist of defects. Most of them are clerical, and every one can be fixed before the deed leaves your hands.

  • The acknowledgment date falls before the date on the caption.
  • The acknowledgment leaves out the county, state, date, the names and titles of the people appearing, or the notary's signature, seal and expiration date. The office treats that acknowledgment as defective.
  • The deed does not name the township, county and state where the property sits.
  • The amount written in words differs from the amount in numbers.
  • A document that refers to an earlier mortgage does not give that mortgage's book and page.
  • A set of papers for one transaction is not numbered in the order they should be recorded.
  • Property crossing two municipalities does not show the split of local transfer tax in dollars.
  • The deed lacks the grantee's address, or the grantee address is unsigned.
  • A foreign language document arrives without a written English translation.

If you are selling by yourself without a closing attorney, read this list against your deed line by line. The re-recording costs from a wrong document order fall on whoever submitted it.

How much transfer tax applies to a Pike County sale?

Pennsylvania charges a state realty transfer tax of 1 percent of the value of the property transferred. Under the state's rules, grantor and grantee answer for it together, and the county recorder collects it along with any local tax.

Local transfer tax is the part that varies. Municipalities and school districts may add their own share, and Pike County deeds can cross municipal lines, which is why the recorder asks for the local split in dollars. Get the combined rate for your township or borough from the recorder before you sign a settlement sheet.

Some transfers pay nothing. The state's exemption list covers certain family transfers, transfers to governmental units and property that passes through an estate. If an heir later deeds the inherited house to a buyer, that second deed is an ordinary taxed sale.

Recording facts from official Pike County and Pennsylvania pages
ItemWhat the page saysSource

Where is Pike County and what is its housing like?

Pike County lies along the Delaware River at Pennsylvania's northeastern edge. It is the only Pennsylvania county that borders both New York and New Jersey. Pike became a county in 1814, takes its name from General Zebulon Pike and has Milford as its seat. Matamoras is the largest borough, and the four largest settlements in the 2020 count are census-designated lake communities: Saw Creek, Hemlock Farms, Pocono Woodland Lakes and Pine Ridge.

The county covers 567 square miles, of which 545 are land. The terrain climbs from the river valley in the east to the foothills of the Poconos in the west, and the climate is humid continental. Interstate 84, US 6, US 209 and US 206 are among the major highways, and Census figures show a mean commute to work of 42.3 minutes.

  • Mid 2025 headcount: 62,808 people, a gain of 7.3 percent on the 2020 base
  • Homes counted: 40,861, with 24,262 households at 2.48 people each
  • Share of occupied homes lived in by their owners: 87.0 percent
  • Typical owned home: $272,600 in value
  • Typical household income: $81,323
  • Typical gross rent: $1,378 a month

The numbers above are drawn from Census QuickFacts for Pike County, using the 2020 to 2024 survey period except where the 2025 estimate is named. With owners living in 87 percent of occupied homes, a typical Pike County sale is an owner selling to another buyer rather than a landlord exiting a rental.

How can I watch for fraud on my Pike County deed?

The recorder offers a fraud alert service through the county's online land records. You sign in at the Uslandrecords site, choose Pennsylvania and Pike County, register, and then use the Alerts menu to be told when a document is recorded under a name you choose. Setting up alerts does not need a credit card. Viewing or downloading images does.

This is worth doing before and after a sale. Before closing, an alert under your own name shows whether anything unexpected gets recorded against your property. After closing, it confirms that your sale deed reached the index. Copies of recorded deeds are available by contacting the office or through the Property Record Search.

What should an heir or a landlord with a Pike County house do before selling?

Start with the title. After an owner's death, the estate has to show who holds authority to sign, which is a question for the Register of Wills and an attorney. The Recorder of Deeds only records what is presented.

Next, check for open mortgages. A mortgage that was paid off years ago may still look open in the index until its satisfaction is recorded, and the recorder's office files satisfactions as part of its normal work. A title company will want that cleared before closing.

Finally, think about timing. Tax bills, rent and repairs keep running while a deed waits for signatures. A seller who wants a fast, as-is closing can ask a buyer to accept the house without repairs, and the recording of the deed still follows the same steps described above.

More questions about Pike County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Which office takes a deed for filing in Pike County?

The Recorder of Deeds at 506 Broad Street in Milford, or an electronic vendor. The county names Simplifile and CSC for online filing, and the counter keeps weekday hours.

What is the return fee on a rejected deed?

$10. The Pike County recorder charges that service fee on every returned document, so checking the acknowledgment and the amounts before you submit saves money and time.

Who is on the hook for transfer tax at a Pike County closing?

Both parties are liable together under state rules, though the sale contract usually assigns the cost. The state's share is 1 percent, and local taxes can add to it. The recorder can tell you the local amount.

Does inheriting a Pike County house trigger transfer tax?

No, title that passes through an estate is on the state's exempt list. A later sale to a buyer is a separate transfer and is taxed like any other, unless another exemption applies.

How do I obtain a copy of a recorded Pike County deed?

Call the Recorder of Deeds at 570-296-3508 or use the Property Record Search on the county's land records site. Viewing or downloading images online requires registering a credit card.

Mercer County by the numbers

Where do Mercer County deeds get recorded, and what are the office hours?

The Mercer County Recorder of Deeds works from Suite 109 of the courthouse complex at 125 S. Diamond Street in the borough of Mercer, the county seat. The phone number is 724-662-3800, and the counter keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30, holidays excepted.

The same counter takes deeds, mortgages, leases, powers of attorney, easements, subdivision plans and notary bonds. For a house sale the order is simple: the deed is signed at closing, a Uniform Parcel Identifier is certified, and the closing agent files the deed with the transfer tax and the fee. The county's fee bill also says recordings can be checked online through the Land Records Search on the county website, with the index and images going back to 1972.

Mercer County covers 673 square miles of land in northwest Pennsylvania along the Ohio line, and its largest city is Hermitage. Sellers in Sharon, Grove City, Greenville or Farrell all record through this one office.

School district names matter on a deed because local transfer tax can be shared with the district. Mercer County is served by Commodore Perry, Farrell Area, Greenville Area, Grove City Area, Hermitage, Jamestown Area, Lakeview, Mercer Area, Reynolds, Sharon City, Sharpsville Area, West Middlesex Area and Wilmington Area, so the property description should place the parcel in the right municipality and district. Interstates 79, 80 and 376 and US routes 19 and 62 cross the county.

What changed with the UPI ordinance in Mercer County in 2026?

Mercer County certifies a Uniform Parcel Identifier for every document that affects title before it can be recorded. The commissioners passed Ordinance No. 2026-001 on November 20, 2025, and it took effect on January 5, 2026.

The UPI is simply the county tax parcel number already assigned to the property. The Tax Assessment Office certifies it, and a document mailed or e-recorded to the Recorder is forwarded there first, so the identifier is settled before the deed reaches the Recorder's desk.

  • The charge is $20.00 for each UPI certification, paid separately to Mercer County Tax Assessment, not to the Recorder.
  • Including the parent parcel number costs nothing extra.
  • When only part of a property is being conveyed, two UPI numbers are needed: one for the new piece and one for the parent parcel.
  • Deeds, quitclaim deeds, mortgages, releases, easements, leases, court decrees and powers of attorney to sell are all covered.
  • Questions and pre-approval requests go to upi@mercercountypa.gov.

An agent who wants the closing on schedule should send the draft deed to the Assessment Office well before the signing date.

How much does Mercer County charge to put a deed on record?

A deed costs $71.25 under the fee bill revised June 15, 2026. That base fee includes four pages, four names and one parcel, and the county adds $2.00 for each extra page and $0.50 for each extra parcel or name.

Mercer County Recorder of Deeds fee bill, revised June 15, 2026
Document or itemFee
Deed, including corrective deed and decree of distribution$71.25
Mortgage, including amendments and subordinations$71.25
Mortgage assignment, release, satisfaction$59.75

Power of attorney$18.50
Realty transfer tax Statement of Value$2.00 extra

Return of a rejected document$5.00 first time, $10 second, $20 after

Source: Mercer County Recorder of Deeds fee bill. The Statement of Value is not part of the four-page base fee, and the county asks for the original plus one copy.

Payment is by cash or check only, and each check needs the account holder's current address and phone number. A stamped return envelope lets the recorded deed travel back to the right buyer.

How much realty transfer tax applies in Mercer County towns?

The baseline is 1 percent to the Commonwealth plus 1 percent local, which the fee bill describes, and five places charge a different local rate. The recorder collects the whole amount when the deed is filed.

  • Hermitage: 2.5 percent local
  • Sharon: 2.5 percent local
  • Farrell: 2 percent local
  • Greenville: 2 percent local
  • Sheakleyville: 1 percent local, effective May 1, 2019

A deed that covers land in more than one municipality has to state how the transfer tax is divided or what percentage goes to each. The fee bill also prints a common level ratio factor of 9.52 for the period July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, and under state revenue rules the grantor and grantee both stand behind the tax. Some family transfers, deeds to government bodies and inherited property are exempt from the state tax.

What document standards does the Mercer County Recorder enforce?

The office rejects paper that does not meet its standards, and a rejected document costs the return fee shown in the table. Sellers can avoid that by checking the deed against the county's list before closing.

  • Original documents only, with an acknowledgment date that does not come before the date of the document.
  • A 2-inch blank margin at the top of every page for the Recorder's stamp.
  • The municipality, county and state of the property written on deeds and mortgages.
  • A signed certificate of residence on deeds, mortgages, articles of agreement and assignments.
  • No highlighting, and text legible enough to index and copy.
  • When several documents belong to one transaction, a note on each showing the order of recording.

The county also requires either the transfer tax or a fully completed Statement of Value, using the current Pennsylvania form.

How does the Mercer County reassessment affect a house sale?

The last countywide reassessment finished in 1971, and the project to replace those values has slipped by a year. New assessed values take effect for the 2028 tax year instead of 2027, and in 2027 each owner will receive a Final Value Mailer showing land, improvements and the total.

By design, a reassessment does not raise total tax revenue. The county explains that the county, municipalities and school districts are to bill the same total after the change, so millage drops where values rise. In other counties, about a third of owners saw taxes fall, a third saw no change and a third saw an increase. A seller in Mercer County can tell a buyer that the value is likely to be reset soon and that the bill may move in either direction.

Once the mailer arrives, an owner can appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals, and the county code requires formal appeals to be finished by October 31 of the appeal year. For the current tax picture on a parcel, the Assessment Office at 724-662-7551 and the county's GIS parcel viewer show the county, municipal and school bills separately.

More questions about Mercer County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How much is the Mercer County UPI certification fee?

It is $20.00 for each UPI certification, paid to Mercer County Tax Assessment rather than to the Recorder. Naming the parent parcel on a document carries no extra fee.

What is the base price of a Mercer County deed filing?

A deed starts at $71.25, which pays for four pages, four names and one parcel. Each added page runs $2.00, each added name or parcel $0.50, and the Statement of Value tacks on $2.00.

Can Mercer County recording fees go on a credit card?

The county's document standards list cash or checks only. A check should show the account holder's current address and phone number.

Why is Hermitage transfer tax higher than the rest of Mercer County?

The fee bill lists Hermitage and Sharon at 2.5 percent local tax, while Farrell and Greenville charge 2 percent. Other places use the usual 1 percent local share on top of the 1 percent state tax.

When do new Mercer County property values take effect?

The county moved the reassessment to the 2028 tax year. Owners will get a Final Value Mailer in 2027 explaining the new values and how to appeal.

Somerset County by the numbers

Which Somerset County office takes my deed?

Deeds go to the Somerset County Recorder of Deeds, which works out of the County Annex Office Building at 300 North Center Avenue, Suite 400, Somerset, PA 15501. The phone number is (814) 445-1547. The county courthouse sits separately at 111 East Union Street, so a seller who is dropping off paperwork should head to the annex.

The county describes the office as the keeper of records about real property. More than fifty kinds of documents are filed there, among them deeds, mortgages, easements, powers of attorney, leases, agreements of sale, military discharges, subdivision plans and old mine maps. About 12,000 new documents are recorded each year.

What will the Somerset recorder charge on a deed?

The county's fee schedule took effect on November 14, 2025, under Act 45 of 2025. Its stated minimum covers the state fee and the recording fee for one instrument of up to four pages and four names. Any part of a page counts as a whole page, with no exceptions, so a document that spills a few lines onto a fifth sheet is billed for five.

The recorder posts a separate price list for additional pages and a fee sheet for each type of document. Ask the recorder's office for the current total on your deed before closing, since the number depends on page count, names and the type of instrument. The county also asks that the instructions on its fee notice be read closely, so that every filer pays by the same rules.

  • Count pages first, and treat a partial page as a full one.
  • Count every name that has to be indexed.
  • Confirm the fee for any extra document, such as a release or an easement, that comes with the deed.
  • Ask whether the transfer tax is paid separately from the recording fee.

How is transfer tax settled on a Somerset County sale?

The state levies 1 percent of the transferred value, and both the person handing over the deed and the person receiving it answer for the bill. The county recorder collects it, forwards the state's cut and deals with any local piece owed to the municipality or school district. Exemptions exist for some family transfers and for property that passes under a will or by intestacy.

Somerset County's recorder page links to the Department of Revenue's Common Level Ratio page. If your deed involves a gift, an inheritance or a sale well below market, ask the recorder's staff which transfer tax paperwork applies.

What should a Somerset County seller know about the county?

Somerset County is a large, thinly settled county in southwestern Pennsylvania. It was carved out of Bedford County on April 17, 1795, and spreads over 1,074 square miles of land, and has Mount Davis, the highest natural point in the state at 3,213 feet, in its southern part. Wikipedia lists average temperatures in Somerset borough from 24.5 degrees in January to 67.1 in July, a spread that tells a seller to expect a real winter on the roof, gutters and heating system.

Somerset borough is the county seat. By 2010 head count, the biggest municipalities were Somerset Township (12,122), Conemaugh Township (7,452), Somerset borough (6,277) and Windber borough (4,683). The county is known for the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township near Shanksville, and for one of the oldest Amish communities in the country, founded in 1772.

Four in five homes are lived in by their owners and the typical value sits near $150,600, so many sales involve long-held family houses, and probate paperwork shows up often at the recorder's counter.

How can I check records and get alerts from the Somerset County recorder?

The recorder's page offers Landex, an online records service with remote access instructions, plus Record Alert and Notary Alert sign-ups. The office itself cannot enroll anyone, so you register through the Landex links yourself. A Record Alert is useful for homeowners who want to know when anything is filed against their name or property, so a surprise filing does not sit unnoticed.

  • Recorded plat maps are available through the recorder's page.
  • The county GIS parcel viewer draws on Tax Assessment Office and Recorder of Deeds records, and the county warns that it is not for exact measurement.
  • Plans for wind turbines and towers have their own recording rules, including a minimum sheet size of 18 by 24 inches.

How is Somerset County laid out and who lives there?

Somerset County runs along Pennsylvania's southern edge and borders Garrett and Allegany Counties in Maryland, along with Fayette, Westmoreland, Cambria and Bedford Counties in Pennsylvania. Cambria County was split from it in 1804, and its boundaries have held since. Forbes Road, cut through the area in 1758 during the campaign against Fort Duquesne, was one of the early western routes, and settlers from New Jersey reached the Turkeyfoot area around 1770.

Towns beyond the county seat include Windber, Meyersdale, Berlin, Boswell, Central City and Confluence. Census QuickFacts counts 29,344 households with 2.34 people on average, and 93.0% of residents had not moved in the previous year. A bachelor's degree is held by 17.9% of adults, and the typical rent is $753.

  • 1,647 employer establishments employed 18,678 people in 2023.
  • Retail sales totaled about $1.04 billion in 2022.
  • Builders took out 57 permits in 2025, so most buyers choose among existing houses.
  • The mean commute is 24.9 minutes, and 82.0% of households have broadband.

What should I prepare before a Somerset County closing?

Gather the existing deed, the latest tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement and a legible copy of the survey or plat if you have one. Recorded plat maps are available from the recorder's page, and the county parcel viewer helps you confirm the lot lines against the tax map number.

On deed day, count the pages and the names, make sure the notary block is complete, and ask whether your title company will record electronically or in person. A document with a missing acknowledgment costs more time than a lower price ever saves. If a relative died owning the house, the personal representative's authority has to be clear before anyone signs.

What if I want to sell a Somerset County house quickly?

Recording is the last step, so the sale itself comes first. A seller in a hurry can consider a direct cash purchase, which avoids showings, repair requests and financing delays. Expect a lower price than a polished listing, and weigh that against the commission and repairs a listing would cost.

Before any closing, pull your deed, get a payoff letter for any mortgage, and ask the recorder's office whether anything recorded against the parcel needs to be released. A paid-off mortgage with no recorded release is the kind of loose end to find before closing day.

More questions about Somerset County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How do I reach the Somerset recorder in person?

It is at the County Annex Office Building, 300 North Center Avenue, Suite 400, in Somerset. The phone is (814) 445-1547. The courthouse is a separate building at 111 East Union Street.

What does the Somerset minimum recording fee cover?

The minimum covers the state fee and recording fee for one instrument with up to four pages and four names, under the schedule effective November 14, 2025. Call the recorder for the current dollar total for your document.

Is a part of a page billed as a whole page?

Yes. The county's fee notice says any fraction of a page is counted as one page, with no exceptions. Check the page count before you submit so the fee is right the first time.

Can I get an alert when a document is recorded on my property?

Yes. The county links to Landex Record Alert and Notary Alert sign-ups. You must register yourself, because the recorder's office cannot sign people up.

Who pays the state transfer tax on a Somerset sale?

Both sides are liable for the 1 percent state tax. Your sales agreement decides how buyer and seller divide the cost.

Indiana County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Indiana County, Pennsylvania?

Indiana County deeds are recorded at the Register & Recorders Office in the county courthouse, 825 Philadelphia Street, Indiana, PA 15701. The phone is 724-465-3860, the fax is 724-465-3863, and the office is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed on county holidays.

One office combines the Recorder of Deeds, the Register of Wills and the Clerk of Orphans' Court. Its website runs on neumo, formerly GovOS and Kofile, and it takes deeds, mortgages, satisfactions and other land documents in person, by mail or by e-recording through CSC or Simplifile.

The county was formed in 1803 from parts of Westmoreland and Clearfield counties and organized in 1806. Every sale of an Indiana County house ends with the deed going through this counter or its electronic equivalent.

What rules does the Indiana County recorder apply to a deed?

The office publishes a 13-point recording checklist, and it warns that the list may not cover every policy. Reading it before the closing prevents a returned package.

  • The acknowledgment date cannot come before the date on the document, and it must show county, state, date, the name and title of the person appearing, and the notary's signature and expiration date.
  • The municipality, county and state must be stated. For parcels in Blacklick, Canoe or Young Townships, the school district must be named too.
  • The UPI parcel number must appear on every real estate document.
  • Numerals must match the written amount on deeds and mortgages.
  • Mortgages must cite a book and page or instrument number that refers back to the original.
  • Deeds and mortgages need a certified grantee or mortgagee address, and the Certificate of Residence must be signed.
  • A deed with land in more than one municipality must state the percentage split of transfer taxes.
  • When several documents make up one transaction, the order of recording must be marked, for example deed first and then mortgage. Re-recording costs from the wrong order fall on whoever submitted them.

The office does not currently accept e-notarizations. An e-recording that makes staff print extra pages, such as a trust copy filed with a deed or the original deed attached to a corrective one, must be sent on paper or it is rejected. A returned document carries a $5 rejection fee.

What does the Indiana County recorder charge for a deed?

A deed or mortgage is $91.75 on the document listing the office posted for November 1, 2025, which raised its JCS document fees by $1. The office adds that anyone should call to confirm fees, and its fee schedule effective December 1, 2025 sits on the Register & Recorders page.

Indiana County Recorder of Deeds common document fees, November 2025 listing
DocumentFee
Deed, corrective deed, sheriff deed or tax claim deed$91.75
Mortgage or deed of trust$91.75
Mineral rights conveyance$91.75

Release of mortgage or satisfaction piece$81.75
Easement or right of way$81.75
Decree of distribution$81.75

Source: Indiana County Recorder of Deeds JCS document fee listing, effective November 1, 2025.

Add $1 to the total if a stamped, self-addressed return envelope is not included. The office also runs an online fee calculator on its page, and it recommends calling for a firm figure before sending money.

How are checks and transfer tax handled in Indiana County?

Indiana County asks for three separate checks made out to Recorder of Deeds for exact amounts: one for recording fees, one for the 1% municipal transfer tax and one for the state transfer tax. The office's printed fee sheet repeats this by asking for two additional checks on a deed with transfer tax, one for 1% local and one for 1% state.

The deed must either accompany a Statement of Value or state its exemption, for example a transfer between family members. One Statement of Value counts as a page of the document, and a second completed copy must be included for the Department of Revenue.

The state's own page says the 1% rate applies to the value of the real estate and that both grantor and grantee are liable. It also lists exemptions for certain family transfers, transfers to government units and property that passes by will or intestate succession.

What scams should Indiana County owners watch for?

The Register & Recorders Office warns that scammers have tried to sell property in the county, and it urges owners to sign up for its free Property Alert, which notifies them of fraudulent recordings. It also advises watching for drivers who collect information from vacant properties while claiming to work for utility companies.

A second warning covers text messages that say delinquent taxes must be paid or a property will be sold. The county calls these fraudulent, explaining that the tax claim office does not text or call owners. All its notices are written and mailed, and questions go to 724-465-3810.

A seller who has left a house empty while preparing to list can use the alert to see every document recorded against the parcel.

How does an Indiana County estate affect the sale of an inherited house?

The Register of Wills asks anyone opening an estate to make an appointment before arriving, by emailing the office to calculate costs and receive forms. For probate the office wants a copy of the petition, the death certificate, the will and any renunciations, plus the number of short certificates desired, so it can quote a total.

  • Inheritance tax payments can be mailed, and the postmark date is treated as the payment date.
  • Short certificates are the papers a bank asks for, according to the county's FAQ headings.
  • The same courthouse office records the deed that follows, so heirs can finish both steps in Indiana.

Because the county will not change a deed once it is recorded, any correction to a name needs a new, corrective deed. The posted fee for a corrective deed is $91.75, the same as a regular deed, and a corrective deed that needs a copy of the original attached must be filed on paper if it is e-recorded.

Heirs who plan to sell should phone 724-465-3860 first, since probate in this office runs by appointment.

What does Indiana County look like for a home seller?

Indiana County covers 827 square miles of land, with an estimated 82,878 residents in July 2025, nearly flat from the April 2020 base. Census QuickFacts puts the median owner-occupied value at $152,800 and the owner-occupied rate at 72.1% for 2020 to 2024.

Median household income is $60,208, and 16.0% of residents live in poverty, the highest rate among the four counties in that comparison. Only 40 building permits were issued in 2025. Monthly owner costs are $1,266 with a mortgage and $540 without, while the median gross rent is $800.

The borough of Indiana is the seat, and the county calls itself the Christmas Tree Capital of the World, shipping over one million trees a year. Agriculture is a large part of the economy, and the county is part of the Pittsburgh media market. A farm or acreage sale here may involve more than one parcel, and each parcel needs its own UPI number on the deed.

More questions about Indiana County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Does Indiana County accept e-recording?

Yes, through CSC and Simplifile. The office does not currently accept e-notarizations, and an e-recording that needs extra pages printed must be submitted on paper.

What is the rejection fee in Indiana County?

Blacklick, Canoe and Young Townships. The recording requirements say the school district must be stated for parcels in those townships.

Three, each payable to Recorder of Deeds: one for recording fees, one for the 1% municipal transfer tax and one for the state transfer tax.

Armstrong County by the numbers

Which office records deeds in Armstrong County, PA?

In Armstrong County the Register and Recorder handles it, from Suite 102 of the courthouse at 500 E. Market Street in Kittanning. One office combines three jobs: the Recorder of Deeds, the Register of Wills and the Clerk of Orphans' Court. The main phone number is (724) 548-3280.

Counter service for transactions runs from 8:00 a.m. to 3:45 p.m., while records research continues until 4:15 p.m. The office takes cash or check only, with no debit or credit cards.

The recorder's side keeps real estate records safe from loss, theft and damage. It records land documents, veterans' discharges, notary bonds and commissions, and powers of attorney that deal with real estate.

How does a deed get recorded in Armstrong County?

It can be recorded electronically or on paper. The office lists four e-recording vendors: Simplifile, CSC Recording, ePN and Indecomm. A title company that already uses one of them can send the deed without a courier.

The staff checks every document against a fixed list before accepting it.

  • The document date has to fall on or before the acknowledgment date.
  • Deeds and mortgages need a legal description that names the municipality, county and state.
  • The tax map number is required. It is not the same as a parcel number, and the Mapping Department, at (724) 548-3234, can supply it.
  • The acknowledgment needs the notary's signature, a readable stamp and the expiration date.
  • A Certificate of Residence must be completed and signed.
  • Documents with shaded areas are not recorded.

The office says there are no refunds, so the fee has to be right the first time. Multiple documents in one transaction must show their intended recording order on each page, and any re-recording expense caused by wrong order falls on whoever submitted them.

What does transfer tax look like in Armstrong County?

The office describes it as a 1% tax for the state and another 1% for the local governments and school district, paid on separate checks, with a third check for the filing fee. All three are written to the Recorder of Deeds.

A Statement of Value, filed in duplicate, is needed in three situations: the full price is missing from the deed, the deed is a gift or has no consideration, or an exemption is claimed. It is also needed for rights of way and easements. A transfer that is wholly exempt on family grounds does not require one, provided the relationship is written on the deed. The office forwards one copy to the Department of Revenue.

A deed that names a price of $1.00 triggers the form, because the real value is not shown. When land spans more than one municipality, the deed must state each one's percentage so the local tax divides correctly.

The state can later revisit a sale. If an investigator decides the property was worth more than stated, or that an exemption was invalid, the Department of Revenue sends a determination directly to the parties, collects the extra tax and interest itself, and issues a receipt for the recorder to file.

What fees and facts should an Armstrong County seller know?

The recorder's fee schedule is posted as a PDF on the county's Register and Recorder page. Ask the office for the current sheet before closing.

Armstrong County Register and Recorder, facts from the county's own page

Common Level Ratio, July 1, 2025 to June 30, 20263.27

The Common Level Ratio changes each July 1, so the 3.27 factor applied to the year that ended June 30, 2026. Ask the office which factor applies to the date on your deed.

Record searches are by first and last name or by book and page. The office cannot search by tax map number or street address, and its staff do not give searches or legal advice.

Does Armstrong County offer protection against deed fraud?

Yes. The recorder runs a free Record Alert System through Landex, the recording vendor. Anyone who signs up gets an email whenever a document is recorded under their name, and businesses can sign up as well.

The same Landex site holds the county's records for people who search often, with a paid remote subscription for frequent users and a pay-per-document web store for occasional ones. Landex sets those charges, not the county.

Property owners who inherit or sell land in the county can use the alert to catch an unexpected deed or mortgage.

What are the Depreciation Lands in Armstrong County deeds?

The recorder's page explains that the Depreciation Land Program was created for soldiers, sailors and prisoners of war who served in the American Revolution and had been paid in Continental money that lost its value. Pennsylvania set aside roughly 720,000 acres in 1783 for that purpose, per the Depreciation Lands Museum, which the office cites.

Two framed prints of the Depreciation Lands from the Pennsylvania State Archives hang in the recording office. Staff will show a visitor how to use the computer system to locate an old document, though employees do not run searches or give legal interpretation, so a seller who needs a title history should hire a title company or attorney.

What is Armstrong County like?

Armstrong County covers 653 square miles of land in the Greater Pittsburgh region, with the Allegheny River running through it, and it was organized on March 12, 1800, from parts of Allegheny, Westmoreland and Lycoming counties. Kittanning is the county seat. Ford City sits three miles downriver and began as a plate glass company town. Parker, in the northwest corner, is an incorporated city of fewer than 800 people. Worthington, west of Kittanning on U.S. Route 422, is the farming hub.

Coal, natural gas, plate glass, brick and ceramics built the local economy, and gradual population decline set in during the 1970s and 1980s. January averages about 27 degrees in Kittanning and July about 73,.

MeasureArmstrong County

Median household income, 2020-2024$65,008

Only 29 building permits were issued in 2025, so most buyers choose among existing homes. At the $157,300 median value, a combined 2% transfer tax would come to about $3,146.

More questions about Armstrong County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Where is the Armstrong County Recorder of Deeds office?

It is inside the Register and Recorder's office, Suite 102 of the Armstrong County Courthouse at 500 E. Market Street, Kittanning, PA 16201. The telephone is (724) 548-3280.

Can I pay with a credit card at the Armstrong County recorder?

No. The office accepts cash or check only, and it posts that rule in capital letters. Plan checks ahead for the state tax, the local tax and the filing fee.

Is e-recording available for Armstrong County deeds?

Yes. The office lists Simplifile, CSC Recording, ePN and Indecomm as current vendors, so title companies using any of them can submit a deed electronically.

What is a tax map number and why does a deed need one?

It identifies the property in the county's mapping system and has to appear on deeds and mortgages. It is not the parcel number. The Mapping Department at (724) 548-3234 can provide it if you lack it.

Do I need a Statement of Value to record a deed?

You need one if the deed omits the full price, is a gift, or claims an exemption, and it must be filed in duplicate. A transfer wholly exempt because of family ties does not need one when the relationship appears on the deed.

Who records deeds in Lawrence County, Pennsylvania?

The Register of Wills and Recorder of Deeds, a combined office serving the county seat of New Castle. Its page on the county website calls the Recorder's main duty recording, protecting, preserving and reproducing legal documents that relate to real estate.

The same office collects county recording fees, the Real Estate Transfer Tax owed to the state, local municipalities and school districts, and the fees that state law sends to the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts. For anyone selling a house in Lawrence County, that means one counter takes the tax and the fee and files the deed.

Ask the office for its current hours and its last time to accept a deed on a given day, since a title company's schedule depends on it.

How far back do Lawrence County land records go, and can I search them online?

Records reach back to the founding of the county in 1849, and all real estate records are open to the public. Staff say older books are searched in the office, while more recent years can be searched online.

The online service runs on CountyFusion and lets you search, view and print documents dating to about 1970. The county also offers a quick land-records search from its cloud search page, and a free property alert service launched in October 2022 that warns an owner when a document is recorded against their property.

  • Use the online index to pull the previous deed and copy the legal description exactly.
  • Check that the name on the old deed matches the name of the person signing the new one.
  • Look for old mortgages that still show as open, and ask the lender for a satisfaction if one was paid off.

Can a Lawrence County deed be recorded electronically?

Yes. The office tells submitters that e-recording is simple, fast and saves money, and it names four vendors on its website: Simplifile, CSC, Indecomm and EPN. Closing agents who already use one of these can send the deed in without a courier.

Paper still works. A deed can be carried in or mailed to the Recorder, but then you need the exact total in the right form, so call the office for a figure before you write a check. The county's Recorder page links notices about about a state-mandated fee increase dated November 28, 2025 and a separate increase in the parcel ID fee.

What does recording a deed cost in Lawrence County?

A fee sheet from the county's Redevelopment Authority, dated September 29, 2026, gives a concrete picture for a deed. It lists deed recording at $87.75 plus $20.00 for each parcel purchased.

That sheet applies to Authority property sales, so a private sale may differ. Treat the numbers as a guide and get the real total from the Recorder, because the add-ons change with the page count and the number of parcels.

The county's Assessment Office assigns parcel IDs, and it provides a form to request a new one. A deed that covers more than one parcel will therefore cost more to record.

How does transfer tax work on a Lawrence County sale?

Pennsylvania imposes a 1 percent state tax on the value of the transfer, and the Department of Revenue holds both grantor and grantee liable. In the Lawrence County fee sheet the local share is another 1 percent, for a combined 2 percent.

The Recorder remits the state's part to Harrisburg and the rest to the municipality and school district. Certain family transfers, transfers to government, and property that passes by will or intestacy are exempt, but a Statement of Value is still filed to show why.

  • For a sale at $100,000, the combined 2 percent tax would be $2,000, before recording fees.
  • A sale to an outside buyer is an ordinary transfer, so an estate selling a house should plan for the tax in its settlement figures.
  • If title first passes to an heir, the Register of Wills side of the same office can say what paperwork it wants.

What does the Lawrence County Assessment Office handle for a seller?

It values the county's roughly 56,000 parcels, which cover 367 square miles across 27 municipalities. One of them is the city of New Castle, with 8 wards, and the others are nine boroughs and sixteen townships. Ellwood City's second ward lies partly in Beaver County.

The office also runs the Act 72 Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion and the Clean and Green program, and it keeps the county's GIS tax maps. Its forms page lists a sales verification form, a change of address form, and a property owner contact form tied to Act 29 of 2026.

The Assessment Board meets monthly, and the county posts agendas for each 2026 meeting. If you sell a homestead property, ask the office how the sale affects the exclusion and update your mailing address with its change of address form.

What is Lawrence County like for someone who has to sell a house?

Lawrence County was created on March 20, 1849, from parts of Beaver and Mercer counties, when New Castle was outgrowing its home county. It covers 363 square miles in the Greater Pittsburgh region and drains through the Shenango and Mahoning rivers into the Beaver River. South New Castle borough was annexed by Shenango Township on January 1, 2026. I-76, I-79, I-376 and US 422 cross the county.

Three in four households own, and the Census Bureau puts the median home value at $147,200. Winters are cold, with New Castle averaging 27.7 degrees in January against 72.2 in July.

What should I bring to record a Lawrence County deed?

Pull these together before the closing date.

  • The signed, notarized deed with the full legal description.
  • The parcel ID for each parcel being conveyed.
  • A Statement of Value if tax is excused or the price is not stated.
  • Payment for the recording fee, the parcel ID charge and the transfer tax, in the form the office accepts.
  • A return address for the recorded deed.

If a title company is handling the sale, confirm that they file electronically through one of the four vendors and ask when the recorded copy will arrive.

More questions about Lawrence County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Does Lawrence County accept electronic recording?

Yes. The Recorder of Deeds lists four e-recording vendors on the county site: Simplifile, CSC, Indecomm and EPN. A closing agent with an account at one of them can submit the deed without a trip to New Castle.

How far back can I search Lawrence County deeds online?

The online system covers documents from about 1970 forward. County records start with the formation of the county in 1849, and the older volumes are searched in the office.

How much is transfer tax on a Lawrence County home sale?

The combined rate in the county's fee sheet is 2 percent, made up of 1 percent state tax and 1 percent local tax. On a $100,000 sale that is $2,000. Exempt transfers, such as some family transfers, file a Statement of Value instead.

Is there a way to be warned if someone records a document on my property?

Yes. The county announced a free property alert service in October 2022. It is meant as fraud protection, and the Recorder's page lists it among its press releases.

What office issues parcel IDs in Lawrence County?

The county Assessment Office. It posts a Request for a New Parcel ID Number form, and it can tell you which parcels a deed must name. Every parcel on a deed adds to the recording cost.
