Where do you record a deed in Wayne County, PA?

At the Recorder of Deeds office in the Wayne County Courthouse Annex, 925 Court Street, Honesdale, PA 18431. The phone is 570-253-5970, extension 4040. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and nothing is accepted for recording after 4:00 p.m.

Wayne County calls the office the custodian of the records and indexes for land transfers. It keeps deeds, mortgages, subdivision plans, rights-of-way and easements, and it also records the commissions and oaths of county officials, district justices and notaries, plus military discharges. A house sale in Wayne County ends here: after closing, the signed deed is recorded in Honesdale, and the new owner appears in the public record from that point.

The county asks one thing of readers up front. Staff cannot give legal advice or attorney referrals, so questions about how to word a deed belong with a lawyer, and the Wayne County Bar Association keeps a member list.

What new Uniform Parcel Identifier rule started in Wayne County in November 2026?

UPI certification began on November 2, 2026, at $20.00 per UPI number. The county posted the start date and the fee at the top of its recorder page, and its tax sale page notes that the Wayne County UPI Ordinance was adopted, with a $20.00 fee for each Uniform Parcel Identifier beginning that date.

For a seller, the practical effect is simple. A deed for a parcel now involves a certification step, and a sale that covers more than one parcel pays the $20.00 once per UPI number. Ask the recorder's office for the UPI notice, and have your closing agent or attorney confirm when the certification has to be completed.

The same date changed another number. The county's tax sale page says the deed recording fee became $94.75 as of November 2, 2026. That figure appears in the context of a tax sale deed, so ask the office to confirm the charge for an ordinary private sale deed.

What charges does Wayne County name on its recorder and tax sale pages?

Wayne County posts a fee schedule as a spreadsheet and a PDF, and the figures below are the ones stated on the county's web pages themselves.

Wayne County fees stated on county web pages
ItemAmountApplies to
UPI certification$20.00 per UPI numberDocuments recorded from November 2, 2026

Deed preparation fee, tax sale$25Added to a repository sale purchase

For a plain deed, the county's page does not print one total, so call 570-253-5970, extension 4040, or open the fee schedule on the county's Recorder of Deeds page. The schedule is dated November 2026, and it lists fees by document type.

How can a Wayne County deed be e-recorded?

Through one of two vendors: CSC at 866-652-0111 or Simplifile at 800-460-5657. Most land-related documents can be sent that way without a trip to Honesdale.

Two kinds of document cannot be e-recorded and must be delivered on paper: subdivision plans, and deeds that are taxable in more than one jurisdiction. The second exception comes up when a parcel lies in more than one municipality: the deed then has to state the percentage in each so the local transfer tax divides correctly.

  • E-recorded transactions with a REV-183 Statement of Value attach helper pages, and those pages cost $0.50 each.
  • Paper filings go to the courthouse annex before the 4:00 p.m. cutoff.
  • Faxed or emailed copies are not accepted for recording.

What does the Wayne County recorder require on a deed?

The county publishes a checklist, and it is stricter than many sellers expect. An acknowledgment must show the county, state, date, the people or corporate officers appearing, and the notary's signature, stamp and expiration date. If any of those is missing, the acknowledgment is treated as defective.

  • The written amount of consideration has to match the number on the deed.
  • Every deed, mortgage and assignment needs a signed certification of the grantee's address with zip code.
  • Transfer taxes or a completed Statement of Value must accompany every deed.
  • Black ink and white or manila paper only, since the office scans everything.
  • Documents may not exceed 8 1/2 by 14 inches, and maps may not exceed 24 by 36 inches.
  • Recorded papers come back by mail only if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

What is Wayne County like for a house sale?

It is a rural, lake-and-hill county in the Poconos with a small population. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 51,703 people on about 726 square miles of land, which works out to roughly 70 people per square mile. The county was formed in 1798 from part of Northampton County, and Honesdale is both the seat and the largest borough.

QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows 80.5 percent owner-occupancy, a median owner-occupied home value of $242,100, median gross rent of $1,038 and median household income of $62,381. Residents aged 65 or older make up 27.2 percent of the population, which is high, and 32,637 housing units serve only 20,877 households.

The county's boroughs are Bethany, Hawley, Honesdale, Prompton, Starrucca and Waymart. Terrain varies from rugged ground along the New York border to a wide central plain, and the Delaware River separates the county from New York. Winters are cold, with Honesdale averaging about 22.8 degrees in January, so heating systems and roofs draw attention at inspection. Six school districts serve the county: Forest City Regional, North Pocono, Susquehanna Community, Wallenpaupack Area, Wayne Highlands and Western Wayne.

What should a Wayne County seller know about assessments and unpaid taxes?

The Assessment Office maintains property records and prepares the tax rolls, and it does not set millage rates or collect taxes. It sits at 925 Court Street in Honesdale, phone 570-253-5970, extension 4010, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The county has 28 municipalities and 6 school districts, all of which draw on those rolls.

Back taxes go to the Tax Claim Bureau, extension 4000, at the same address. It runs sales under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, and unsold properties go on a repository list. Repository sales are held quarterly in February, May, August and November, and the owner can pay up to the day of the sale. Buyers at a repository sale pay costs, a $25 deed preparation fee and 2 percent transfer tax, and Act 33 requires every bidder to pre-register.

If a back-tax balance sits on the house you want to sell, ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff figure before closing.

More questions about Wayne County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What are the Wayne County Recorder of Deeds hours?

The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., but it takes no documents for recording after 4:00 p.m. It is in the Courthouse Annex at 925 Court Street in Honesdale, and the phone is 570-253-5970, extension 4040.

Is there a new fee for parcel identifiers in Wayne County?

Yes. Uniform Parcel Identifier certification began on November 2, 2026, and costs $20.00 per UPI number. The county's recorder page links a UPI notice that explains the process.

Can I e-record a Wayne County deed?

Yes, with exceptions. Use CSC (866-652-0111) or Simplifile (800-460-5657). Subdivision plans and deeds taxable in multiple jurisdictions cannot be e-recorded and must go in on paper.

Does Wayne County mail back a recorded deed?

Only if you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope when you submit it. Without one, the Recorder's Office does not mail recorded documents.

Where do I see who owns a Wayne County parcel?

Search recorded documents on Landex, which the county uses for online records. Index searching is free, and you pay only when you buy copies of documents to download or print.

Who records deeds in Huntingdon County, Pennsylvania?

The Huntingdon County Register & Recorder handles deed recording. The county is sixth class, and its Register & Recorders Office covers three jobs: the Register of Wills, the Recorder of Deeds and the Clerk of the Orphans' Court. The post is elected for a four-year term.

Call (814) 643-2740 and choose option 2 for fee schedules, deeds, wills and marriage licenses. Recorded documents in this office run from 1787 to the present, which matches the year Huntingdon County was created from the northern part of Bedford County plus a strip from Cumberland County.

Deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, releases, subdivision plans, agreements and easements, highway maps and secured transactions all live here. A seller in Huntingdon County meets the office at the end of a sale, when the signed deed is recorded and the new owner enters the public index.

What is a UPI number and why does Huntingdon County require it?

A UPI is the Uniform Parcel Identifier, and Huntingdon County has required one on real estate documents since October 1, 2014 under county Ordinance 2014-2. It is the same number that appears as the tax parcel number on a tax bill and in the County Assessment Office.

The Assessment Department, acting through its Mapping Department, compares the document against county records and either accepts or rejects it based on the accuracy of that number. The county says the check exists to keep recorded documents accurate and to help later real estate searches.

  • The UPI must be the first line on the document, below the top margin.
  • The top margin must be at least 2 inches.
  • The certification fee is $20 for each UPI number certified, paid along with the other recording fees to the Recorder of Deeds.

A deed that covers a house and a separate lot can carry two parcel numbers, and each certified number adds $20 to the recording bill.

How does the UPI certification process work in Huntingdon County?

Walk-in customers take documents to the Mapping Department at 233 Penn Street in Huntingdon, PA 16652, between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. on weekdays except holidays. A submission made after 4:15 p.m. is processed on the next business day.

Mail-in and e-file customers send documents to the Recorder of Deeds, which processes them in the order received. The Mapping Department collects mail-in documents daily and returns them to the recorder within one business day.

This split matters for timing. A closing agent who delivers a deed in person at 4:20 p.m. has missed the same-day certification window, while a package submitted electronically goes through the recorder first and does not need a trip to Penn Street. Ask the Register & Recorders Office which route fits the closing schedule.

What does it cost to record a deed in Huntingdon County?

The base recording fee for a deed or mortgage is set by the county's fee schedule, and the office quotes it by phone at (814) 643-2740, option 2. One add-on is fixed on the county page: $20 per UPI number certified.

Ask for the full total before the closing, including any per-page charge, transfer tax and the UPI line for each parcel. Whoever runs the closing sends these amounts with the deed, and the figures belong on the settlement statement.

Realty transfer tax is the larger cost. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue puts the state rate at 1% of the value of the real estate, collected by county recorders, usually along with an additional local tax. Both grantor and grantee are liable for the tax, and the recorder passes the state's 1% along to the Department.

The state page lists transfers that are exempt, among them certain transfers between family members, transfers to government units, deeds to burial sites, and property that passes by will or intestate succession.

What should a Huntingdon County seller check before the deed is signed?

Start with the parcel number. Look at the latest tax bill, or ask the County Assessment Office, so the number typed on the first line of the deed matches the records the Mapping Department will compare it with.

  • Confirm the margin: at least 2 inches at the top of the first page, with the UPI number on the first line below it.
  • Decide how the deed will travel. In person it goes to the Mapping Department first, while mail and e-file documents go to the recorder, who passes them along for certification.
  • List every parcel being conveyed, because each UPI number certified is $20.
  • Ask the Register & Recorders Office for the total recording fee before the closing date.
  • If the transfer claims an exemption from realty transfer tax, ask the Department of Revenue or the closing attorney which paperwork supports it.

The county also notes that documents recorded in its office cover subdivision plans. A seller who divided off a lot should check whether the plan was recorded, because a deed that references a lot needs a recorded description to point to.

Are military discharge papers public in Huntingdon County?

No. Military discharge records are recorded in the Recorder of Deeds office, but they are secure records closed to the public. A DD-214 is given only to the veteran, who must show proper identification.

Anyone else asking for the information is directed to the Veterans' Affairs Officer at (814) 643-1360. Census QuickFacts counts 2,980 veterans in Huntingdon County for 2020 to 2024.

A seller who is a veteran and needs the document for a loan or a benefit should bring identification to the recorder's office in person.

What do the Census numbers say about Huntingdon County homes?

Huntingdon County has an estimated 43,001 residents in 2025, down 2.4% from the April 2020 base, and 79.2% of homes are owner-occupied. The county covers 874.65 square miles of land, making population density about 50 people per square mile.

Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024$183,200
Owner costs with a mortgage, monthly$1,336
Owner costs without a mortgage, monthly$501
Median gross rent$810

Housing units, July 202521,148
Building permits, 202564
Mean commute, minutes31.2

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, Huntingdon County, Pennsylvania.

Wikipedia's county page shows 19.2% of housing units were vacant in the 2020 census, and 74.3% of residents lived in rural areas. The Census commute figure of 31.2 minutes is the longest of the four counties compared in that QuickFacts table, so a typical Huntingdon County worker spends more than half an hour getting to a job.

What is the setting around the Huntingdon County courthouse?

Huntingdon County sits in central Pennsylvania, with the borough of Huntingdon as its seat and its own micropolitan statistical area. It spans 875 square miles of land and 15 square miles of water, and its humid continental climate runs from an average of 27.8 degrees in January to 72.3 in July at Huntingdon borough.

The Kishacoquillas Valley has Amish and Mennonite communities, and Pennsylvania Dutch is heard there. With three-quarters of residents in rural areas, a Huntingdon County deed often describes land in more than one tax parcel, and each parcel needs its own UPI certification.

The county's population fell between the 2010 and 2020 censuses from 45,913 to 44,092, a loss of 1,821 residents. Sellers weighing a sale in that setting should ask early what the deed and recording will cost.

More questions about Huntingdon County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Where do I record a deed in Huntingdon County?

Record it with the Register & Recorders Office, reachable at (814) 643-2740, option 2. UPI certification for walk-ins happens at the Mapping Department, 233 Penn Street in Huntingdon.

How much is UPI certification in Huntingdon County?

It is $20 per UPI number certified. The fee is submitted to the Recorder of Deeds with the other recording fees.

What is the cutoff for same-day UPI certification in Huntingdon County?

A walk-in submission to the Mapping Department after 4:15 p.m. is processed on the next business day. Walk-in hours run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays.

How far back do Huntingdon County recorded documents go?

The county says recorded documents in the Recorder of Deeds office date from 1787 to the present day.

Who can get a military discharge record in Huntingdon County?

Only the veteran, with proper identification. Others contact the Veterans' Affairs Officer at (814) 643-1360.

Union County by the numbers

Where do I take a deed in Lewisburg?

You will find the office inside the Union County Courthouse, 103 South Second Street, Lewisburg, PA 17837. Call (570) 524-8762 with questions. It shares space with the Register of Wills, and the same elected office covers both jobs. The counter is open from 8:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon, though the county notes that document recording concludes at 4:15 p.m.

That fifteen minute gap trips up closings. A deed brought in at 4:20 is not recorded that day, so a title agent or seller who needs same-day recording should plan to arrive well before the cutoff.

What does the Union County recorder do?

Its job is to record paperwork tied to land and buildings: deeds, mortgages, releases, easements and rights of way, subdivisions and restrictions. It also records notary and county officer information and military service discharges. Records from January 1, 1962 to the present can be searched online, and anything earlier is on microfilm.

The recorder also collects the real estate transfer tax for the state, the townships, the boroughs and the school districts. That makes it the last stop in a sale: the buyer and seller sign at closing, then the deed is recorded here and the taxes are paid at the same time.

What are the recording rules for a deed in Union County?

The county publishes a short list of recording requirements, and a document that misses one comes back unrecorded. Mailed documents that cannot be recorded are returned with a letter of explanation and a $3.00 charge.

  • The acknowledgment must show the county, state, date, the people or corporate officers who appeared, and the notary's signature, seal and expiration date.
  • The notary stamp must be clear, and the stamp, seal and signature must not overlap one another.
  • Every deed, mortgage and mortgage assignment needs a signed certificate of address for the grantee, mortgagee or assignee.
  • A re-recorded document needs fresh acknowledgments and a note on why it is being filed again.
  • A Statement of Value, when one is required, must be filed in duplicate, fully completed, signed and dated.
  • Each recorded document and each transfer tax payment gets its own check, payable to Union County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Blanket documents are refused, and checks must be for the exact amount because no refunds are given.
  • Return by mail needs a stamped, self-addressed envelope supplied at the time of recording.

What will Union County charge to record my deed?

The county posts a recorder's fee schedule on its website, and the amount depends on the type of document, its page count and the number of names. Ask the office at (570) 524-8762 for the current total on your deed before you write the check, since checks must match the fee exactly.

On top of that, the state takes 1 percent of the property's value as transfer tax, with buyer and seller sharing the legal duty to pay. The recorder sends the state portion onward, and local governments may divide their own tax between municipalities and school districts. Some family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt.

What does a Union County seller need to know about the county?

Union County is one of the smallest counties in Pennsylvania, the fourth smallest by area, at 316 square miles of land. Wikipedia reports that it was created on March 22, 1813 from part of Northumberland County. Mifflinburg was the first county seat, New Berlin took over in 1815, and Lewisburg has held the role since 1855.

It is also far more densely settled than Somerset or Venango County, with 135.1 residents per square mile in 2020 against 69.0 and 74.8 there. The county has four boroughs, Hartleton, Lewisburg, Mifflinburg and New Berlin, and its main roads include Interstate 80, US 15 and PA 45. In 2010 Lewisburg had 5,792 residents and Mifflinburg 3,540.

A typical owned home at $240,100 is worth well over the Somerset and Venango figures, and 27.7% of homes are rented, so a house sold with a tenant in place is a real possibility. Tenant questions belong in the sales contract, not at the recorder's counter.

How is Union County laid out and who lives there?

Union County sits in central Pennsylvania and borders Lycoming, Northumberland, Snyder, Mifflin, Centre and Clinton Counties. R. B. Winter State Park and Sand Bridge State Park lie within its borders, and the overlook at Shikellamy State Park is in the county as well. Wikipedia lists average temperatures in Lewisburg from 27.2 degrees in January to 72.7 in July.

Census QuickFacts counts 14,546 households averaging 2.30 people. Residents move more often than in the other two counties, since only 79.3% stayed in the same house over the prior year, and 26.5% of adults have a bachelor's degree. The average commute is a short 17.9 minutes, and 11.0% speak another language at home.

  • 960 employer establishments employed 16,233 people in 2023.
  • Health care businesses took in about $566 million in 2022.
  • Median monthly owner costs are $1,625 with a mortgage and $585 without one.
  • The county recorded 63 building permits in 2025.

Why does Union County recording go smoothly for some sales and not others?

Rejected recordings usually trace back to the acknowledgment or the checks. The county's own list shows how specific the office is: a legible notary stamp, a seal that does not overlap the signature, a certificate of address and exact payment. Two sellers closing on the same day can have different outcomes simply because one deed had a clean notary block and the other did not.

If a house is being sold by an estate, the Register of Wills sits in the same office and handles probate and inheritance tax, with checks for inheritance tax payable to Union County Register of Wills, Agent. A seller settling an estate can often resolve both matters on one visit to the courthouse in Lewisburg.

What should a seller bring to the Union County recorder?

Most sales are recorded by the title company, but a seller who handles the paperwork should assemble the signed and notarized deed, the certificate of address for the buyer, a Statement of Value when the tax is not paid in full, separate checks for the recording fee and for each tax payment, and a stamped return envelope. Having every item on this list in one folder is what keeps a closing from slipping a day.

  • Deed with a complete, legible notary block.
  • Signed certificate of address for the grantee.
  • Checks written to Union County Recorder of Deeds, one per document and per tax.
  • Statement of Value in duplicate, if it applies.

A seller who wants to skip showings and repairs can ask for a direct cash purchase on a timeline of their own choosing, and the recording steps above are the same either way.

More questions about Union County, PA Recorder of Deeds

When does the Union County recorder stop taking documents?

Recording ends at 4:15 p.m., even though the office stays open for fifteen minutes longer. Anything that arrives after 4:15 waits for the next business day.

Will the Union County office accept a deed by mail?

Yes, as long as you enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope and the right checks. A document that cannot be recorded is returned with a letter of explanation and a $3.00 fee.

How far back do Union County online records go?

Records from January 1, 1962 to the present can be searched online. Earlier records were placed on microfilm and are available through the office.

Can one check cover everything?

No. The recording requirements call for separate checks for each recorded document and for each realty transfer tax payment, all in the correct amount.

Which Union County office collects the transfer tax?

The Recorder of Deeds collects it for the state, townships, boroughs and school districts. The state rate is 1 percent, and local shares are added by the municipalities and districts.

Venango County by the numbers

Which Venango County office takes my deed?

The Register and Recorder office handles deeds from the county courthouse, 1168 Liberty Street, Franklin, PA 16323, with a mailing box at P.O. Box 831. It opens on weekdays at 8:30 in the morning, closes at 4:30 in the afternoon and shuts for legal holidays.

The same elected office also serves as Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court, so probate filings, marriage licenses and real estate recordings all run through one courthouse counter. A seller dealing with an inherited house will often visit for both reasons.

Can Venango County deeds be recorded electronically?

Yes. The county says electronic filing of real estate documents is handled by CSC eRecording Solutions, reachable at 866-652-0111. Title companies and attorneys commonly use e-recording because it skips the courthouse trip and the mail time, and it fits well when buyer and seller sign in different places.

The Register and Recorder's page does not print the recording fees in the text of the page. It tells filers to contact the office for fees or a fee schedule, and the county also posts a Recorder of Deeds fee schedule dated November 2025 in its document library. Call the office for the exact total on your deed before you send payment.

How is transfer tax handled in a Venango County sale?

The recorder collects it when the deed is filed. The state's cut is 1 percent of the value, and the person conveying and the person receiving the property both answer for it. Local governments can add a tax of their own and split it between school districts and municipalities.

  • Exempt transfers include some family gifts, transfers to government bodies and property passed by will or intestacy.
  • Of what the state collects, 15 percent is set aside for the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund and most of the remainder reaches the General Fund.
  • The sales contract sets who pays in practice, so read that clause before you sign.

Venango County has two cities, Franklin and Oil City, plus boroughs and townships, and the local share depends on where the parcel sits. Ask the recorder which municipality and school district your parcel falls in before you work out your net proceeds.

Why does oil history matter for a Venango County house?

Venango County was created in 1800 and organized in 1805, and its name comes from a Native American word for otter. The county is tied to the start of the oil industry. On August 28, 1859, George Bissell and Edwin L. Drake used the first successful drilling rig near Titusville, and the well sat less than a mile inside the Venango County line. Oil boom towns followed, among them Franklin, Oil City and the now vanished Pithole City.

The industry also shaped the land. French Creek, which runs 117 miles, joins the Allegheny River near Franklin, and Riverfront Park in Franklin sits at that meeting point. A seller with an older house in the two cities should expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at the foundation, wiring and plumbing.

What do the Venango County housing numbers show?

Venango County has been losing residents for decades. Its population peaked at 65,328 in 1950 and stood at 50,454 in 2020. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 49,346, down 2.2% from the 2020 base. By 2018 estimates, Oil City (9,897), Cranberry Township (6,789), Franklin (6,231) and Sugar Creek borough (5,008) were the largest places.

With a median value near $119,800 and 26,293 housing units serving 21,397 households, a house that needs work faces a modest price ceiling, and repair costs can eat most of the gain.

How is Venango County laid out and who lives there?

The county covers 683 square miles, 674 of them land, in northwestern Pennsylvania. It borders Crawford, Warren, Forest, Clarion, Butler and Mercer Counties. The Drake Well Museum stands in Cherrytree Township, and the area around Oil City and Franklin is known as the Oil Region.

Census QuickFacts shows a settled, older population. Households average 2.28 people, 90.5% of residents did not move in the past year, and 27.2% are 65 or older. Just 19.1% of adults have a bachelor's degree, and the average commute is 23.1 minutes. Median household income is $61,522, and 13.2% of residents live in poverty.

  • 1,134 employer establishments employed 14,230 people in 2023.
  • Health care businesses took in about $361 million in 2022, and retail sales reached about $754 million.
  • The county recorded 50 building permits in 2025, a sign of how little new construction competes with existing houses.

How has the Venango County population changed over time?

The county grew fast during the oil boom, from 25,043 residents in 1860 to 47,925 in 1870. After a dip to 43,670 in 1880 it climbed past 56,000 by 1910 and peaked at 65,328 in 1950. Since then each census has counted fewer people, ending at 59,381 in 1990, 54,984 in 2010 and 50,454 in 2020.

One early oil figure is worth knowing: Henry Huttleston Rogers started his first refinery venture, the Wamsutta Oil Refinery, in 1861 at McClintocksville in Cornplanter Township, before he joined Standard Oil. Stories like that explain why so many Venango County properties have old deeds, old easements and mineral questions, and why a title search matters on a long-held parcel. Ask your title company to look for recorded easements, rights of way and releases ahead of closing.

Which Venango County communities do sellers come from?

The county has two cities, Franklin, which is the seat, and Oil City, the largest place. Boroughs include Sugar Creek, Pleasantville, Polk, Emlenton, Rouseville, Clintonville, Cooperstown, Barkeyville and Utica. Cranberry and Cornplanter are the two most populous townships, and Hasson Heights, Woodland Heights and Seneca are census-designated places.

Because each of these has its own municipal government, a parcel's zoning, permit rules and local tax shares depend on the address. Before listing, call the borough, city or township office that covers your house and ask what an inspector or buyer is likely to raise. The recorder's staff can tell you which municipality and school district a parcel belongs to when the deed is filed.

How do I look up real estate tax rates in Venango County?

The county publishes a Real Estate Tax Millages page with a PDF for every year from 2005 through 2026. Check the latest sheet for your municipality and school district, since the millage that applies to a house depends on where it sits. Ask the county's Tax Assessment Office, also in the courthouse complex, about the assessed value behind that bill.

Buyers will ask for the figures, so keep your last tax bill handy when you talk to a title company. A seller who would rather skip repairs can consider a direct as-is cash purchase, since fixing an older home can cost more than the market returns.

More questions about Venango County, PA Recorder of Deeds

When is the Venango County recorder open?

Weekdays from 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., closed on legal holidays, in the courthouse at 1168 Liberty Street in Franklin.

Is e-recording available in Venango County?

Yes. The county names CSC eRecording Solutions as the processor of electronic real estate filings, at 866-652-0111. Your title company or attorney can usually set this up.

Where are the Venango County recording fees listed?

The county posts a Recorder of Deeds fee schedule from November 2025 in its document library, and the Register and Recorder's page tells you to contact the office for fees. Call before you send a check.

Who handles probate for a Venango County house?

The Register of Wills handles probate and collects inheritance tax for the Commonwealth. In Venango County that office is combined with the Recorder and the Clerk of Orphans' Court.

What transfer tax rate applies in Venango County?

The state's piece is 1 percent of the value. A municipality and school district may add shares, so ask the recorder for the combined rate on your parcel.

Who records deeds in Elk County?

Elk County deeds are recorded by the Recorder of Deeds, which shares an office with the Register of Wills and the Clerk of Orphans' Court. The delivery address is 250 Main Street, Ridgway, PA 15853, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 314, Ridgway, PA 15853.

Ridgway is the county seat, while St. Marys is the largest city. A seller who lives in St. Marys or Johnsonburg and mails a deed to Ridgway should allow time for delivery, and a title company will usually handle that step through e-recording instead. The office lists Simplifile and CSC as its current e-recording partners.

The office describes its mission as recording, protecting and reproducing legal documents that relate to Elk County real estate. It also acts as collecting agent for the Commonwealth, the local school districts and the municipalities when realty transfer tax is due. Records since 1843 are open to public inspection, except military discharges.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Elk County?

A standard Elk County deed costs $92.75 to record under the schedule that took effect December 1, 2025. That price covers four names, four pages and one parcel, and the schedule lists the fees as exclusive of state and local realty transfer tax.

Elk County Recorder of Deeds fees, schedule effective December 1, 2025
DocumentFee
Deed or mortgage$92.75
Quit claim deed or easement$79.75
Satisfaction or release of mortgage$81.75
Assignment of mortgage$81.75
Sheriff's deed or correction deed$81.75
Tax claim deed$79.75
Power of attorney$18.50
UCC filing$100.00

Extra pages are $2.00 each, extra names are $0.50 each, and extra parcels on deed documents are $0.50 each. A subdivision or survey map 18 by 24 inches or smaller is $50.00, and a larger map is $62.50.

The office accepts credit and debit cards through AllPaid for transactions that do not involve realty transfer tax or inheritance tax. AllPaid adds a convenience fee of 2.5% of the transaction, with a $3.99 minimum.

What does the Elk County recorder require on a deed?

The office has a short list of rules that title agents and do-it-yourself sellers both run into. Check the document against it before you send it.

  • Leave a 1-inch top margin on every page, because the office stamps recording data automatically.
  • Put the tax parcel identifier (UPI) on any instrument that affects land.
  • State the true consideration on every deed.
  • Pay state realty transfer tax with its own check or electronic payment.
  • Attach an original signed Statement of Value (REV-183) plus a copy if you claim an exemption from tax, unless the deed itself states the reason.

If the property lies in more than one taxing jurisdiction, the person recording must state the percentage of the property in each. Fees and taxes are due when the document is recorded, so a closing agent should bring payment with the package.

How is realty transfer tax handled in Elk County?

The recorder collects state and local realty transfer tax at recording, and the state share has to be paid separately from the other fees. The office page asks check payers to put the state tax on its own check.

Elk County's municipalities and school districts set their own local share, and the rate depends on where the house is. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate for your township, borough or the city of St. Marys before you set a net-proceeds figure. The county's municipal list includes Benezette, Fox, Highland, Horton, Jay, Jones, Millstone, Ridgway and Spring Creek townships, along with Johnsonburg and Ridgway boroughs and St. Marys.

Heirs who sell an inherited house deal with the same office, which also issues letters and keeps wills. That is useful when a deed cannot be signed until someone has authority to act for the estate.

How do you search Elk County deeds online?

Deeds from 1864 to the present can be searched online, while anything older has to be searched at the office. Guests can view records with some information redacted. An account with a credit card lets you save or print an unredacted copy, and the price is 50 cents per page, the same as in the office.

Older books lettered A through Z need four zeros ahead of the letter in the search tool, for example 0000B. The search page also has a live chat link to the software vendor if the search tool misbehaves.

  • Records open to inspection: since 1843, except military discharges
  • Online searchable: 1864 to present
  • Older than 1864: search in person at the office

What estate paperwork sits alongside a deed in Elk County?

The Register of Wills fee schedule effective December 1, 2025 shows the filing costs an estate faces before a house can be sold. Letters testamentary or of administration start at $76.25 for an estate not exceeding $1,000 and rise with the value of the estate. The fee includes the $41.25 judicial computer and access to justice surcharge.

  • Probate of a will only: $15.00 for the first page, $2.00 for each added page
  • Short certificates: $5.00 each
  • Certified copy of a will: $10.00 for the first 10 pages
  • Inheritance tax return filing: $15.00
  • Certification of inheritance tax paid, issuing: $15.00

Ask the Register of Wills which of these filings your estate needs. A buyer's title company will want letters in hand before it closes on a deed signed by an executor or administrator.

What is Elk County like for a home seller?

Elk County covers 832 square miles, most of it wooded rolling hills, and part of the Allegheny National Forest lies inside it. The county was created on April 18, 1843 from parts of Jefferson, Clearfield and McKean Counties and takes its name from the eastern elk that once lived here. Bendigo State Park and Elk State Park are both inside the county.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 29,926 people, down 3.4% from the 2020 base, and 26.5% of residents are 65 or older. There are 16,968 housing units, 79.5% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $133,600. Median gross rent is $719.

Elk County's assessment office says the county has used a 50% ratio since the countywide reassessment of 2005, which took effect in 2006. Its FAQ lists total county, municipal and school mills at 16.15 for 2025 and 18.40 for 2026 in its example. Highways serving sellers and buyers include US 219 and PA 120, PA 255 and PA 948.

Ridgway averages 23.2 degrees in January and 67.4 in July, so winters are long. A mean commute of 18.3 minutes and a density of 37.5 people per square mile show how different this market is from southeast Pennsylvania.

More questions about Elk County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How much does it cost to record a deed in Elk County?

A deed costs $92.75 under the December 1, 2025 schedule, with four names, four pages and one parcel included. Extra pages are $2.00 each and extra names or parcels are $0.50 each.

Where is the Elk County Recorder of Deeds?

It is at 250 Main Street, Ridgway, PA 15853, in the office shared with the Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court. Mail goes to P.O. Box 314, Ridgway, PA 15853.

Does Elk County accept e-recording?

Yes. The office lists Simplifile and CSC as its current e-recording partners. Title companies usually submit seller deeds this way.

Can I pay Elk County recording fees by credit card?

Yes, for transactions that do not involve realty transfer tax or inheritance tax. AllPaid charges a convenience fee of 2.5% of the transaction, with a $3.99 minimum.

How far back do Elk County online deed records go?

Online deed search covers 1864 to the present. Deeds recorded before 1864 must be searched in the office at this time.

Bedford County by the numbers

Who records deeds in Bedford County, Pennsylvania?

The Recorder of Deeds division of the combined Register and Recorder office handles every deed, mortgage, lease, survey, financing statement and right of way in Bedford County. It is in Room 106 on the first floor of the Bedford County Courthouse, 200 S Juliana St, Bedford, PA 15522. The phone is (814) 623-4836 and the email is randr@bedfordcountypa.org.

The county describes its holdings as permanent records dating back to 1771, the year Bedford County was created from part of Cumberland County. The office also keeps records for several neighbors listed on the county site: Huntingdon, Somerset, Centre, Cambria, Blair and Fulton. Seven public workstations let title searchers, lenders and genealogists look documents up on their own, though staff do not run title searches for visitors.

Closing agents can file electronically through Simplifile and CSC, so a seller usually never visits the counter. The office also offers FraudSleuth, a free service that lets owners confirm which recordings are authorized.

What are the office hours and same-day recording cutoff?

The counter is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and closed on designated county holidays. Same-day recording stops at 4:00 p.m., and the register and recorder page describes recording as taking place from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Plan around that earlier cutoff. For a quick close, ask the title company to submit the deed well before 4:00 p.m. rather than carrying paper in at the end of the day.

  • Same-day cutoff: 4:00 p.m.
  • Mail goes to Recorder of Deeds Division, Bedford County Courthouse, 200 S Juliana St, Room 106, Bedford, PA 15522.
  • Every mailed filing needs a self-addressed stamped envelope for return of the documents.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Bedford County?

A deed is $59.75 on the fee bill effective November 20, 2025. That figure already includes the state and county taxes the schedule folds in, and it assumes a document with no more than four names and four pages. Each additional name adds $0.50 and each additional page adds $2.00.

Bedford County recording fees, from the Recorder's fee bill effective November 20, 2025
DocumentFee
Deed$59.75
Mortgage$59.75
Satisfaction piece$59.75
Release of mortgage$61.75
Assignment of mortgage$61.75
Easement$59.75
Power of attorney$18.50
Photocopy, per page$0.25
Certified copy$1.00 plus $0.25 a page
Soldier discharge (DD-214)Free

Fees have to be exact. The office cannot refund and keeps overages of $5.00 or less, and if an overage is larger the document comes back. No more than five documents can ride on a single check.

What does the realty transfer tax cost in Bedford County?

The county brochure states a state tax of 1% and a local tax of 1% of the consideration, due when the deed is recorded. That makes 2% in total, and it is paid on top of the recording fee. The office accepts checks, money orders, cash, and credit or debit cards, and checks are made payable to the Register Recorder named on the fee bill.

One check is enough: the county says it does not require separate checks for transfer tax and recording fees. If the property spans more than one municipality or school district, the deed has to state in whole numbers how the local tax is divided between them.

  • Deeds must show the true consideration or carry a completed Statement of Value.
  • Deeds, mortgages and assignments all need a signed Certificate of Residence.
  • The county web page links a Common Level Ratio sheet and the realty transfer tax forms.

What does Bedford County look like to a home seller?

Bedford County is the largest of the four counties on these pages by land, at 1,017 square miles, but the smallest by population. Census QuickFacts estimates 47,480 residents for 2025, roughly flat against the 2020 base of 47,567, and a density of about 47 people per square mile. The county seat is Bedford, and the landscape is ridge and valley country, with Blue Knob the highest mountain and limestone quarries in the Morrison Cove area.

Housing is mostly owner-occupied. QuickFacts counts 23,836 housing units, 19,750 households and an owner-occupied rate of 77.5%. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $179,000 for 2020 to 2024, median gross rent was $784, and only 75 building permits were issued in 2025. Households with a broadband subscription came to 83.1%, lower than the other three counties compared here, which a buyer working remotely may weigh.

Historic travel routes shaped the county. The old Forbes Road is now US 30, and the Pennsylvania Turnpike, I-70, I-76 and I-99 all run through. Bedford Springs once drew wealthy vacationers in the late 19th century.

Which other documents does the Bedford County office record, and at what price?

Beyond deeds and mortgages, the fee bill lists a long run of real estate and miscellaneous instruments. Most affidavits, agreements, covenants, declarations, notices, restrictions and orders are $18.50. Amendments, cancellations, modifications, subordinations and terminations run $20.50, and leases of 30 years or longer, installment sales agreements, memorandums and oil and gas leases are $59.75.

Maps and plans are priced separately. A plat under 24 inches is $9.00 and one over 24 inches is $13.00. State highway and mining plans are $16.50 for the first page, with additional pages at $3.00. UCC financing statements and their ancillary filings are $100.00 each.

  • Notary public bond and commission: $39.50, which includes the commission tax and writ tax.
  • Notary name change or address change: $18.50.
  • Clean and Green filing: $18.50.
  • Partial release: $61.75.

For a home seller the practical lines are the deed, the mortgage satisfaction and any easement. If a title search turns up an old right of way or an unreleased mortgage, those are the instruments your closing agent will ask the office to record or clear.

What should a Bedford County seller check before the deed goes in?

Start with the paperwork the office will reject if it is missing. Every deed, mortgage and assignment needs a Certificate of Residence completed and signed, and the deed must state the true consideration or come with a fully completed Statement of Value. The county also asks that fees be exact, so confirm the number with the office or your closing agent instead of rounding up.

Next, check how the sale will be paid. Settle ahead of time who brings the 2% tax and the recording fee, whether the closing runs through a title company or privately. The brochure says all fees and taxes are payable in advance, so a deed cannot be recorded first and paid later.

  • Confirm the grantee name and mailing address spelling.
  • Ask which municipality and school district the parcel falls in.
  • Call (814) 623-4836 with questions about the fee bill.
  • Keep a recorded copy for your records after closing.

How do you get a copy of a recorded Bedford County document?

Records can be viewed online through the Recorder of Deeds Records Online link on the county page, or at the public workstations in Room 106. Photocopies are $0.25 a page at the counter, pages larger than 11 by 17 inches are $2.00, and a certified copy is $1.00 plus $0.25 for each page.

The office does not take part in title searches and cannot offer legal advice, so the county suggests an attorney for questions about what a document means. Originals go back to whoever presented them, unless the filer directs otherwise, and mailed documents must come with a postage-paid return envelope. Military discharge papers are kept confidential, available only to the veteran or a veterans organization, and recording a DD-214 and any certified copies are free.

More questions about Bedford County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the recording fee for a deed in Bedford County?

It is $59.75 for a deed with up to four names and four pages, under the fee bill effective November 20, 2025. Each added name is $0.50 and each added page is $2.00.

Is the transfer tax included in the Bedford County deed fee?

The fee bill says its listed fees include state and county taxes. The realty transfer tax itself is 1% state and 1% local of the consideration, collected at recording, so ask the office how your deed's total is calculated.

Can I record a Bedford County deed electronically?

Yes. The office accepts e-recording through Simplifile and CSC, along with mail and in-person filing. Most sellers leave this to the title company.

When does same-day recording stop in Bedford County?

Same-day recording stops at 4:00 p.m. even though the office stays open until 4:30 p.m. Call (814) 623-4836 if a closing is running late.

Does the Bedford County office return my original deed?

Yes. Originals go back to the person who presented them unless the office is told otherwise, and mailed documents need a postage-paid return envelope.
